docs.title: AI Landing Zones
docs.text:
Build AI applications and agents on a secure, resilient Azure foundation. AI Landing Zones provides workload landing zone reference architectures and deployable implementations. Start with Agent Landing Zone, centralize model access with AI Gateway Landing Zone, or combine both.

Note

Designed and tested for Azure public cloud. Validate government and sovereign deployments separately. Some included services may be in preview.

docs.title: AI Landing Zone for Azure Container Apps
High-Level Architecture Design: AI Workloads on Azure Container Apps
Executive Summary
docs.text: This article defines a production-ready landing zone architecture for deploying AI workloads on Azure Container Apps. It lists the design considerations and recommendations when using Azure Container Apps for AI workloads.

docs.title: Infrastructure & Compute
docs.text: This section covers the recommendations for the infrastructure and compute design area for the landing zone.

docs.title: Environments & Workload Profiles
docs.text:
The Container App Environment serves as the administrative and security boundary. To cater for different workload performance and cost requirements, we utilize multiple workload profiles within a single environment:

  • Consumption Profiles: Best for variable or unpredictable traffic patterns. scale to zero to minimize costs during idle periods.
  • Dedicated Profiles: Best for steady-state workloads or background workers that require reserved compute for consistent latency.
  • Serverless GPUs vs. Dedicated GPUs:
    • Serverless GPUs: Ideal for bursty inference where you only pay for the duration of the request.
    • Dedicated GPUs: Necessary for long-running training, fine-tuning, or supporting larger inferencing models.

The architecture organizes workloads into five distinct workload profiles:

Workload Profile Resource Type GPU Strategy Typical Workloads Latency-sensitive inferencing Container Apps Dedicated GPUs Real-time inference with Ollama, Foundry Models, or similar open-source inference runtimes requiring guaranteed low-latency responses Cost-sensitive inferencing Container Apps Serverless GPUs Bursty inference workloads using Ollama, Foundry Models, or similar open-source inference runtimes where pay-per-request is more economical ML and training Container App Jobs Serverless GPUs Batch training jobs, fine-tuning, embedding generation, and periodic model retraining as run-to-completion tasks. Use dedicated GPUs when latency is critical. Design jobs to be idempotent with checkpointing so that retries or restarts resume safely without reprocessing completed work or corrupting artifacts Apps Container Apps Consumption (CPU) Front-end UIs, MCP servers, and AI agents AI Gateway Container Apps Dedicated (CPU) AI Gateway for routing and load balancing across model endpoints, agents and MCP servers. Runs on a dedicated profile with minimum replicas to avoid cold starts and ensure consistent latency on the critical inference path

docs.title: Networking & Security
docs.text: This section covers the recommendations for the networking and security design area for the landing zone.

docs.title: VNet Integration & Egress Control
docs.text:
For enterprise security, we implement "Bring Your Own VNet" to apply custom security controls: - Dedicated Subnet: The Azure Container Apps environment requires a dedicated subnet delegated to Microsoft.App/environments. - Internal vs. External Access: - Internal: The environment is hidden from the public internet; traffic is routed via a Private IP. - External: The environment is reachable via a public load balancer managed by Azure Container Apps. - Egress Control: Route all outbound traffic through an Azure Firewall for inspection and centralized policy enforcement.

Note: Azure NAT Gateway is also supported for egress in workload profile environments with custom VNet integration. Use NAT Gateway when the primary requirement is a static outbound IP without the need for Layer-7 traffic inspection. For scenarios requiring outbound traffic filtering, FQDN-based rules, or threat intelligence, Azure Firewall remains the recommended approach.

docs.title: Private Access & Secret Management
docs.text:
• Private Endpoints: Ensure all communication to back-end services (Cosmos DB, Storage, Key Vault) stays on the Microsoft backbone.
  • Key Vault: All sensitive data (API keys, access tokens, SSL certs) must be stored in Azure Key Vault and referenced as secrets in Azure Container Apps.
  • Managed Identities: Use User-Assigned Managed Identities for all resource-to-resource authentication (e.g., Azure Container Apps pulling from ACR) to eliminate the need for hardcoded credentials.

docs.title: Ingress Security
docs.text:
• HTTPS Enforcement: Set allowInsecure: false on all ingress configurations to enforce TLS and automatically redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
  • IP Restrictions: Configure IP allow/deny rules when relevant to restrict inbound access to known CIDR ranges (e.g., corporate VPN, Azure Front Door backend IPs).
  • Mutual TLS (mTLS): Enable mTLS for service-to-service communication between container apps within the environment to encrypt traffic and verify both client and server identities.
  • CORS: Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing policies for front-end AI chat UIs that call backend inference APIs from browser clients.

docs.title: GenAI Application Dependencies
docs.text:
The architecture relies on a set of Azure services that support the AI workloads:

  • Azure Cosmos DB: Persistent storage for conversation history, agent state, session metadata, and application data.
  • Azure Key Vault: Centralized secret management for API keys, model access tokens, and certificates.
  • Azure Storage Account: Durable storage for model weights (via Azure Files mounts), training datasets, and artifacts.
  • Azure Container Registry (ACR): Private registry for container images. Deploy in the same region as the Azure Container Apps environment for minimal pull latency.
  • Managed Identities: User-Assigned Managed Identities for all service-to-service authentication, eliminating hardcoded credentials.
  • Azure App Configuration: Centrally manage applications' configuration.

docs.title: AI Workload Optimization
docs.text: This section covers the recommendations for optimizing the AI workloads to be deployed in the landing zone.

docs.title: Model Serving & Deployment
docs.text:
• Foundry Models: Leverage built-in integrations for turnkey deployment of Microsoft-managed foundry models.
  • Open-Source Model Serving: Deploy open-source model serving runtimes such as Ollama, vLLM, or Hugging Face Text Generation Inference (TGI) as container apps on GPU-enabled workload profiles. These runtimes provide flexible, self-hosted inference for open-weight models (e.g., Llama, Mistral, Phi) and can be paired with either dedicated or serverless GPUs depending on latency and cost requirements.
  • AI Gateway: Deploy an AI Gateway (e.g., Azure API Management, Envoy-based proxies, or custom routing middleware) to centralize traffic management across model endpoints. The gateway enables load balancing, rate limiting, request routing, and failover across multiple backend model deployments, agents and MCP servers.
  • Dynamic Sessions: Provide secure, isolated sandboxes (Hyper-V based) for executing AI-generated code safely.
  • MCP (Model Context Protocol) Servers: Host MCP servers within Azure Container Apps to allow AI agents to securely query internal databases or execute tools via a standardized interface.

docs.title: Reducing Cold Starts & Storage
docs.text:
Loading multi-gigabyte models (Foundry or open-source) into memory can lead to significant latency.

  • Azure Files Volume Mounts: Download model weights to a persistent Azure File Share once. Mount this share to the container so the model is available instantly on startup without re-downloading.
  • Azure Container Registry (ACR): Deploy Azure Container Registry in the same region as the Azure Container Apps environment to reduce latency.
    • Use the Premium SKU for global distribution and Artifact Streaming to further accelerate container startup times.
  • Optimize Container Image Size: Audit inference container images to remove training-only dependencies, development tools, and unnecessary libraries. Use multi-stage Docker builds to minimize image size.
  • Custom Startup Probes: For AI model containers that take minutes to load large models into GPU memory, configure custom startup probes with extended initialDelaySeconds and failureThreshold to prevent premature container kills during initialization.
  • Proactive Wake-Up: Use scheduled Container App Jobs to send warm-up requests to inference endpoints ahead of peak usage (e.g., a daily job at 9 AM) to eliminate cold starts while still benefiting from scale-to-zero during off-hours.

docs.title: AI Agents & Orchestration
docs.text:
Deploy AI agents as individual container apps within the Apps workload profile. Each agent runs as an independent, scalable microservice that can be updated and versioned separately. Use open-source agent orchestration frameworks to build and manage agent workflows, such as Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph, and others.

Agents communicate with model endpoints via the AI Gateway, and leverage MCP servers for tool access and external data retrieval.

docs.title: Autoscaling
docs.text:
• Scaling Rules: Define KEDA-based autoscaling rules tailored to each workload profile:
    • HTTP scaling for front-end UIs and AI Gateway (based on concurrent request count).
    • Custom scaling for event-driven workloads.
  • Min/Max Replicas: Set minimum replicas ≥ 1 for latency-sensitive inference endpoints to avoid cold starts. Set maximum replicas based on GPU availability and cost budget.
  • Session Affinity: Enable sticky sessions for stateful AI chat applications that maintain conversation context in-memory, ensuring subsequent requests from the same user route to the same replica.

docs.title: Deployment & Release Strategy
docs.text:
• Blue-Green Deployment: Use revision labels and traffic weights to implement blue-green deployments. Deploy new model versions or application code to a "green" revision, validate via the labeled FQDN, then shift 100% of traffic. Roll back instantly by re-routing traffic to the "blue" revision.
  • Traffic Splitting: Use percentage-based traffic splitting to gradually roll out new revisions, enabling canary testing of updated inference endpoints.
  • Revision Management: Set maxInactiveRevisions to automatically clean up old revisions and avoid hitting the revision limit (default max of 100 per container app).

docs.title: Resiliency & Global Availability
docs.text: This section covers the recommendations for resiliency and availabilitys for the workloads to be deployed in the landing zone.

docs.title: Availability Zones
docs.text:
Enable zone redundancy on the Container App Environment to distribute replicas across multiple physical availability zones within a region. This protects against datacenter-level failures.

  • Environment-Level Setting: Zone redundancy must be enabled at environment creation time — it cannot be added after the fact.
  • Minimum Replicas: Configure a minimum of three replicas for critical workloads to ensure at least one replica runs in each zone.
  • Dependency Alignment: Ensure dependent services (Cosmos DB, Key Vault, Storage) are also configured for zone redundancy to avoid single-zone bottlenecks.

docs.title: Service Resiliency & Health
docs.text:
• Health Probes: Define liveness, readiness, and startup probes to detect unhealthy instances and enable automatic recovery.
  • Resiliency Policies (Preview): Configure retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers for service-to-service communication. Ensure services (inference endpoints, databases, MCP tool,..etc) are idempotent so that retried requests do not cause duplicate side effects.

docs.title: Operational Excellence
docs.text:
• Planned Maintenance Windows: Configure maintenance windows on the Container App Environment to schedule non-critical platform updates during off-peak hours, minimizing disruption to AI inference workloads.
  • Service Discovery: Container apps within the same environment can communicate using their app names as internal DNS hostnames. Use internal ingress for backend services to restrict access to within-environment traffic only.

docs.title: Multi-Region Architecture
docs.text:
For business continuity against full regional outages, deploy across two or more Azure regions:

  • Active-Active: Both regions serve production traffic simultaneously via Azure Front Door. Provides near-instant failover (seconds) but requires globally replicated data stores and synchronized deployments. Best for mission-critical serving workloads (inference endpoints, front-end apps, AI agents, AI Gateway). Training and batch jobs should remain single-region due to data locality requirements and run in the secondary region only during failover.
  • Active-Passive: The secondary region remains on warm standby, activated during failover. Lower cost and complexity, with failover measured in minutes. Suitable for most production workloads. However, cost savings depend on the workload profile types deployed in the standby region. Pre-deploy the environment with consumption-based and serverless GPU profiles in the standby region. Use Infrastructure as Code (Bicep/Terraform) to rapidly provision dedicated GPU profiles only during failover, balancing cost efficiency against recovery time.

Key design considerations:

  • Deploy one Container App Environment per region, each with zone redundancy enabled.
  • Use Azure Front Door for global Layer-7 traffic routing, SSL termination, and automatic health-probe-based failover.
  • Replicate stateful data (conversation history, agent state, model weights) across regions using geo-redundant services (e.g., Cosmos DB multi-region writes, GRS storage accounts).
  • Mirror network topology (VNets, subnets, firewall rules) and identity configuration (Managed Identities, RBAC) consistently across regions.
  • Ensure CI/CD pipelines deploy to all regions in sync to avoid version drift.

docs.title: Observability & Monitoring
docs.text: This section covers the recommendations for monitoring, logging, and observability for the workloads deployed in the landing zone.

docs.title: Logging & Diagnostics
docs.text:
• Log Analytics Integration: Configure a Log Analytics workspace as the default log destination for the Container App Environment. Use KQL queries to analyze system logs, container console output, and scaling events.
  • Diagnostic Settings: Configure Azure Monitor diagnostic settings to stream logs and metrics.
  • Azure Monitor Alerts: Set up alerts for critical conditions: failed health probes, high error rates, replica restarts, GPU utilization thresholds, and scaling failures. Use action groups to trigger automated incident response.

docs.title: Distributed Tracing & Metrics
docs.text:
• OpenTelemetry: Configure OpenTelemetry data agents at the environment level to collect distributed traces and metrics from AI agent workflows. This provides end-to-end visibility across multi-agent orchestration chains.
  • Metrics: Monitor platform metrics including CPU/memory utilization, replica count, request count, and response latency. Use these metrics to validate scaling rules and detect performance regressions in model inference endpoints.

docs.text:
Agent Landing Zone v4.3.0 released.

  • Independent ingestion deployment — fresh, supported native-ingestion deployments omit the ingestion Container App. Existing and custom deployments retain their component choices; disabling deployment does not delete existing applications or document data. See ingestion application selection.
  • Ingestion-aware uploads — UI v3.3.0 disables upload controls and rejects attachments server-side when the ingestion application is disabled. Text chat, authentication and retrieval remain available.

No unrelated or target-side connections are approved automatically. See private native Blob ingestion.
  • Explicit shared-source permissions — deliberately shared, non-ADLS Blob sources can use empty ingestion permission options; protected defaults remain unchanged. Review the shared-source permission guidance before opting in.
  • Isolated image builds and DNS — build-subnet-only HTTPS egress now covers the pinned Microsoft npm feeds and package-download CDN without requiring firewall DNS proxy. The separate ENABLE_FIREWALL_DNS_PROXY option defaults to false and does not change client DNS. See image builds and firewall DNS proxy.

docs.title: Agent Landing Zone
docs.text:
Agent Landing Zone provides a secure Azure foundation and an extensible agent application built on Microsoft Foundry. Deploy the foundation on its own, use the bundled application, or bring your own application.

Source code: Azure/agent-landing-zone

docs.title: Foundation and application
docs.text:
The template separates Azure resource provisioning from application deployment. Deployment parameters and application selection determine what is created.

Layer What it contains Deployed by Foundation Azure resources, identities and service configuration selected by the deployment inputs azd provision and its configuration hooks Application The selected application components and, for hosted orchestration, the agent version azd deploy and its deployment hooks

For the file layout and lifecycle, read How the template works. For the exact resource inventory, see Deployed resources and cost estimates.

docs.title: Agent application
docs.text:
The Agent App Orchestrator coordinates models, knowledge sources and configured tools through a selected orchestration strategy. Extend its strategies and tools to implement your workload's behavior. The Agent App UI provides the conversational interface.

flowchart LR
    user[User] <--> ui[Agent App UI]
    ui <--> orchestrator[Orchestrator and selected strategy]
    orchestrator --> models[Models]
    orchestrator --> tools[Configured tools]
    orchestrator --> knowledge[Knowledge sources]

docs.title: Strategies and hosting
docs.text:
A strategy determines how the agent uses models, obtains context and invokes tools. Hosting determines where the orchestrator runs. These are separate choices, and not every strategy supports both hosts.

Hosting option Execution model Foundry hosted agent The default for a fresh environment. Foundry Agent Service runs the orchestrator image with a supported strategy. Azure Container Apps Runs the orchestrator as a Container App, including strategies that are not yet supported by the hosted runtime.

See Agent hosting for supported strategies and the differences in history, continuity and optional administration features.

docs.title: Knowledge ingestion
docs.text:
The optional Agent App Ingestion provides application-managed document processing, including format-aware chunking, embeddings and configured SharePoint ingestion. Native Foundry IQ can instead ingest configured Blob sources without that application.

These paths are not feature-equivalent. Conversation attachments require the ingestion app and the existing upload eligibility checks. SharePoint has separate connector and permission requirements; the native Blob path does not establish ingestion-free SharePoint support. See Ingestion choices before selecting or changing the ingestion path.

docs.title: Deploy applications with Azure DevOps
docs.text:
Use this optional CI/CD runbook when you want to promote one reviewed application revision through DEV → TEST → PROD with protected approvals. It automates the platform's application and foundation lifecycle; Azure DevOps is not required for an interactive deployment.

For interactive execution, use Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack. For component changes, see Custom applications.

Choose the right pipeline

The downloadable example below verifies the same source commit in every job and enforces successful prior stages. It is not a build-once image promotion pipeline. The separate foundation pipeline guide explains upstream service connections and Environment setup; those assets provision infrastructure only, allow independent environment selection and do not automatically execute their preview template.

docs.title: 1. Prepare the repository and runners
docs.text:
Use your reviewed platform revision. Keep manifest.json, app-definition.json, main.parameters.json, azure.yaml, infra/, config/, contracts/ and scripts/ together at its root. Infrastructure is incorporated under infra/; do not deploy it from a second foundation checkout. Commit your configuration and compatible component pins before queuing a pipeline. Do not commit credentials or local azd environments.

The downloadable example initially deploys the bundled application with hosted-no-panel, native Blob ingestion and private endpoints. Set the same reviewed topology and ingestion selection across the three environments:

Input Choices and effect DEPLOYMENT_TOPOLOGY hosted-no-panel, hosted-panel, or classic. Classic runs orchestration in Container Apps. HOSTED_AGENT_RESOURCE_SCOPE Required before first provision for hosted modes: the deployed Foundry delegated-user audience followed by /.default. It has no implicit runtime default. DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP Explicit 'false' in this example; set 'true' if the optional app and conversation uploads are required. Native source ingestion is not feature-equivalent. Retain an existing environment's selection during upgrades. NETWORK_ISOLATION Explicit 'true'. Do not change it merely to make a pipeline pass. BUILD_MODE acr-task; private image builds use the foundation's ACR Tasks pool. Local Docker is not required.

See Configuration, Hosted agents and ingestion compatibility. An explicit topology overrides legacy flags; fresh environments otherwise default to hosted, existing recorded topologies remain sticky, and unmarked older environments are treated as classic. This example deliberately makes the choice explicit: do not use it to switch an existing classic environment to hosted without the migration and recovery review.

docs.title: Runner requirements
docs.text:
Create authorized Linux self-hosted Azure Pipelines agent pools, with a runner able to reach each environment's private endpoints through its VNet or a peered hub/VPN. Bootstrap the deployment network before this full-stack pipeline: an agent cannot depend on the VNet it is about to create to become reachable. Use Network isolation for DNS, routing and egress checks. The CI-only pool need not reach Azure data-plane endpoints.

Every runner needs Bash, PowerShell 7 (pwsh), jq, Git, curl, Azure CLI with Bicep, Azure Developer CLI (azd), and Python 3.12+ with pip and venv. Hosted deployment also needs an azd version supporting the pinned hosted-agent/azure.yaml service. Install and pin approved tool versions in your agent image; record them in your release evidence. Populate the self-hosted agent's Python tool cache for UsePythonVersion@0 (3.12), rather than assuming it can install Python. Allow package, source and container-build dependency egress. Hooks themselves bootstrap a temporary pip environment during post-provision.

From the agent's Bash shell, verify:

python3 --version
pwsh --version
jq --version
git --version
az version
az bicep version
azd version

The YAML uses pool.name, not pool.vmImage. A private ACR Tasks agent pool is a different resource from an Azure Pipelines agent pool: it builds images, but does not run azd, topology discovery or post-provision hooks. A Microsoft-hosted public agent is not the default private deployment runner. For an intentionally public deployment, review network inputs and runner policy separately.

Use dedicated, preferably ephemeral agents. workspace.clean isolates jobs; the final cleanup removes only explicitly listed runtime state directories and temporary tool configuration, leaving source checkouts intact. Do not place unrelated files in the agent workspace or run untrusted pull requests on deployment agents.

docs.title: 2. Establish identities and permissions
docs.text:
Create an Azure Resource Manager workload identity federation (WIF) service connection per environment, following the foundation setup. Restrict each connection to this pipeline and its target subscription/scopes. The AzureCLI@2 task authenticates noninteractively; all azd and hook commands run inside it, with azd config set auth.useAzCliAuth true. Do not add interactive az login, azd auth login, client secrets or exported federation tokens.

Set AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID to the connection identity's enterprise application / service principal object ID, not its application/client ID or app-registration object ID. Set AZURE_PRINCIPAL_TYPE=ServicePrincipal; the default parameter type is User and is wrong for this job. A connection that can read the subscription does not necessarily have deployment or data-plane permissions.

Have an administrator approve the minimum role plan:

Identity Required access to review Deployment service principal Contributor for resource deployment plus scoped role-assignment authority (for example User Access Administrator) wherever Bicep and hooks create grants. Subscription-scope deployments, provider registration and hub/shared resources can require additional scope; use the foundation guide's scope review. Do not solve data-plane denials by adding Owner. Deployment service principal, configuration/build operations App Configuration Data Owner for publishing settings; required Key Vault secret access when resolving references; Search service/index configuration permissions and the Foundry configuration/model/deployment actions used by the enabled hooks. ACR Tasks build/run and registry/Container Apps update permissions must also be authorized. These are separate from ARM Contributor. Check the effective grants from Bicep for the explicit principal and add only missing scoped roles. Deployment service principal, hosted authoring Foundry User (previously Azure AI User) on the exact project, plus account read access; authority to create the scoped runtime assignments in the hosted access plan. Cognitive Services Contributor/OpenAI User alone do not grant hosted-agent data-plane authoring. Runtime managed identities Capability-profile roles and separate hosted project/image-pull/runtime grants. Do not substitute the pipeline identity for the runtime identity. Delegated application users Application consent, Foundry caller/agent access where applicable, and the intended source/document permissions. Pipeline success grants none of these to users.

Also confirm service/model availability, quota, provider registration and Responsible AI acceptance in each target subscription. Do not set preflight bypass flags to work around an unattended failure. Allow RBAC propagation before retrying.

docs.title: Complete the application sign-in setup separately
docs.text:
The pipeline service connection is not the UI's Entra application registration. The inspected root configuration and pinned UI deployment scripts do not create that registration or grant tenant consent. Arrange this with an Entra administrator for each isolated application environment:

  1. Create the confidential application registration; expose its api://<client-id>/user_impersonation scope and request version-2 access tokens.
  2. Register the final HTTPS UI URL with /auth/oauth/azure-ad/callback. Set CHAINLIT_URL to that canonical HTTPS origin without a trailing slash. For a first deployment, discover the assigned frontend URL, finish this setup, and restart the UI before accepting DEV.
  3. Create/rotate its client credential under tenant policy. Store it in Key Vault, publish a Key Vault reference as OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_SECRET, and publish OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_ID, OAUTH_AZURE_AD_TENANT_ID and OAUTH_AZURE_AD_SCOPES under App Configuration label agent-lz. Keep CHAINLIT_AUTH_SECRET stable and protected as well.
  4. Configure and consent the downstream delegated permissions for the deployed audience, including Foundry OBO for hosted mode. Graph scopes are not a replacement for the UI's single-token API scope. Grant intended caller access.
  5. Review conflicting unlabelled/service settings, restart affected components, then perform actual user sign-in and document allow/deny tests.

Follow delegated authentication for the exact keys and consent boundaries, and runtime settings for publishing/restart behavior. Tenant consent and this configuration are an unattended onboarding gap, not work automatically performed by YAML or by granting Azure subscription roles. Use a separately reviewed administrative procedure or automation; do not give the deployment connection broad Microsoft Graph permissions to hide the gap.

docs.title: 3. Fill the pipeline inputs
docs.text:
Download both files, then place them beside each other in .pipelines/ in your platform repository, not in its infra/ folder:

  • azure-pipelines.yml
  • deploy-stage.yml
  • Optional local check: validate.py

Replace the following values before authorization. DEV, TEST and PROD must have separate resource groups, azd environments, connection identities, configuration stores, secrets and data. Apply the environment boundaries, including runtime identities, sign-in, test data and network isolation.

Never copy DEV's .azure state into TEST or PROD. Initialize or securely restore the intended environment on each runner, refresh its outputs when needed and reapply approved inputs. Keep .azure and sibling child state private.

Exact example input Required replacement / source REPLACE_CI_LINUX_POOL Authorized Linux validation pool with the toolchain above. REPLACE_DEV_VNET_LINUX_POOL, REPLACE_TEST_VNET_LINUX_POOL, REPLACE_PROD_VNET_LINUX_POOL Authorized, connected Linux deployment pool for each target. May be the same pool only if its connectivity and isolation policy cover all targets. REPLACE_DEV_WIF_SERVICE_CONNECTION, REPLACE_TEST_WIF_SERVICE_CONNECTION, REPLACE_PROD_WIF_SERVICE_CONNECTION Exact Azure DevOps WIF service connection names, authorized for this pipeline only. REPLACE_DEV_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, REPLACE_TEST_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, REPLACE_PROD_SUBSCRIPTION_ID Target subscription GUIDs matching those connections' allowed scopes. REPLACE_DEV_RESOURCE_GROUP, REPLACE_TEST_RESOURCE_GROUP, REPLACE_PROD_RESOURCE_GROUP New target names for first provision, or the exact previously azd-provisioned groups for redeployment. REPLACE_DEV_REGION, REPLACE_TEST_REGION, REPLACE_PROD_REGION Supported foundation locations (AZURE_LOCATION). REPLACE_DEV_FOUNDRY_REGION, REPLACE_TEST_FOUNDRY_REGION, REPLACE_PROD_FOUNDRY_REGION Foundry/model locations with quota (AZURE_AI_FOUNDRY_LOCATION). REPLACE_DEV_COSMOS_REGION, REPLACE_TEST_COSMOS_REGION, REPLACE_PROD_COSMOS_REGION Cosmos locations supported by the selected topology/foundation (AZURE_COSMOS_LOCATION). REPLACE_DEV_SERVICE_PRINCIPAL_OBJECT_ID, REPLACE_TEST_SERVICE_PRINCIPAL_OBJECT_ID, REPLACE_PROD_SERVICE_PRINCIPAL_OBJECT_ID Connection service principal object IDs; keep AZURE_PRINCIPAL_TYPE: ServicePrincipal. REPLACE_DEV_HOSTED_RESOURCE_SCOPE, REPLACE_TEST_HOSTED_RESOURCE_SCOPE, REPLACE_PROD_HOSTED_RESOURCE_SCOPE Explicit delegated-user Foundry scope ending in /.default, matched to the deployed audience and consent (for example https://ai.azure.com/.default where that is the target audience). Required for both hosted topologies before provisioning; not the UI's api://<client-id>/user_impersonation scope. Classic does not consume this hosted input. environment: agentlz-dev, agentlz-test, agentlz-prod Precreated Azure DevOps Environment resource names. Rename consistently if required; these are approval resources, not azd environments. AZURE_ENV_NAME: agentlz-dev, agentlz-test, agentlz-prod Unique azd names, retained exactly for subsequent refresh/deploy runs. variableGroup: agentlz-dev-secrets, agentlz-test-secrets, agentlz-prod-secrets Create these Library variable groups and authorize only this pipeline. Each must contain the secret variable AGENTLZ_SECRET_SETTINGS_JSON, initially the string {}. AGENTLZ_SECRET_SETTINGS_JSON in each group JSON object of additional documented azd/hook inputs, with string values. It cannot override the inline deployment controls. Empty {} is valid for the bundled example. This is not automatic publication of OAuth/runtime settings or a private Git credential mechanism. Inline settings in each stage Review topology, ingestion, isolation and regional settings. Add required configuration inputs for your approved network, source, models or reused resources. Keep nonsecret configuration reviewable here; never put secret values in YAML.

The settings maps are intentionally inline, not an unexplained external configuration file. Values are reapplied after environment refresh on every job. RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX=true requires the connected-host check; it does not create connectivity. The example leaves AZURE_SKIP_NETWORK_ISOLATION_WARNING=false. The inspected POSIX preProvision hook's interactive warning checks the legacy AZURE_NETWORK_ISOLATION variable, not the example's NETWORK_ISOLATION input. Do not inherit that legacy alias in the runner or environment. If an existing workflow must retain a truthy legacy alias, explicitly review setting the warning flag to true for unattended execution while retaining RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX=true. The warning flag alone can defer configuration when RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX is not truthy; never use that combination as a private deployment shortcut.

Protect variable-group edits as well as YAML changes. Secret masking is not a data-loss prevention system; keep pipeline debug and shell tracing off. Use Key Vault references for runtime secrets instead of literal secret JSON wherever the contract supports them.

docs.title: Private component repositories and custom definitions
docs.text:
The platform connection authenticates Azure, not GitHub or Azure Repos Git. See Private Git authentication for repository access. The root deploy hook clones selected bundled components as sibling checkouts using manifest repository/tag pins, then verifies the expected commit. Use approved read-only Git credentials for those private repositories separately. The example does not install a private-Git credential: before adopting private component pins, add your organization's reviewed, job-scoped credential-helper or SSH-agent/known-host setup inside the authenticated task, with guaranteed cleanup. Test the exact repository/tag access without printing tokens. Source checkout authorization alone does not authorize the hook's new clones.

Never put tokens in manifest URLs, command-line URLs, url.insteadOf global configuration, .azure, or downloadable artifacts. Keep persistCredentials: false; the example uses a temporary GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL because hooks can write safe-directory entries. Do not rely on an agent owner's persistent Git credentials. If using an Azure Repos job token, separately grant the build identity read access to the required repositories and review job-token scope before explicitly mapping it into the credential mechanism. It is not a GitHub credential.

For a custom application, adapt CI validation to the selected definition and add AGENTLZ_APP_DEFINITION to each stage before first provision. Keep the application ID stable. Custom definitions accept local sources or immutable image digests, not remote repository URLs.

Materialize local source in every job with a clean Git checkout at its declared source.commit, preserving .git metadata and the definition's relative layout. Explicitly check out pinned component repositories or pinned submodules if needed, using the separate Git credentials above. Do not feed these hooks a git archive tree without Git metadata: they check the component's actual git rev-parse HEAD. Source commit checks do not reject uncommitted edits; validate clean trees.

Extend the template's fixed cleanup list with the custom definition folder's explicit .azure and .logs paths; never add a source or workspace root.

Custom hosted services follow their own definition/image contract, not an assumed bundled orchestrator build. The downloaded template's preparation branch is for the bundled application; replace that branch with the documented custom hosted workflow before using it for a custom hosted definition.

docs.title: 4. Protect and register the pipeline
docs.text:
1. In Pipelines → Environments, create the three exact Environment names. On agentlz-test and agentlz-prod, configure Approvals and checks outside YAML, with accountable reviewers, no self-approval where policy requires it, and restricted administrator/pipeline permissions. Approval for TEST accepts DEV evidence; approval for PROD accepts TEST evidence. Configure branch control and an exclusive lock where appropriate, and avoid overlapping release runs.
  2. Authorize this pipeline, not all pipelines, to use the environments, pools, WIF connections and variable groups. Protect the release branch and require review of pipeline/template changes.
  3. In Pipelines → New pipeline, select your platform repository and Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file, then .pipelines/azure-pipelines.yml. Save it without starting a production run until all inputs/checks are ready.
  4. Queue a run from a reviewed branch/commit. This sample has no automatic trigger. Leave all stages selected; never use stage selection as a promotion bypass.

CI validates the application definition and manifest JSON, installs the hook dependencies, and compiles Bicep without deploying. It is not a complete security scan, Bicep what-if, Azure readiness test, or real-user acceptance test. Add your existing unit/contract tests and review gates before extending it.

Each deployment stage requires succeeded() and an explicit result equal to Succeeded for every prerequisite. Failed, Canceled, Skipped and SucceededWithIssues cannot promote. Do not replace these conditions with always(), succeededOrFailed() or independent stage-selection parameters. Azure DevOps Environment approvals remain external protected-resource checks; the YAML does not create or prove their existence.

docs.title: 5. Understand what runs on a fresh job
docs.text:
The template checks out Build.SourceVersion again and fails if HEAD differs. It activates Python 3.12 and installs config/requirements.txt in that job; a CI virtual environment is not available on a later agent.

Inside AzureCLI@2, it initializes a local azd environment (or explicitly selects one already present), sets the intended resource group, and checks group existence:

  • New group: no refresh is attempted before the first provision.
  • Existing group: azd env refresh --environment <name> --no-prompt must reload the previous azd deployment outputs. Access, discovery or refresh errors fail the job; there is no || true. An existing empty/unrelated resource group is not a prior azd deployment. Use a fresh target for this example or explicitly onboard/review the existing foundation before using it.

The same azd name and subscription must locate the previous deployment. Review the refreshed target and outputs for an existing environment; do not create a second deployment by renaming the environment. Local .azure is disposable here, not a promoted artifact or backup. Review migration state and application binding before adopting an existing environment into CI.

After refresh, reviewed environment settings are applied, then the template runs:

Topology Ordered commands from the platform root Classic azd hooks run preup --no-prompt → azd provision --no-prompt → azd deploy --no-prompt Bundled hosted azd hooks run preup --no-prompt → azd provision --no-prompt → bash scripts/prepareHostedDeployment.sh → azd provision --no-prompt → azd deploy --no-prompt

Preup validates/checks binding before standalone provisioning. Preprovision resolves topology using python -m config.deployment.topology and composes infra/main.parameters.json; subsequent hooks use --describe to read its JSON. Post-provision configures application services and roles. The first hosted provision prepares prerequisites, preparation records an image digest, the second provision materializes that digest in the deployment handoff, and deploy creates the hosted version plus the other selected components.

This full workflow is deliberately repeatable on fresh agents. A hosted preparation may reuse a compatible digest when its provenance is available, but disposable local state and different environment registries can cause rebuilding. Bundled Container App scripts build per environment. This is immutable source promotion, not build-once immutable-image promotion: mutable base images, package feeds, tool versions, generated configuration and credentials can affect results. Pin dependencies/base images and record actual image digests per environment. If identical images are mandatory, design and validate a separate digest-based application contract and cross-registry availability/permissions; do not claim this source workflow already provides it.

No build artifacts are published or downloaded. Do not add a whole-workspace publish step: hooks copy .azure to sibling components and create .logs. Exclude .azure, .env/environment files, logs, secret files, credential/config caches, .git credentials and Python dependency environments from any future artifact. If changing to CI artifacts, deploy from the downloaded validated tree and explicitly solve the Git metadata requirement for local custom sources.

Cleanup runs even after failure. Its fixed path list removes .azure and .logs from the platform root, hosted-agent/, and the three manifest component sibling checkouts (agent-app-ui, agent-app-orchestrator, agent-app-ingestion). It leaves their source files intact and removes the job-specific temporary Python environment, azd config and Git config. Update the explicit state-directory list when changing component names or adding a custom definition folder; do not replace it with recursive deletion of source/workspace roots. AzureCLI@2 owns its isolated Azure CLI authentication context. Abrupt agent loss can prevent cleanup: reimage ephemeral agents or securely clean their disks before reuse.

docs.title: 6. Verify DEV, approve TEST, then approve PROD
docs.text:
Expected pipeline results are a green CI job, successful DEV deployment, TEST waiting for its protected Environment check, then PROD waiting after successful TEST. Check the recorded Build.SourceVersion and reviewed manifest pins; do not approve a different run just because its branch name is the same.

Before each promotion, record the following against the preceding environment in your release evidence:

  1. azd env get-value AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP identifies the intended target. App Configuration has the expected platform outputs and effective settings under label agent-lz; the selected apps have real, healthy image revisions, not just provisioned placeholders. Record image digests and hosted routed version.
  2. Complete Entra setup above. Verify HTTPS login/callback, authenticated API access and (for hosted mode) real-user OBO invocation. The hook's managed-identity greeting alone is not proof of these.
  3. Ingest a controlled document through the selected configured source. With an authorized user, retrieve its expected content/citations. With a user lacking that document's permission, verify the content is not returned. Also verify unauthenticated requests are rejected where required. Check that logs do not contain tokens or protected document bodies.
  4. Exercise selected ingestion/upload, history, panel and continuity features; check disabled surfaces are actually unavailable. Native Blob ingestion does not imply conversation uploads work without the optional app.
  5. Inspect service health, RBAC and private endpoint resolution, and attach sanitized evidence to the run/change record. See application health and diagnostics and document authorization guidance.

Do not approve TEST or PROD until the preceding environment meets these checks. Hook exit status is necessary but not sufficient: some post-provision setup sections currently log a configuration failure and continue. Add organization-owned acceptance checks before promotion; this sample does not pretend those sections are fail-closed end-to-end tests.

docs.title: Troubleshoot, redeploy and recover
docs.text:
Symptom Action Connection login fails, or azd asks for sign-in Verify WIF issuer/subject/audience, pipeline authorization and connection scope. Keep azd CLI-auth configuration and commands inside the authenticated task. Do not add interactive login. ARM succeeds but App Configuration/Search/Foundry returns 403 Check the deployment principal's scoped data-plane roles and propagation. For hosted authoring, check exact project access. Do not substitute subscription Owner or disable authorization. Private DNS/connectivity check fails Verify the Azure Pipelines runner's network/DNS/firewall path. An ACR Tasks pool does not connect the pipeline agent. Keep post-provision nondeferred. Refresh fails Check the azd environment name, subscription, prior deployment and read permission. Stop; do not swallow the error or silently provision another group. Stale sibling checkout / source mismatch Use the clean workspace and exact manifest/local source commits. Do not remove commit validation or update pins only in PROD. Hosted handoff/digest missing Complete provision → prepare → provision → deploy; see hosted redeployment. Do not skip the second provision after a source change. Green deploy but UI login/retrieval fails Complete registration/consent/runtime settings, inspect sanitized hook/service logs and run the real-user positive/negative checks. See Troubleshooting. TEST or PROD starts without the expected approval Stop the run and fix Environment checks/permissions outside YAML before restarting.

For an application-only redeployment with unchanged compatible foundation/binding and hosted handoff, use the same initialization/authentication procedure and azd deploy, following Redeploy applications only. Do not replace full provisioning with deploy-only for infrastructure, RBAC, topology or ingestion-selection changes.

For recovery, select the last accepted complete pinned combination and review configuration/data compatibility before rerunning the protected flow. Follow Roll back to a previous release. Rechecking an old commit does not reverse schema, infrastructure or data changes. Back up required data/configuration under a separate authorized process, retain known-good images, and do not use azd down --purge as rollback.

docs.title: Local example validation
docs.text:
With Python and PyYAML installed, run from the downloaded example directory:

python -m pip install PyYAML==6.0.3
python validate.py

This checks YAML/template wiring, stage conditions against prerequisite result combinations, embedded Bash/Python syntax, and the exact cleanup targets with rm intercepted (no real deletion) without Azure. It is not the Azure DevOps template-expansion service and cannot check real service connections, approvals, RBAC, private connectivity, tenant consent or application behavior. The example has not been executed against Azure or registered as a live pipeline as part of this documentation change.

docs.title: Custom applications
docs.text:
You can extend a bundled component or bring a different application to the foundation. Choose the contract that matches your change:

Goal Approach Change a documented setting Use Configuration; no source fork is needed. Extend the bundled UI, agent strategies/tools or ingestion code Fork only the component you change and update its coordinated pins below. Deploy a different application composition Supply an application definition and its matching azure.yaml.

The orchestrator is an extensible agent architecture. Its registered strategies include model/tool coordination, MCP, NL2SQL, multimodal and retrieval-oriented behavior. A strategy is not a hosting topology: Foundry hosting versus Container Apps is a separate choice, and each strategy still needs its own configured tools, data sources and authorization.

The platform owns identity, networking, and permissions. Your application declares only what it is, where its code lives, and which capabilities it needs.

For the platform-wide mechanism, read How the template works. For execution, use Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack.

docs.title: Customize a bundled component
docs.text:
An unmodified deployment does not require four forks. Fork or mirror the platform when you need versioned deployment inputs, automation or platform changes. Fork only the runtime repositories whose source you change. The platform fetches the selected components; changing its Git remote does not change their repository URLs.

Prefer configuration over source changes. Forking the orchestrator to add a strategy does not require forking the UI, ingestion or upstream infrastructure. Keep your platform changes in its repository-owned infra/ tree when needed, with upstream provenance recorded separately in manifest.json.

Updating older repository remotes

Older clones can still use the previous repository names. Update your remotes and automation to the current names even where GitHub redirects still work:

Previous Current Azure/GPT-RAG Azure/agent-landing-zone Azure/gpt-rag-ui Azure/agent-app-ui Azure/gpt-rag-orchestrator Azure/agent-app-orchestrator Azure/gpt-rag-ingestion Azure/agent-app-ingestion

Changing a remote does not update component pins or migrate an Azure deployment. Use the upgrade runbook for that.

docs.title: Pin the modified component
docs.text:
For example, when using your organization's orchestrator fork:

  1. Test and commit the component change, then publish a stable tag that resolves to its intended full 40-character SHA. The fetch path selects a published tag, or a branch when no tag is set, and verifies that HEAD matches the SHA. A SHA alone is not a selectable fetch ref.
  2. Update that component's repo, tag and commit together in the platform manifest.json. Keep unchanged components at their coordinated release pins.
  3. Set the bundled app-definition.json orchestrator source.commit to the same SHA. Keep application ID agent-lz-default. A manifest-only change fails bundled definition validation.

  4. Validate both files with the existing hook dependencies installed:

    python -m config.appdefinition --validate app-definition.json

  5. Commit the two pin files together and validate the complete combination before promotion. Upstream release validation does not cover your modified component.

Keep manifest names agent-app-ui, agent-app-orchestrator and agent-app-ingestion, and bundled definition names ui, orchestrator and ingestion. Hooks use those names to map entries and sibling folders.

Existing sibling checkouts are verified, not advanced automatically. Preserve local work and relocate stale checkouts before allowing hooks to fetch selected versions. Keep deployment working trees clean: a matching HEAD does not prove there are no uncommitted changes.

Bundled hosted image preparation fetches and verifies the manifest-pinned orchestrator separately. It builds the hosted entrypoint from that source, not a different platform implementation. Changing only a startup variable does not convert a classic image into a supported hosted image. See Image provenance and redeployment.

docs.title: Private Git authentication
docs.text:
Azure authentication does not authorize GitHub or Azure Repos clones. The actual deployment runner needs noninteractive read access to every selected private repository, including hosted image preparation's orchestrator checkout.

Use an approved credential helper, short-lived token or SSH identity with explicit repository access. Test access using that runner identity. Never embed tokens in manifest URLs, definitions, environment files or logs. Avoid shared write-enabled credentials when read-only access is sufficient. For a protected promotion pipeline, see the optional Azure DevOps runbook.

docs.title: Application binding and selection
docs.text:
An application definition is validated against contracts/app-definition-v1.schema.json. Its folder supplies the matching azure.yaml. Select AGENTLZ_APP_DEFINITION before the first provision, not just before deployment. When omitted, the bundled application is selected.

The platform's preup hook rejects invalid definitions and changed application IDs before the deployment pipeline can create Azure resources, including an empty resource group. The preprovision hook repeats validation for standalone azd provision, but that later hook cannot guarantee rejection before azd's own resource-group initialization. For a strict no-Azure-change check before standalone provisioning, run azd hooks run preup first.

Note

One azd environment hosts exactly one application. To deploy a different application, create a new azd environment.

Ingestion and additive composition

DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP selects the bundled app, not components in an explicit custom definition. Custom definitions keep their declared intent, including any component named ingestion.

Current foundation composition is additive: bundled Container App placeholders, including ingestion, remain alongside custom resources even with the bundled-only switch set to false. Deployment uses the definition's declared components. The effective published ingestion capability is true; it is not evidence that your custom app implements uploads.

Preserve your application's upload/source/authentication contracts. Native source ingestion does not replace conversation uploads or every application ingestion feature. Applications reusing the bundled UI must also meet its upload-gate migration requirements.

docs.title: Application definition
docs.text:
Minimal Container App example, taken from samples/custom-app/containerapp/app-definition.json:

{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "id": "sample-containerapp",
  "displayName": "Sample custom application (Container App)",
  "components": [
    {
      "name": "web",
      "kind": "containerapp",
      "path": "src",
      "source": { "commit": "0000000000000000000000000000000000000000" },
      "profiles": [],
      "ingress": "external",
      "resources": { "cpu": 0.5, "memory": "1.0Gi" }
    }
  ],
  "settings": [
    { "key": "SAMPLE_GREETING", "value": "Hello from the sample application" }
  ]
}

The all-zero commit is a placeholder. Replace it with the commit you deploy (see Source pinning).

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Required Rules schemaVersion Yes Must be 1. id Yes Application identifier matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,39}$. Bound to the environment at the first provision. displayName No Human-readable name. components[].source Yes Either commit (40 lowercase hex characters) or imageDigest (sha256: followed by 64 lowercase hex characters). components[].name Yes Matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,23}$. Must match the service name in azure.yaml. components[].kind Yes containerapp or azure.ai.agent. components[].path Yes Relative path to the component source. Must not contain ... components[].profiles No Capability profiles. See Capability profiles. components[].ingress No external or internal. Default internal. Container Apps only. components[].resources.cpu No 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, or 2.0. Default 0.5. Container Apps only. components[].resources.memory No One of 0.5Gi, 1.0Gi, 1.5Gi, 2.0Gi, 3.0Gi or 4.0Gi. Default 1.0Gi. Container Apps only. settings[] No Each entry requires an uppercase key of 2 to 64 characters that does not start with AGENTLZ_. Optional value and secret: true are mutually exclusive. components[].settings[] No Component settings with the same key and value rules as application settings. They cannot duplicate an application setting.

Components of kind azure.ai.agent run as Foundry hosted agents and cannot set ingress or resources. The hosted sample in samples/custom-app/hosted/app-definition.json defines one component named agent with profiles: ["model-user"].

Settings are validated against the schema. They are not published to App Configuration by the platform.

docs.title: What a definition cannot contain
docs.text:
• Lifecycle hooks.
  • Remote URLs in definition fields, including setting values. The optional $schema field is exempt. Configure runtime endpoints outside the definition, and keep source code in the local working tree.
  • Azure role names. Permissions come only from capability profiles.

docs.title: Capability profiles
docs.text:
Every component receives the base profile. Add the others only when the component needs them.

Container App profile assignments are reconciled during post-provisioning. For custom hosted services, foundation provisioning prepares registry pull access for the existing Foundry project managed identity. This is separate from capability-profile reconciliation for each hosted instance: deployment first verifies the actual routed agent version and its instance identity against the selected Foundry project, then reconciles the declared profiles before running the greeting smoke. No bundled orchestrator permissions are substituted for the custom definition, and this runtime check does not mean all instance grants precede image pull. The deployment identity needs permission to create these scoped role assignments. Denied or ambiguous assignments fail deployment. RBAC propagation may require an explicit, idempotent retry with the same application and image after the reported failure. Deployment does not silently bypass reconciliation.

Key Vault profile assignments use the explicit AZURE_KEY_VAULT_NAME override when present, otherwise the foundation's KEY_VAULT_NAME output, followed by the vault endpoint inputs. The named vault must exist in the selected resource group. If no name is supplied and more than one vault exists, deployment fails rather than guessing which vault should receive application permissions.

Profile Roles assigned to the component identity base (always applied) App Configuration Data Reader, AcrPull, Key Vault Secrets User model-user Cognitive Services User, Cognitive Services OpenAI User retrieval-reader Search Index Data Reader, Storage Blob Data Reader conversation-store Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor blob-delegator Storage Blob Data Reader, Storage Blob Delegator ingestion-writer Search Index Data Contributor, Storage Blob Data Contributor

For reference, the default application uses these profiles:

Component Profiles UI blob-delegator Orchestrator model-user, retrieval-reader, conversation-store Ingestion (when selected) model-user, conversation-store, ingestion-writer

docs.title: Folder layout and azure.yaml
docs.text:
The folder that contains the definition must also contain a root azure.yaml with one service per component. Service names must equal component names, and the file must not declare hooks.

components[].path points to the service source, not to another azd project. Keep azure.yaml next to app-definition.json and set each service's project to its source folder. The pre-deploy hook reuses the selected environment in the definition folder and deploys each declared service by name, rather than deploying all services repeatedly.

name: sample-containerapp
services:
  web:
    host: containerapp
    project: ./src
    language: docker
    docker:
      remoteBuild: true

docs.title: Source pinning
docs.text:
• components[].source.commit: must equal the HEAD commit of that component's local source folder. Nothing is cloned. The platform builds from the working tree and refuses to deploy if HEAD differs. Keep the working tree clean because the commit check does not reject uncommitted source changes.
  • components[].source.imageDigest: deploys a prebuilt image. Set the corresponding service's image in azure.yaml to a qualified registry and repository, such as myregistry.azurecr.io/my-app:v1. The platform replaces its tag or existing digest with the definition's exact digest and deploys it with docker.imagePassthrough: true. It does not build a different image. Environment substitutions in image must resolve before deployment.

With NETWORK_ISOLATION=true, source-pinned Docker components build through the foundation's dedicated ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL, and the platform deploys the immutable digest returned by the completed ACR task. The service project must match components[].path, with Dockerfile and context . in that folder. Other Docker options or source-build layouts fail with actionable guidance to supply a prebuilt digest instead. They are not silently ignored. Public source builds keep the service's normal azd build behavior.

For image handoff, the platform temporarily updates the selected service's image and Docker settings in the child azure.yaml, then restores the original file even if deployment fails. It deploys that service by name. Do not run concurrent deploys or edit that file during a deployment. For a custom Container App using the platform ACR, deployment automatically wires registry pull authentication to the component's existing sole attached managed identity before deploying an immutable image. This adds no identity or RBAC assignment. The automatic wiring is specific to Container Apps and the platform ACR. Configure access separately for other private registries. Hosted agents use the existing Foundry project managed identity for image pull, with the foundation's declarative AcrPull assignment on the platform ACR, not Container App registry wiring or a per-instance preactivation grant. Digest pinning does not bypass registry authorization.

Foundation provisioning publishes the Foundry project and registry deployment outputs whenever those resources are enabled, even in classic topology.

Selecting any custom azure.ai.agent component must also prepare the hosted foundation (prepareHostedAgent=true), even when the bundled orchestrator topology is classic. This does not deploy the bundled hosted orchestrator (deployHostedAgent=false for that classic topology) or change the topology. The current platform prepares these prerequisites for custom hosted components independently of the bundled orchestrator topology.

For recovery, retain the same application definition and immutable image, then apply the current coordinated platform's foundation through the full-stack runbook. Provisioning applies the declared project-identity pull grant; refreshing outputs alone cannot create it.

Use a connected host for private environments. Never substitute another environment's endpoints, broad manual grants, registry admin credentials or an OIDC connection workaround. See Custom hosted image-pull recovery.

When an older environment has an empty project output, the quota preflight can discover a single existing Foundry project in the selected resource group. It credits only matching, successfully provisioned model allocations after verifying the account scope and region. Ambiguous projects receive no credit. Select the intended project explicitly instead of bypassing the quota check.

docs.title: Reading platform outputs at runtime
docs.text:
Components find platform resources through App Configuration. Each component receives APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT and reads the AGENTLZ_PLATFORM_OUTPUTS key with label agent-lz. Both samples show the pattern: the Container App sample serves GET /health and GET /, and the hosted sample answers the Responses protocol.

The platform-output publisher discovers the provisioned Container App identities for the selected definition and publishes their client IDs in identities and the matching AGENTLZ_IDENTITY_<COMPONENT>_CLIENT_ID keys. Hosted-agent instance identities are not available during foundation provisioning. Missing or ambiguous Container App identities fail publication rather than producing an empty map. See Platform outputs.

Custom hosted services must declare an explicit agent name and either invocations or responses in their azure.yaml service definition. The greeting smoke uses the selected service name and declared protocol, preferring invocations when both are available. For Responses services, it validates either Responses SSE or a completed JSON response with nonempty assistant output. A greeting is not evidence of document retrieval or authorization.

docs.title: Validate and select a definition
docs.text:
From the platform root, with the hook dependencies installed:

python -m config.appdefinition --validate path/to/your-app

The deployment input is a file or its containing folder:

azd env set AGENTLZ_APP_DEFINITION path/to/your-app/app-definition.json

Apply it to a new environment before provisioning, following Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack. Pre-deploy revalidates the definition and binding; a mismatch exits with code 2.

Selecting the bundled foundation's classic topology avoids a bundled hosted orchestrator handoff. It does not prevent custom azure.ai.agent components from receiving their own hosted prerequisites. Custom hosted services use their own definition and service configuration, not the bundled image preparation script.

docs.title: config.appdefinition reference
docs.text: Option Description --validate [PATH] Validate a definition file or folder. Without a path, validates the definition selected for the environment. --bind Bind the selected definition to the environment. --check-binding Verify that the environment is bound to the selected definition. Cannot be combined with --bind. --assign-roles Assign capability-profile roles to the identities of containerapp components. --env-name NAME azd environment. Defaults to AZURE_ENV_NAME or the azd default environment. --azure-dir PATH azd folder. Defaults to <repo>/.azure.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Agent Landing Zone has two kinds of configuration:

  • Deployment inputs are azd environment variables read by Bicep or the lifecycle hooks. They control resource provisioning, application selection and image builds.
  • Runtime settings are Azure App Configuration keys read by applications at startup. Some bootstrap values must be container environment variables because they are needed before remote configuration can load.

Set deployment inputs with azd env set <NAME> <value> before provisioning. Inspect only the keys you need with azd env get-value <NAME>; a complete environment dump can contain secrets.

This is a settings reference, not another deployment procedure. Follow Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack for the ordered workflow.

Note

main.parameters.json is the checked-in input to composition. The preprovision hook generates infra/main.parameters.json from it and the selected environment. Do not edit the generated file. In a Git checkout, the hook attempts to hide local regeneration from git status with skip-worktree.

docs.title: Environment boundaries
docs.text:
Use separate azd environments and resource groups for DEV, TEST and PROD. Separate subscriptions provide a stronger administrative and quota boundary. An environment name or App Configuration label alone is not a security boundary.

Boundary Keep separate Target and deployment access Resource group/subscription, azd environment and environment-scoped deployment identity. DEV must not deploy to PROD. Runtime access Component identities, grants and Entra registrations, or explicitly separated callbacks and consent. Configuration and secrets App Configuration store/endpoint and Key Vault. The agent-lz label is shared by convention, not an environment separator. Data Sources, indexes, conversation/history stores and retention. Use approved test data instead of copying production documents. Network and builds DNS, routes, private endpoints and a connected runner. An ACR build pool does not connect the deployment host.

Keep nonsecret, approved inputs in version control. A folder such as environments/ is your convention, not an automatically loaded platform input: apply its settings explicitly. Local .azure is private deployment state, not a promoted configuration artifact. Hooks copy it to child projects; protect those workspaces too. Never copy DEV state into TEST or PROD.

docs.title: Values set by azd or by you
docs.text: Variable Description AZURE_ENV_NAME Environment name. Set by azd env new. Used to derive resource names. AZURE_LOCATION Primary Azure region. azd asks for it on the first azd up. AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID Object ID of the deployment identity that receives roles for service setup and access. Set by azd from your signed-in account.

docs.title: Inputs that use Bicep defaults
docs.text:
These mappings have no inline default in main.parameters.json. When unset, they use the template defaults shown below.

Variable Template default Description NETWORK_ISOLATION false Enables private networking. Jumpbox, Bastion and firewall deployment also depend on their component flags. See Network isolation. AZURE_AI_FOUNDRY_LOCATION Deployment region Region for the Microsoft Foundry account. AZURE_COSMOS_LOCATION Deployment region Region for application Cosmos DB. USE_UAI false Uses user-assigned managed identities instead of system-assigned identities. ENABLE_AGENTIC_RETRIEVAL false Enables the template's agentic retrieval resource configuration. This is separate from the application setting RETRIEVAL_BACKEND. USE_EXISTING_VNET false Deploys into a virtual network you already have when network isolation is enabled. EXISTING_VNET_RESOURCE_ID Empty Resource ID required when reusing a virtual network. DEPLOY_SUBNETS true Creates the required subnets in the selected virtual network. SIDE_BY_SIDE true Uses the deployment resource group for private endpoints and DNS zones rather than placing them in the existing VNet's resource group.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
Variable Default Description AZURE_PRINCIPAL_TYPE User Type of AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID. Use ServicePrincipal in pipelines. DEPLOYMENT_MODE standalone Declares deployment intent for tags and preflight. ailz-integrated does not automatically attach a hub or override component flags. Supply the hub, routing, resource reuse and DNS inputs explicitly. RESOURCE_NAMING_MODE caf caf uses Cloud Adoption Framework prefixes. legacy keeps the naming of older environments. USE_CAPP_API_KEY false Enables the optional classic Container App API-key mechanism. It does not configure Entra ID sign-in. Hosted composition disables this key mechanism. APP_RUNTIME_CONFIGURATION_MODE appConfig Applications read runtime settings from App Configuration. ENABLE_COSMOS_ANALYTICAL_STORAGE false Enables the Cosmos DB analytical store. AZURE_SEARCH_LOCATION Empty Region for both the general Azure AI Search service and the Search service created for Foundry Agent Service. Leave empty to use AZURE_LOCATION. AZURE_SPEECH_LOCATION Empty Region for Azure AI Speech. Leave empty to use the deployment region. AZURE_PE_LOCATION Empty Region for private endpoints. Leave empty to use the deployment region. AZURE_PE_RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME Empty Resource group for private endpoints. Defaults to the deployment resource group, or the existing VNet's resource group when USE_EXISTING_VNET=true and SIDE_BY_SIDE=false. EXISTING_APPLICATION_INSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING None Sends telemetry to an Application Insights resource you already have.

Parameters that start with EXISTING_ reuse a resource instead of creating one. They are listed in Network and security.

docs.title: Ingestion application selection
docs.text:
Variable Fresh-environment default Description DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP false Selects the optional Agent App Ingestion Container App in the bundled application, independently of DEPLOYMENT_TOPOLOGY.

The boolean is persisted by pre-provision and published under label agent-lz. Existing environments retain their selection; they do not silently adopt the fresh default. Custom definitions retain their declared intent and additive foundation composition.

Selection Effect false Omits the bundled ingestion app from subsequent composition/deployment and reconciliation. The UI disables attachment controls and upload paths, not text chat, authentication or retrieval. true Selects the app and retains the UI's existing upload eligibility checks. It does not grant every caller permission to upload.

Opt-out supports native Foundry IQ azureBlob, or an explicitly bound, independently populated SEARCH_RAG_INDEX_NAME for ai_search / Foundry IQ searchIndex. It does not select a strategy, configure SharePoint, rewrite source bindings, populate an index or remove authorization. FOUNDRY_IQ_CONVERSATION_UPLOAD_ENABLED=true requires the app.

See Ingestion and conversation uploads for source choices, SharePoint distinctions, custom-definition behavior and older-UI migration and safe retirement. Disabling the component does not delete existing resources or revoke old grants.

docs.title: Search region and quota
docs.text:
AZURE_SEARCH_LOCATION resolves the effective Bicep searchServiceLocation. An unset or empty value falls back to AZURE_LOCATION. Both newly created Search services use this effective region. Provider availability and Search quota checks must use that same region, not the primary region when an override is set.

Search quota must cover the complete enabled service count: one general service when deploySearchService (DEPLOY_SEARCH_SERVICE) is enabled, plus one Foundry Search service when deployAiFoundry and deployAAfAgentSvc (DEPLOY_AAF_AGENT_SVC) are enabled and aiSearchResourceId is not supplied. When both creation paths are enabled, the check requires quota for two services. Reusing a Foundry Search resource does not request a new service for that path. Do not bypass preflight to work around a region mismatch or insufficient quota. See Search preflight region and quota.

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text:
Variable Default Description RETRIEVAL_BACKEND foundry_iq Retrieval implementation used by the orchestrator. FOUNDRY_IQ_PATTERN azureBlob Foundry IQ pattern. FOUNDRY_IQ_KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_KIND azureBlob Kind of knowledge source. FOUNDRY_IQ_API_VERSION 2026-05-01-preview Azure AI Search API version used for Foundry IQ objects. FOUNDRY_IQ_IS_ADLS_GEN2 false true when the source storage account has a hierarchical namespace. KNOWLEDGE_BASE_NAME knowledge-base Knowledge base name. KNOWLEDGE_BASE_CONNECTION_NAME knowledge-base-connection Foundry project connection to the knowledge base. FOUNDRY_IQ_KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_NAME knowledge-base-blob-ks Knowledge source name. FOUNDRY_IQ_SEARCH_INDEX_NAME agent-lz-index Search index name.

Other retrieval defaults: billing plan free, semantic configuration default, security field metadata_security_id, storage container documents, content extraction mode standard, ingestion permission options ["rbacScope"], and the filter add-on disabled.

For network-isolated native Blob configuration, infrastructure publishes SEARCH_SHARED_PRIVATE_LINKS as a JSON array under label agent-lz. This is post-provision metadata, not an operator switch or a runtime retrieval setting. Each entry records the template-owned name, groupId and privateLinkResourceId. Configuration cross-checks these against SEARCH_SERVICE_RESOURCE_ID, STORAGE_ACCOUNT_RESOURCE_ID and AI_FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT_RESOURCE_ID. This manifest identifies the exact source GETs for readiness. It is not an automatic target approval allowlist. Pending links require administrator approval. Do not substitute unrelated resources or edit the manifest to bypass the gate. See Private native Blob ingestion.

The exact ARM resource IDs can include Azure-valid resource-group names with parentheses, Unicode letters and decimal digits. Resource-group validation does not relax the expected resource type or allow extra path segments, query strings, URL hosts or encoded path separators.

docs.title: Explicit shared-source permission options
docs.text:
FOUNDRY_IQ_INGESTION_PERMISSION_OPTIONS controls the configured source's ingestion permission metadata. It is an existing setting, not a new runtime key. Omission or an actual null value retains the protected default ["rbacScope"]. An explicit JSON empty array, [], is an opt-in for a deliberately shared source when native Blob ingestion is active. It is not treated as a missing value.

For active native Blob ingestion, the shared-source empty list is accepted with RETRIEVAL_BACKEND=foundry_iq, FOUNDRY_IQ_PATTERN=azureBlob (or the historical managed compatibility alias), azureBlob knowledge source kind and a recognized non-ADLS source. Active ADLS Gen2, mismatched source configuration and ambiguous ADLS configuration fail closed. Nonempty Blob permission lists accept only rbacScope and sensitivityLabels.

The infrastructure also publishes [] as unused metadata for inactive native Blob ingestion: ai_search with any pattern, or foundry_iq with the searchIndex pattern. Those empty lists remain accepted because no native Blob knowledge source is rendered. They are not shared-source opt-ins and do not change the independently populated index's authorization.

Malformed JSON, scalar values, textual null, non-string or blank list entries, and unsupported permission names fail with actionable diagnostics. Invalid input fails closed rather than silently falling back or removing protection. An actual null value and the text null are not interchangeable.

For active native Blob ingestion, use [] only when policy permits the source's documents to be shared without that ingestion permission metadata. It does not grant document access by itself or change other sources, application authentication, Entra ID/OBO, retrieval authorization, RBAC or private network restrictions. Do not use it to work around an authentication or private-link failure. Review the source's intended audience and verify allow/deny behavior before enabling it.

To restore protected ingestion, set ["rbacScope"] and rerun the source configuration. Verify the resulting source/index permission metadata and document authorization. Do not assume changing a setting alone has repaired already-ingested documents. See Private native Blob ingestion.

docs.title: Network and security
docs.text:
These parameters matter mostly when NETWORK_ISOLATION=true. Read Network isolation first.

Variable Default Description DEPLOY_AZURE_FIREWALL true Deploys Azure Firewall for egress control. ENABLE_FIREWALL_DNS_PROXY false Enables the deployed firewall's DNS proxy only when both Azure Firewall deployment and network isolation are enabled. Does not modify VNet or VPN DNS settings. DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL true Deploys an Azure Container Registry agent pool inside the virtual network so images can be built without a local Docker host. The pool is created only when NETWORK_ISOLATION=true. DEPLOY_JUMPBOX Same as NETWORK_ISOLATION Deploys a Windows jumpbox virtual machine. DEPLOY_BASTION Enabled with network isolation and jumpbox deployment Deploys Azure Bastion unless an existing Bastion is selected. BASTION_SKU_NAME Standard Bastion SKU. DEPLOY_NAT_GATEWAY Enabled with network isolation and jumpbox deployment Deploys a NAT gateway unless an existing gateway is selected. ENABLE_ACS_MEDIA_EGRESS false Opens firewall egress for Azure Communication Services media. DEPLOY_GROUNDING_WITH_BING false Deploys Grounding with Bing Search. DEPLOY_KEY_VAULT true Deploys the application Key Vault. DEPLOY_VM_KEY_VAULT false Deploys a separate Key Vault for the jumpbox. DEPLOY_LOG_ANALYTICS true Deploys a Log Analytics workspace unless an existing workspace is selected.
