Independently populated Search index Your own ingestion pipeline populates a compatible index You bind SEARCH_RAG_INDEX_NAME explicitly, using ai_search or Foundry IQ searchIndex. Disabling the bundled app does not create this pipeline or populate the index. Agent App Ingestion The optional ingestion Container App processes documents and writes Search content You need the application's processing pipeline, its SharePoint jobs, or the conversation-upload path. Review the selected component's supported formats and configuration.

Agent App Ingestion provides format-specific chunking, text/image embeddings and application-managed ingestion jobs. It is not simply a deployment wrapper for native Foundry IQ ingestion. Neither path is a drop-in replacement for the other.

docs.title: SharePoint is a separate integration
docs.text:
The optional application's Graph-based SharePoint jobs and Foundry IQ's preview indexedSharePoint knowledge source are different implementations. Configuring native Blob ingestion does not configure SharePoint.

The platform can register the preview indexed SharePoint source when its required identifiers are supplied. It still requires an Entra application, a federated identity credential for the configured managed identity, Graph administrator consent and, for Sites.Selected, explicit site access. Incomplete identifiers cause that source to be omitted with a warning. Registration is not evidence that the manual permissions work.

The bundled ingestion opt-out validator supports native azureBlob, or an explicit independently populated index. It does not establish SharePoint-only ingestion-free support or parity with the application's SharePoint jobs. Validate the chosen integration and its document authorization before removing an existing ingestion dependency.

docs.title: Select the optional application
docs.text:
DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP accepts only true or false:

Environment Resolution New bundled application Defaults to false. Existing bundled application Retains its recorded selection. A populated older environment without a selection retains ingestion. A failed state lookup requires restored access or an explicit choice, not a guess. Explicit custom definition Retains its declared component intent and the current additive foundation composition. The bundled-only switch does not remove its components.

An empty azd-created resource group is considered fresh. Pre-provision persists the resolved choice, and configuration publishes the effective value under App Configuration label agent-lz.

Contextual setting, applied before the matching deployment runbook:

azd env set DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP false

For the bundled application, opt-out excludes ingestion from subsequent provisioning, checkout, build, deployment, endpoint reconciliation and identity/role reconciliation. It does not change the retrieval backend, source/index bindings, strategy, topology or document authorization.

An ingestion-free ai_search deployment needs SEARCH_RAG_INDEX_NAME. For Foundry IQ with an independent index, also select both FOUNDRY_IQ_PATTERN=searchIndex and FOUNDRY_IQ_KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_KIND=searchIndex. The index must pass the existing schema/upgrade guards. Unsupported combinations, including FOUNDRY_IQ_CONVERSATION_UPLOAD_ENABLED=true with ingestion disabled, fail validation.

docs.title: Conversation uploads are not native source ingestion
docs.text:
The bundled UI reads the effective ingestion flag:

  • false hides attachment controls and rejects server uploads and client preflight before ingestion endpoint or Dapr fallback resolution.
  • true retains upload eligibility checks. It does not give every caller permission to upload.
  • Missing retains legacy behavior, not a safe opt-out.

Text chat, delegated authentication and retrieval remain available when uploads are disabled. When enabled, authenticated-mode eligibility, anonymous Copilot restrictions, conversation ownership/eligibility, supported file types and size/count limits still apply. Hosted upload eligibility also requires a conversation identifier. Native source ingestion does not implement this chat attachment path.

Custom applications own their upload contract. A published capability flag does not prove that a custom application implements uploads.

docs.title: Upgrade and retirement safety
docs.text:
Before changing an existing selection, record the current platform revision, manifest, source/index bindings and ingestion dependencies. Back up relevant configuration and data. Apply selection changes through the full deployment workflow, not deploy-only or a manually edited runtime key. Private environments need a connected runner.

Older UI compatibility

The upload gate was introduced in the coordinated Agent Landing Zone v4.3.0 / agent-app-ui v3.3.0 combination. On v4.2.3 / UI v3.2.2, retain explicit DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP=true: that UI sends attachments to ingestion in both hosting modes and does not enforce the new gate. An empty endpoint can fall back to a derived URL or Dapr. Changing Chainlit TOML or authentication policy is not a supported opt-out.

Upgrade the complete manifest-pinned combination before disabling ingestion. Check that App Configuration publishes the resolved flag and the deployed UI consumes it. Verify attachment controls are hidden and stale/direct uploads are rejected, while sign-in, chat, retrieval and document allow/deny tests still work.

Opt-out does not delete an existing app, documents or indexes, or revoke existing identity permissions. Resource retirement and RBAC cleanup require separate, deliberately authorized actions after validation.

To restore ingestion, restore the previous explicit selection and source/index configuration, rerun the matching full workflow and retest. Enabling the app alone does not repair bindings. Before rolling back to a UI without the upload gate, restore ingestion and its required endpoint/source configuration first. Rollback must not delete documents or indexes.

docs.title: Authorization remains a design requirement
docs.text:
Preserve authentication, Entra ID/OBO, RBAC and document-level authorization across ingestion and retrieval. Test with both an allowed user and a user who must not see the document. A successful indexer, greeting or hook is insufficient.

The default native Blob permission metadata is ["rbacScope"]. An explicit [] is a deliberate shared-source choice only for supported active non-ADLS native Blob ingestion, not a private-link or login repair. See permission options and private Blob connectivity.

docs.text:

docs.title: Network isolation
docs.text:
With NETWORK_ISOLATION=true, Agent Landing Zone uses private endpoints and private DNS for the deployed workload services. With the default empty allowedIpRanges, public access to those service endpoints is disabled. This is not a blanket block on every public endpoint: Azure Resource Manager remains public, and telemetry and optional public ingress have separate settings.

An explicit, nonempty allowedIpRanges in main.parameters.json enables IP-restricted public access on services that support those rules, even with isolation enabled. Review that exception and any existing network or DNS resources before describing a deployment as private-only.

Use this reference to plan connectivity, DNS and image builds. For the ordered procedure, follow Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack. Optional pipeline automation is covered separately in the Azure DevOps runbook.

Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot publication

Publish to Teams and M365 adds a manual, source-IP-filtered public exception for the Foundry Activity route while Foundry and Bot Service PNA stay disabled. Channel delivery does not use Private Link; other Foundry APIs remain private. The template does not enable this exception.

For a Copilot Studio agent calling Foundry, use Connect Copilot Studio. That runbook uses an authenticated agent flow and Power Platform VNet delegation to reach the Foundry private endpoint; it does not require the Activity-route public exception.

docs.title: What changes with isolation
docs.text:
Area NETWORK_ISOLATION=false NETWORK_ISOLATION=true Workload service access Public endpoints, with service authentication and authorization Private endpoints by default DNS Public DNS Private DNS zones linked to the VNet Jumpbox, Azure Bastion, NAT gateway Not deployed by default Deployed by default Container image builds Local Docker or regular ACR Tasks ACR Task agent pool inside the VNet by default Post-provision and deploy Run from an authorized host that can reach the endpoints Run from an authorized host connected to the VNet

Note

The ACR Task agent pool is created only for isolated deployments. When isolation is off, supported components can build with local Docker or regular ACR Tasks. No pool is created, even if DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL is true.

docs.title: Enable isolation
docs.text:
Set the flag before the first provision:

azd env set NETWORK_ISOLATION true

The ARM resource deployment uses a public control plane, but azd provision also runs lifecycle hooks. Existing-environment topology discovery can require private App Configuration access before ARM deployment, and post-provision configuration requires private connectivity afterward. Provisioning therefore does not always succeed from an unconnected workstation.

Use a connected host for the matching canonical runbook. A new hosted deployment also needs the image preparation and handoff stages described in Deploy the full stack.

docs.title: Reach the private network
docs.text:
Use one of these options:

  • Point-to-site or site-to-site VPN into the landing zone VNet, or into a hub that is peered with it.
  • A VM or build agent inside the VNet, or inside a peered VNet with access to the private DNS zones.
  • The jumpbox VM deployed by the landing zone, reached through Azure Bastion.

docs.title: Use the jumpbox
docs.text:
The default jumpbox is a Windows VM. Unless overridden, its administrator user is testvmuser. The password is supplied through the secure vmAdminPassword provisioning input, not a documented Key Vault secret. If it is unavailable, have an authorized administrator reset it through your approved credential procedure. Do not expose a new password in shell history or command logs.

Connect through Azure Bastion from the Azure portal, then install the deployment prerequisites. Docker is not installed on the jumpbox by default, and it is not required: image builds run in the ACR Task agent pool.

docs.title: Connected-host requirements
docs.text:
Use the same reviewed platform revision and approved inputs on the connected host. Restore/select the intended azd environment and refresh its provisioning outputs using the infrastructure runbook. Refreshing outputs is not provisioning or application configuration.

Signing in with the jumpbox's managed identity does not prove that all deployment permissions are present. Verify its existing configuration and build roles, then have an authorized administrator grant only the missing permissions required by the selected application. For hosted-agent authoring, the runner needs Foundry User (previously Azure AI User) on the exact Foundry project, plus read access to the Foundry account. Cognitive Services Contributor and OpenAI User alone do not grant the agent data-plane actions. Do not grant subscription or resource-group Owner to resolve this denial. See Foundry RBAC for the current role catalog and scopes. Allow role propagation before retrying.

An infrastructure-only deployment stops after provisioning and post-provision configuration. It can contain placeholder Container Apps without running the selected applications. Continue with Deploy the full stack when you are ready to deploy application code.

docs.title: Post-provision can be deferred
docs.text:
When isolation is enabled, post-provision can be deferred instead of failing. Set RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX to false (or 0, no, skip), or set AZURE_SKIP_NETWORK_ISOLATION_WARNING=true while RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX is not truthy. A truthy RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX, such as true, requests the connectivity check even if the warning flag is set. Deferral produces:

Post-provision configuration explicitly deferred; application setup is incomplete.

If the other provisioning stages succeed, azd provision reports success, but the application is not configured. Deferral does not bypass earlier topology or provisioning checks. Clear it and rerun configuration from a connected host: see Complete a deferred post-provision.

When the deferral settings are not set and the private endpoints cannot be reached, post-provision fails with:

Private post-provision prerequisites failed. Connect through VPN/VNet and rerun postProvision; configuration has not started.

Warning

RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX only controls whether post-provision is deferred. It does not provide connectivity. azd deploy always checks private reachability, and fails with "Private deployment prerequisites failed" when the host cannot reach the endpoints.

docs.title: Image builds in isolated deployments
docs.text:
With the default private registry configuration, public build agents cannot reach the registry. Remote builds use an ACR Task agent pool inside the VNet. It is created by default (DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL=true), and the root hosted topology composition selects it for isolated deployments.

If the pool is missing, azd deploy stops before building and offers two fixes:

  1. Create the pool (recommended): select DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL=true and apply it through the matching deployment runbook.
  2. Use local builds where supported: BUILD_MODE=local needs a VNet-connected host with working Docker.

The local alternative applies to component scripts that support BUILD_MODE=local. Automatic hosted orchestrator image preparation and isolated custom source builds still require the private pool. Supplying an already-built immutable digest can skip those builds, but does not bypass the root pre-deploy pool guard unless BUILD_MODE=local is selected. That guard is not proof that the remaining services can build locally.

docs.title: Application-specific package feeds
docs.text:
The root deployment defaults include dependency-verified package feed destinations alongside common language and OS package registries, through the scoped foundation build-egress configuration. This is a build-only allowlist, not a runtime or general Internet exception. It does not allow every mirror recorded in a custom application's lockfile. Check the resolved URLs and download redirects for the exact component commit before building.

For additional dependencies, set parameters.additionalAcrTaskBuildFqdns.value in main.parameters.json and provision the updated configuration. This is an explicit array, not an azd environment variable. Copy the same parameter file to a VNet-connected runner so a later provision preserves the setting.

The bundled orchestrator frontend lockfile uses ms-feed-2.pkgs.visualstudio.com, ms-feed-12.pkgs.visualstudio.com, ms-feed-17.pkgs.visualstudio.com, and ms-feed-25.pkgs.visualstudio.com. Their public package downloads redirect to *.vsblob.vsassets.io. These four exact feeds and the redirect CDN are included in the Agent Landing Zone default build allowlist. packages.microsoft.com is already included in the OS-package rule and does not need an additional entry.

With extendFirewallForAcrTaskBuilds=true (the default) and an effective ACR Task agent pool, the feeds, redirect CDN, and additional hosts are allowed only from the build-agent subnet over HTTPS on port 443. They are not added to jumpbox, application, or agent-subnet rules. The additional-host array defaults to empty.

Disabling the build-egress extension removes these package rules. Re-enabling it restores them. This egress rule has no DNS-proxy dependency and does not change client DNS.

Do not enable public registry access, allow all Internet egress, disable TLS verification, or change dependency integrity hashes to work around a failed build.

See Package installation fails inside the build pool for diagnosis.

docs.title: Verify private connectivity
docs.text:
Run these checks from the host you will deploy from. Use the endpoint host names from azd env get-value <NAME>, for example APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT.

Check Command Expected result DNS nslookup <service-host> Only private IPv4 addresses (10.x, 172.16 through 31.x or 192.168.x) TCP Test-NetConnection <service-host> -Port 443 TcpTestSucceeded : True TLS curl -sv https://<service-host>/ -o /dev/null TLS handshake completes. HTTP 401 or 403 is fine.

If DNS returns a public address, the host is not using the private DNS zones. Check the VNet link of the zone, or the DNS forwarder on your VPN or hub.

On Windows, also check resolution through the operating system resolver, especially when a VPN uses NRPT rules. nslookup alone can differ from the resolver used by the Python prerequisite check. That check rejects public, mixed public/private, IPv6, loopback and link-local answers, then verifies TCP 443 and TLS with the original hostname and normal certificate validation. It sends no HTTP request or credentials. Passing it does not prove API health, RBAC, OBO or document authorization.

docs.title: Opt-in firewall DNS proxy
docs.text:
Use the platform's repository-owned infrastructure tree. Upstream infrastructure provenance alone does not include platform-owned changes or establish a compatible application combination.

ENABLE_FIREWALL_DNS_PROXY defaults to false and maps to the Bicep boolean enableFirewallDnsProxy (also default false), which sets dnsSettings.enableProxy. It applies only when the existing deployAzureFirewall and networkIsolation gates enable firewall deployment. Opt in only for a topology that deliberately uses the firewall as its DNS forwarding path:

azd env set ENABLE_FIREWALL_DNS_PROXY true

Apply the selection through the matching deployment runbook. It persists through normal provisioning. Enabling the proxy does not redirect VNet or VPN clients to the firewall or rewrite their DNS configuration. It is independent of the build-feed egress allowlist.

Confirm the actual client DNS path and private-zone resolution separately from proxy enablement. A proxy cannot repair missing private DNS zone links, VPN routes or application authentication. For rollback, set ENABLE_FIREWALL_DNS_PROXY=false and provision only after confirming that the deployed DNS path does not depend on it.

docs.title: Private native Blob ingestion
docs.text:
Private azureBlob ingestion uses Search-managed outbound shared private links. Before dependent Search cleanup/mutation and again before native knowledge source creation, configuration verifies the exact deployment-owned Search shared links, their expected targets and groups. This guarded implementation does not automatically approve target-side connections: pending links require authorized administrator approval.

The gate is limited to NETWORK_ISOLATION=true, RETRIEVAL_BACKEND=foundry_iq and rendered native azureBlob sources, excluding the searchIndex pattern. It checks the application Search link to deployment Blob storage (blob) and the links to the deployment Foundry account (openai_account, foundry_account, cognitiveservices_account). It does not configure the separate Foundry Search service or unrelated services. Exact names come from the template's SEARCH_SHARED_PRIVATE_LINKS manifest, including bounded Foundry names. The exact Search shared-link GET must return the expected name, target and group. If its body includes a resource ID, that must match too.

Microsoft documents that the backend endpoint is provisioned in a Microsoft-managed tenant. A target PEC can contain an opaque Microsoft.Network/privateEndpoints ID and omit a source Search/link binding. Its name or request message alone is not proof of ownership. Configuration therefore does not enumerate target PECs, follow their pagination links, or write approvals. See Microsoft's approval and shared-link status procedure, sections 2 and 3.

A Pending source link stops immediately with its exact Search ID, target ID, group and link name for administrator investigation and approval. After approval, rerun configuration. An approved source still needs to be ready. ARM visibility alone does not prove readiness. A timeout or denied Search read permission is a configuration failure, not a reason to enable public access or bypass readiness. See Search shared private links are not ready.

Polling has a 600-second total readiness budget, a 10-second interval and ARM request timeouts of at most 30 seconds (limited by the remaining budget). Each exact Search shared link must be Approved and Succeeded, the documented source-side readiness signal. Approved links whose provisioning is still propagating use bounded polling. Pending approval does not spend this budget waiting for an unprovable target match. Administrator-approved links are usable even when target PECs are paginated, opaque or unreadable by the runner. The existing Azure CLI/managed-identity credential is reused. The runner needs Search shared-link read permission, with no new secret, target PEC read/write requirement or automatic RBAC grant.

Native ingestion supports configured Foundry IQ source kinds and is not feature-equivalent to Agent App Ingestion. Choosing it does not remove Entra ID/OBO, RBAC or document-level authorization. In particular, FOUNDRY_IQ_INGESTION_PERMISSION_OPTIONS=[] is a deliberate shared-source metadata choice for active, supported non-ADLS native Blob ingestion, not a workaround for a private connection failure. Infrastructure-published [] for ai_search (any pattern) or foundry_iq / searchIndex is accepted as unused metadata, not a shared-source opt-in: no native Blob source is rendered. See Explicit shared-source permission options.

docs.title: Integrate with an existing hub
docs.text:
To place the landing zone in an existing hub-and-spoke network, use the ailz-integrated deployment mode:

Setting Purpose DEPLOYMENT_MODE=ailz-integrated Declares integration intent; does not attach a hub or override component flags by itself HUB_INTEGRATION_HUB_VNET_RESOURCE_ID Hub VNet to peer with HUB_INTEGRATION_CREATE_HUB_PEERING Create the peering (default true) HUB_INTEGRATION_PEERING_ALLOW_GATEWAY_TRANSIT Allow gateway transit (default false) HUB_INTEGRATION_PEERING_USE_REMOTE_GATEWAYS Use the hub gateway (default false) HUB_INTEGRATION_EGRESS_NEXT_HOP_IP Next hop for egress, for example the hub firewall HUB_INTEGRATION_EXISTING_ROUTE_TABLE_RESOURCE_ID Existing route table to attach AZURE_PE_RESOURCE_GROUP_NAME, AZURE_PE_LOCATION Where to place private endpoints EXISTING_* Reuse the existing VNet, private DNS zones, jumpbox, Bastion, NAT gateway or monitoring resources

Supply the peering, routing, DNS and reuse settings explicitly. See Configuration for the full list, the hub-and-spoke design for design detail, and Deploy infrastructure only to execute the deployment.

docs.title: Publish to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot
docs.text:
Publish an agent already hosted in Microsoft Foundry to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot. Start with a tested agent in a private-network Foundry project, then use its endpoint, identity and version throughout this runbook. The agent can be part of your own application.

You will create a Bot Service resource, enable channel access and publish the agent's app listing. These are manual post-deployment tasks; the landing zone template does not perform them.

Messages from either client follow the same path:

  1. Teams / Microsoft 365 Copilot
  2. Azure Bot Service
  3. Foundry Activity endpoint

Foundry and Bot Service keep public network access (PNA) disabled. Following the Foundry REST publishing flow, you enable a restricted public HTTPS exception for the Activity route. Foundry allows only service-managed Microsoft channel source ranges and still requires authentication and authorization. Channel delivery uses this exception, not the Foundry private endpoint. Management requests still use the private endpoint.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Agent: Have a working hosted agent in a Foundry project, with its own agent identity, a stable endpoint and a version you have tested. If you still need to deploy an application, start with Full stack deploy or Custom applications, then return here.
  • Network access: Run the commands from a VNet-connected host that resolves and reaches the Foundry project's private endpoint. This procedure requires Foundry PNA to be disabled. For a project with public access enabled, use the Foundry portal publishing procedure instead.
  • Tools: Install Azure CLI, Bicep CLI and PowerShell 7.4 or later. Run Steps 1-4 in the same PowerShell session; later blocks use variables set by earlier ones.
  • Azure permissions: You need Foundry User on the project, plus Azure Bot Service Contributor Role and permission to create deployments in the target resource group. Resource-group Contributor covers both bot creation and deployment. A subscription administrator must register Microsoft.BotService if it is not already registered.
  • Microsoft 365 access: Use member accounts in the same tenant as Foundry, with access to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot and app policies that allow the agent. Guest accounts cannot call these agents. Tenant-wide publication requires a Microsoft 365 administrator's approval.

Licensing and costs

To use the agent in Microsoft Copilot Chat, users need an eligible Microsoft 365 subscription. The Microsoft 365 Copilot add-on is optional:

  • With the add-on: No additional Microsoft 365 usage charge for using this agent.
  • Without the add-on: Access to shared tenant data, such as SharePoint or Copilot connectors, can incur usage-based charges in Copilot Credits.

In both cases, Azure costs are separate: the license does not cover Foundry model usage, agent hosting or other Azure services. See licensing and costs for custom engine agents.

Approve the data flow first

Obtain your organization's approval before sending data through this channel. Microsoft 365 processes publishing metadata and conversations under its own compliance and data-residency commitments. Validate how the agent authenticates users and enforces data permissions through this channel; tests through another client do not establish those guarantees.

docs.title: Step 1: Select the agent and save its configuration
docs.text:
In the Azure portal, collect the subscription ID, resource group name, Foundry resource name and project name. Then open the agent in Foundry and record its name and tested version. Use these values for the agent you want to publish.

Expand the block below, replace every placeholder and run it on the connected host. The commands check the agent's identity and save its configuration before you change it.

PowerShell: select the target and save a backup 
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true

$subscriptionId = "<subscription-id>"
$resourceGroup = "<foundry-resource-group>"
$foundryName = "<foundry-resource-name>"
$projectName = "<foundry-project-name>"
$agentName = "<agent-name>"
$agentVersion = "<tested-agent-version>"
$botName = "<globally-unique-bot-name>"
$publishScope = "Shared"

az login
az account set --subscription $subscriptionId
$tenantId = az account show --query tenantId --output tsv
az account show --query "{subscription:id,tenant:tenantId}" --output table

$pna = az cognitiveservices account show --name $foundryName `
    --resource-group $resourceGroup --query properties.publicNetworkAccess --output tsv
if ($pna -ne "Disabled") { throw "This runbook requires Foundry PNA Disabled." }

$work = Join-Path $HOME ("teams-publication-" + (Get-Date -Format "yyyyMMdd-HHmmss"))
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $work | Out-Null
Set-Location $work

$projectEndpoint = "https://$foundryName.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/$projectName"
$agentUri = "$projectEndpoint/agents/$([uri]::EscapeDataString($agentName))"
$token = az account get-access-token --resource https://ai.azure.com `
    --query accessToken --output tsv
$headers = @{ Authorization = "Bearer $token" }
Remove-Variable token

$agent = (Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers).Content | ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable
if (-not $agent.instance_identity.client_id -or -not $agent.agent_endpoint) {
    throw "The agent needs a unique identity and stable endpoint. Stop before publishing."
}
$agent | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 100 | Set-Content agent-before.json
@{
    subscriptionId = $subscriptionId
    tenantId = $tenantId
    resourceGroup = $resourceGroup
    foundryName = $foundryName
    agentUri = $agentUri
    botName = $botName
} | ConvertTo-Json | Set-Content target.json
$agent.agent_endpoint | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 100
"Working folder: $work"

Expected result: The commands complete without errors and display the intended tenant and subscription, the endpoint configuration and a working-folder path. Record that path. Keep target.json and agent-before.json in that folder, outside source control; neither file contains the bearer token.

Before continuing, choose who can use the agent. The block starts with $publishScope = "Shared", which is the recommended pilot scope. Your choice controls both catalog visibility and permission to call the agent:

$publishScope Who can call the agent Store visibility Shared Only identities with the required Foundry permissions can invoke it, through BotServiceRbac. The publisher finds it under Your agents and can share the link with authorized testers. Publishing approval is not required. Tenant Everyone in the Foundry tenant can invoke it, through BotServiceTenant. It appears under Built by your org after Microsoft 365 admin approval.

For tenant-wide distribution, set $publishScope = "Tenant" in the same session before Step 3, and only after your organization approves that access. For a Shared pilot, ask an administrator to grant selected testers Foundry Agent Consumer at the agent scope. Sharing an app link does not grant invocation permission.

If the agent identity check fails

Stop and follow the Foundry migration guidance. Bot Service needs the agent identity's client ID (instance_identity.client_id), not the project's managed identity or an application registration belonging to another client.

docs.title: Step 2: Create the bot and Teams channel
docs.text:
Complete the three sections below in order. This creates a separate Bot Service resource and its Teams channel; the same channel also serves Microsoft 365 Copilot. You do not need to add a bot runtime or modify the landing zone template.

1. Check Bot Service provider registration

Run this command in the PowerShell session from Step 1:

az provider show --namespace Microsoft.BotService --query registrationState --output tsv

Expected result: The provider state is Registered. If it is not, ask a subscription administrator to run az provider register --namespace Microsoft.BotService --wait, then check again. Do not deploy the bot until registration is complete.

2. Save bot-service.bicep in the working folder

Create a file named bot-service.bicep in the $work folder created in Step 1, and paste the following template into it:

param botName string
param displayName string
param msaAppId string
param tenantId string
param endpoint string

resource bot 'Microsoft.BotService/botServices@2022-09-15' = {
  name: botName
  kind: 'azurebot'
  location: 'global'
  sku: {
    name: 'F0'
  }
  properties: {
    displayName: displayName
    endpoint: endpoint
    msaAppId: msaAppId
    msaAppTenantId: tenantId
    msaAppType: 'SingleTenant'
    publicNetworkAccess: 'Disabled'
  }
}

resource teams 'Microsoft.BotService/botServices/channels@2021-03-01' = {
  parent: bot
  name: 'MsTeamsChannel'
  location: 'global'
  properties: {
    channelName: 'MsTeamsChannel'
  }
}
3. Deploy the bot and verify its network setting

Replace <agent-display-name> with the name users should see. Run the commands from $work to deploy the saved template into the Foundry resource group.

$displayName = "<agent-display-name>"
$activityEndpoint = "$agentUri/endpoint/protocols/activityProtocol"

az deployment group create --resource-group $resourceGroup `
    --name "teams-bot" --template-file bot-service.bicep `
    --parameters botName=$botName displayName="$displayName" `
        msaAppId=$($agent.instance_identity.client_id) tenantId=$tenantId `
        endpoint=$activityEndpoint --output none

$botServiceId = az bot show --name $botName --resource-group $resourceGroup `
    --query id --output tsv
az resource show --ids $botServiceId --api-version 2022-09-15 `
    --query "properties.{endpoint:endpoint,pna:publicNetworkAccess}" --output json

Expected result: The bot's endpoint matches the agent's activityProtocol URL, and its network setting is "pna": "Disabled". The bot uses the agent's identity; you do not need a client secret, public VNet ingress or a custom connector.

docs.title: Step 3: Enable the restricted Activity route
docs.text:
Run the block below to enable the restricted Activity route, apply the Bot Service authorization scheme for your chosen audience and send traffic to the tested agent version. The block reads the current configuration so it can preserve the existing protocols and non-Bot authorization schemes. It also checks for Foundry's default Entra authorization. If you changed that configuration, review the endpoint authorization settings before proceeding.

Preserve access for existing consumers

The API replaces the submitted protocol configuration and authorization array. Keep the protocols and authorization schemes your agent already uses, such as responses, invocations and Entra. Removing them can break other clients. Pinning the version also affects all consumers of the stable endpoint, not just Teams and Copilot. Do not run concurrent agent configuration changes.

PowerShell: enable Activity and pin the tested version 
if ($publishScope -notin @("Shared", "Tenant")) { throw "Choose Shared or Tenant." }
$agent = (Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers).Content | ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable
$protocols = $agent.agent_endpoint.protocol_configuration
if (-not $protocols) { throw "Review the agent's existing protocols before continuing." }
$activity = $protocols.activity
if (-not $activity) { $activity = @{} }
$activity.enable_m365_public_endpoint = $true
$protocols.activity = $activity

$botScheme = if ($publishScope -eq "Tenant") { "BotServiceTenant" } else { "BotServiceRbac" }
$schemes = @($agent.agent_endpoint.authorization_schemes |
    Where-Object { $_.type -notin @("BotServiceRbac", "BotServiceTenant") })
$schemes += @{ type = $botScheme }
if ("Entra" -notin $schemes.type) { throw "Review missing Entra authorization before continuing." }

$patch = @{
    agent_endpoint = @{
        protocol_configuration = $protocols
        authorization_schemes = $schemes
        version_selector = @{
            version_selection_rules = @(
                @{ type = "FixedRatio"; agent_version = $agentVersion; traffic_percentage = 100 }
            )
        }
    }
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 100

Invoke-RestMethod -Method Patch -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/merge-patch+json" -Body $patch |
    Out-Null

Expected result: The update completes without errors and prints no output. You will check the final configuration in Step 5.

docs.title: Step 4: Publish the app
docs.text:
This step submits the listing directly to the catalogs. If your organization requires package review before submission, follow the REST package-download procedure instead of running this publish request.

Replace the placeholders below with approved listing details, including your organization's HTTPS website, privacy statement and terms of use. These details are visible to users; do not include secrets or sensitive information.

PowerShell: publish to Teams and Microsoft 365 Copilot 
$publishRequest = @{
    agentDisplayName = $displayName
    botServiceArmId = $botServiceId
    publishScope = $publishScope
    publishAsAutopilot = $false
    appVersion = "1.0.0"
    shortDescription = "<short-description>"
    fullDescription = "<full-description>"
    developerName = "<organization-name>"
    developerWebsiteUrl = "https://<organization-domain>"
    privacyUrl = "https://<organization-domain>/privacy"
    termsOfUseUrl = "https://<organization-domain>/terms"
}
$body = $publishRequest | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 10
$body | Set-Content publish-request.json
$result = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
    -Uri "${agentUri}/microsoft365/publish?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
$result | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20 | Set-Content publish-result.json
$result

Expected result: The response contains titleId. If you selected Tenant, ask a Microsoft 365 administrator to approve the request in Microsoft 365 admin center > Agents > Requests. Approval is required before tenant-wide discovery, and app policies can still restrict availability.

App version versus agent version

appVersion is the version of the store listing. Increase it when you republish metadata or change publication scope. $agentVersion selects the running agent version; changing that version does not require republishing the listing.

Optional: inspect a copy of the published app package

To inspect or retain the package after direct publication, run this block in the same session. It reuses the publication request:

Invoke-WebRequest -Method Post -Uri "${agentUri}/microsoft365/zip?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body -OutFile appPackage.zip

Extract the ZIP and review its manifest and icons with the package inspection checklist. Keep the generated IDs and agent sections unchanged.

The download call does not submit the app to the catalogs, but it can update the agent's publishing configuration and requires agent write permission. Downloading this copy does not require uploading it again.

docs.title: Step 5: Install and verify
docs.text:
Returning later or using a new PowerShell session?

Use this block only to resume verification or maintenance after the bot has been created. Run it on the connected host, replacing <saved-working-folder> with the path recorded in Step 1. It restores the connection variables and gets a fresh token without recreating the bot or republishing the app.

$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
$PSNativeCommandUseErrorActionPreference = $true
Set-Location "<saved-working-folder>"
$target = Get-Content target.json -Raw | ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable
$resourceGroup = $target.resourceGroup
$foundryName = $target.foundryName
$agentUri = $target.agentUri

az login --tenant $target.tenantId
az account set --subscription $target.subscriptionId
$token = az account get-access-token --resource https://ai.azure.com `
    --query accessToken --output tsv
$headers = @{ Authorization = "Bearer $token" }
Remove-Variable token
$botServiceId = az bot show --name $target.botName --resource-group $resourceGroup `
    --query id --output tsv

After publication, open the agent in both clients. For Shared, sign in with the publishing account. For Tenant, wait for admin approval and find the agent under Built by your org.

Client Open the agent Teams Open Apps, find the agent, add it and open its chat. Microsoft 365 Copilot Open the Agents area, find the agent in the agent store and add it. For Shared, look under Your agents.

Complete these checks in each client before making the agent available to users:

  1. Complete any sign-in prompt. Send a greeting, a representative workload question and a follow-up. Confirm that the expected tools and knowledge sources work; receiving a reply alone is not enough.
  2. For a Shared pilot, test with an authorized user and a tenant member who lacks agent permission. The second user must be denied. Use member accounts, not guests. With Tenant, all tenant members are authorized to call the agent, so this is not a valid negative test.
  3. If the agent handles protected data, test with identities that should and should not access that data. Confirm the intended restrictions in both clients, regardless of publication scope.

Then return to the connected host and run the final configuration check:

PowerShell: verify the endpoint and both PNA settings 
$after = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" -Headers $headers
$after.agent_endpoint | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 30
az cognitiveservices account show --name $foundryName --resource-group $resourceGroup `
    --query properties.publicNetworkAccess --output tsv
az resource show --ids $botServiceId --api-version 2022-09-15 `
    --query properties.publicNetworkAccess --output tsv

Expected result: The tested version receives 100% of traffic. The original protocols and Entra authorization are preserved, activity.enable_m365_public_endpoint is true, and the Bot Service scheme matches your publication scope. Both PNA values must remain Disabled.

Channel limitations

Published agents do not support streaming responses or citations. File uploads and image generation are not supported in Microsoft 365 Copilot, although they are available in Teams. Test the capabilities your agent uses in each client and review the Foundry publishing limitations before rollout.

docs.title: Update or stop publication
docs.text:
Use the following actions to maintain the published agent. If your PowerShell session ended or its token expired, resume the session before running the maintenance commands.

Task Action Release a new runtime version Test the version, then follow the REST API tab in the active-version instructions from the connected host. Keep the existing bot and listing. Roll back agent behavior Use the same REST instructions to select the previous tested version. This changes the version for every consumer of the stable endpoint. Change the listing name, descriptions or URLs Edit publish-request.json, increase appVersion and run Update listing metadata below. Keep botServiceArmId and publishScope unchanged for a metadata-only update. Check publication after redeployment Recheck the active version, Activity exception and authorization, then repeat the client tests in Step 5. The landing zone template does not manage this manual configuration. Update listing metadata

Open publish-request.json in the saved working folder. Update the listing details, increase appVersion and review the entire request before running the block below. A Tenant update can require renewed admin approval.

$body = Get-Content publish-request.json -Raw
$result = Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post `
    -Uri "${agentUri}/microsoft365/publish?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/json" -Body $body
$result | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20 | Set-Content publish-result.json
$result

To stop channel access from both clients, run the block below. It disables only the public Activity exception, leaving the other endpoint protocols and their private access unchanged. Keep Foundry PNA disabled.

Stop Teams and Copilot access

The commands read the current protocol configuration and change only the Activity exception:

$current = (Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers).Content | ConvertFrom-Json -AsHashtable
$protocols = $current.agent_endpoint.protocol_configuration
if (-not $protocols.activity) { throw "No Activity configuration found; review the endpoint." }
$protocols.activity.enable_m365_public_endpoint = $false
$disable = @{ agent_endpoint = @{ protocol_configuration = $protocols } } |
    ConvertTo-Json -Depth 100
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Patch -Uri "${agentUri}?api-version=v1" `
    -Headers $headers -ContentType "application/merge-patch+json" -Body $disable |
    Out-Null

After the update, confirm that new requests from Teams and Copilot no longer reach the agent. Ask the administrator to block or remove the app from the catalogs. Uninstalling the app alone does not revoke endpoint access. Do not delete shared Foundry resources or restore an old backup over later configuration changes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom What to check or do A project GET or PATCH fails or times out. Check private DNS and connectivity, the selected tenant, the Foundry User role and the token audience (https://ai.azure.com). If the token expired, resume the session. Do not enable PNA to bypass the error. The bot deployment is denied. Check Microsoft.BotService registration, bot and deployment permissions, and any Azure Policy denial. The agent is missing from either client. Check the signed-in account, publication scope, admin approval and app policies. Refresh the store or sign out and back in; catalog caching can delay discovery. Activity returns 403 NetworkAccessDenied. Check that the Activity exception is enabled and test through Teams or Copilot. A public curl request from an arbitrary IP remains blocked by design. A user can open the app but receives an authorization error. Check that the user is signed in to the Foundry tenant and, for Shared, has Foundry Agent Consumer access. Do not switch to Tenant just to remove the error. The Teams sign-in card opens, but its redirect page does not load. Ask the network administrator to allow outbound HTTPS (TCP 443) to *.azureml.ms from the user's network, then retry sign-in. The agent replies, but tools or retrieval fail. Check runtime identity permissions, data authorization and outbound access. A successful test in another client does not validate identity propagation through Teams or Copilot. A conversation is stuck or returns no tool output found. In Teams, send /foundry_new_preview; in Copilot, start a new chat with the agent. Previous conversation context cannot be restored after a reset. Publication returns version already exists. Increase appVersion and submit the listing again. Do not change the runtime version to fix a listing-version error.

For other errors, use Foundry publishing troubleshooting and published-agent authorization.

docs.title: Sizing and capacity
docs.text:
Plan capacity around the workload you expect to run, not only the number of people who can sign in. Concurrent agent requests, model calls, tool latency and document processing place different demands on the deployment.

Detailed guidance is planned

A benchmark-backed sizing guide with validated workload profiles is planned. This page provides planning questions, not tested small/medium/large tiers or a throughput guarantee.

docs.title: Establish a workload baseline
docs.text:
Record these inputs before choosing resource capacity.

Area Questions to answer Agent traffic How many requests run concurrently at peak? How long do turns take, and how many model or tool calls does each strategy make? Models Which deployments are required? What are the expected input/output token volumes, token-rate limits and target response times? Knowledge and ingestion How many documents and vectors are stored? What are their sizes, formats, update rate and ingestion completion targets? Will ingestion run alongside peak interactive traffic? Hosting Which strategies must run, on which host? What CPU, memory, concurrency and scaling behavior does representative execution require? Availability and operations What recovery targets, environment separation, telemetry retention and private-network requirements must the deployment meet?

Start with Configuration and Agent hosting to identify the applicable inputs and host constraints. Use the resource inventory to identify enabled resources, then confirm them against your platform's composed parameters: the foundation inventory is not a promise that every Agent Landing Zone topology has the same resource count.

docs.title: Validate the initial capacity
docs.text:
1. Choose explicit targets. Record acceptable response time, error rate, ingestion delay and peak concurrency for representative requests.
  2. Check service limits and quota. Confirm regional availability and capacity for every enabled service. Template defaults and a passing preflight check are not workload sizing evidence.
  3. Measure representative behavior. In a nonproduction environment, exercise the selected strategy, configured tools, document sizes and ingestion path. Include authentication and document allow/deny checks.
  4. Observe the bottleneck. Use service metrics and application traces to distinguish model throttling, Search limits, tool latency and runtime CPU/memory pressure before changing capacity.
  5. Recheck cost and repeat. Change the constrained resource, repeat the same tests and record the chosen settings and results.

Scaling the application host does not increase model quota or Search capacity. Treat those as separate limits, and account for shared demand when ingestion and interactive requests use the same services.

docs.title: Turn the result into a cost plan
docs.text:
Use Cost planning and Deployed resources and cost estimates as starting points. Recalculate for your region, enabled resources, measured usage and availability requirements. The example estimates are not a quote or a validated production sizing profile.

Record the selected configuration with the workload assumptions and test evidence so that a later capacity change can be evaluated against the same baseline. Then follow Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with the first failing stage and its exact error, not the last command that returned success. Provisioning, post-provision configuration, image preparation, application deployment and runtime access are separate checks.

What you see Start here Hosted deployment asks for preparation Hosted handoff Private endpoint or build-pool failure Private prerequisites, package installation Configuration stops after provisioning Post-provision diagnostics Deploy reports success but the application fails Revision health, startup authentication Chat, history or authorization fails Runtime diagnostics

docs.title: Before changing anything
docs.text:
1. Run diagnostics from the platform repository root. Confirm the intended environment with azd env list and the Azure CLI subscription with az account show. Verify the identity used by azd separately from the CLI identity; they need not be the same.
  2. Record the failing command, time, stage, source revision and relevant non-secret settings, such as NETWORK_ISOLATION, BUILD_MODE and DEPLOYMENT_TOPOLOGY.
  3. For private environments, use a host with the required VPN/VNet connectivity. Inspect DNS, TLS and authorization separately.
  4. Preserve local work and data. Do not delete resources, clear bindings, disable authentication or bypass preflight to make an error disappear.

Here, classic means the orchestrator runs in a Container App; hosted topologies run it in Foundry Agent Service. Confirm the selected topology before following a recovery path.

Share useful, redacted diagnostics

Hooks write to the terminal. Bundled Container App component deployments also write child logs under <component>/.logs. Share the exact error and relevant log excerpt, not the full output of azd env get-values. Remove tokens, cookies, credentials, signed URLs, document contents, user identifiers and private environment names.

docs.title: Hosted deployment is not prepared
docs.text:
Symptom: Deployment asks you to run the hosted preparation script or reports an incomplete image handoff.

Diagnose: The first provision creates prerequisites and records HOSTED_AGENT_PREPARED=true. Preparation records an immutable image digest. A subsequent provision materializes the DEPLOY_HOSTED_AGENT=true handoff. None of these steps alone creates the data-plane agent version.

Correct: Follow the hosted sequence in Deploy the full stack from the first incomplete step. For an unchanged, compatible image, use the redeployment guidance. Do not set generated output flags manually.

Verify: Deployment targets the intended digest and routed agent version. Then test authenticated task execution and the retrieval/authorization features you use; a protocol greeting alone is not acceptance.

docs.title: Hosted agent deployment returns an agent permission denial
docs.text:
Symptom: HTTP 403 names Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/AIServices/agents/read.

Diagnose: Compare the denied object ID with the actual deployment principal. Successful ARM provisioning or a TLS connection does not prove Foundry data-plane permission.

Correct: Have an authorized administrator review the minimum project-scoped agent authoring role for that principal. A runner creating/updating agents needs Foundry User (formerly Azure AI User) or the appropriate equivalent custom role. Azure AI Developer targets different hub/workspace scenarios. Allow role propagation before retrying; do not grant resource-group Owner as a substitute.

Verify: The same principal can perform the previously denied operation. Test delegated-user/OBO access separately.

docs.title: Application definition does not match the environment
docs.text:
Symptom: Application definition binding check failed. No changes were made. with exit code 2. An invalid definition instead exits with code 1.

Diagnose: Compare the selected definition's application ID with the existing AGENTLZ_APP_ID binding. A custom hosted component does not automatically require switching the bundled orchestrator's topology.

Correct: Restore the matching definition. For a different application ID, use a separate environment and select the definition before first provision. Do not delete the binding or switch topology to bypass the mismatch.

Verify: Definition validation and binding checks pass for the intended environment. See Custom applications.

docs.title: Custom hosted image pull fails with a classic bundled orchestrator
docs.text:
Symptom: A custom azure.ai.agent service cannot activate its private image, although Foundry project and registry outputs exist.

Diagnose: Check the Foundry project identity's registry pull grant and the exact image/registry. A legacy composition defect omitted hosted foundation preparation when the bundled orchestrator stayed in a Container App. The correction shipped in v4.2.3 (PR #779).

Correct: Use the complete corrected platform combination. Preserve the environment, definition and immutable image, then rerun the full-stack provisioning workflow. Provisioning applies the declarative pull grant; refreshing outputs alone cannot. For an external registry, review its supported pull-role mode and resource scope separately.

Verify: Image activation succeeds and the actual runtime principal receives the declared capabilities. Check the routed version before testing the agent. Do not enable registry admin credentials, grant broad roles or replace delegated-user/OBO authentication with a service identity.

docs.title: Private deployment prerequisites failed
docs.text:
Symptom:

Private deployment prerequisites failed. Use a VPN/VNet-connected host; RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX is not a connectivity bypass.

Diagnose: With NETWORK_ISOLATION=true, the host cannot resolve or establish TLS to App Configuration, or to the Foundry project endpoint for hosted topologies. The gate allows up to 20 seconds per endpoint.

Correct: Move to the approved jumpbox, VPN or peered-VNet runner and inspect the private connectivity path. RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX is not a bypass.

Verify: Resolve and reach each required endpoint from that runner, then retry the failed stage. A reachable endpoint can still reject authorization.

docs.title: ACR Task agent pool is missing
docs.text:
Symptom:

Run 'azd env set DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL true' and 'azd provision', or set BUILD_MODE=local on a VNet-connected host with Docker.

Diagnose: The private environment has no ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL output and BUILD_MODE is not local. This guard also applies to a custom service with a prebuilt digest.

Correct: Select the pool intentionally and run the foundation workflow:

azd env set DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL true
azd provision

For supported Container App builds, local Docker on a connected host is an alternative. The jumpbox does not include Docker by default. Local mode is not a fallback for automatic hosted image preparation or isolated custom source builds. See isolated image builds.

Verify: Confirm the selected environment has the provisioned pool output and that a build runs in it. Then resume the topology's deployment sequence; hosted preparation may still be incomplete.

docs.title: Package installation fails inside the build pool
docs.text:
Symptom: An ACR run starts, but package installation fails. npm can report Exit handler never called!, followed by tsc: not found.

Diagnose: Retrieve the failed ACR run log from a connected host. Correlate timestamps and the build-agent source address with firewall deny logs. Check the pinned lockfile's resolved URLs, including redirect CDN destinations. A pulled base image does not prove package-feed access.

Correct: Confirm the pool and extendFirewallForAcrTaskBuilds are enabled and the shipped firewall changes are provisioned. The platform includes the orchestrator's Microsoft npm feeds, *.vsblob.vsassets.io and the existing packages.microsoft.com OS-package allowance. For additional verified dependencies, use application-specific package feeds. Keep exceptions limited to build-subnet HTTPS traffic.

Verify: Retry the same pinned source and confirm package installation and compilation both complete. Do not upgrade npm speculatively or assume a missing compiler proves a dependency-version defect.

docs.title: Stale component checkout
docs.text:
Symptom: Remove or relocate the stale sibling checkout.

Diagnose: A bundled component's sibling folder exists at a different commit from manifest.json. Matching HEAD alone would not establish that local work is absent.

Correct: Inspect the named checkout, preserve local modifications and move it aside. Retry deployment to obtain the expected source. Delete it only after confirming it contains nothing needed; keep component development elsewhere.

Verify: The deployed source matches the manifest's tag and commit, and the intended application revision is healthy.

docs.title: A component deployment fails
docs.text:
Symptom: One or more components failed. See logs above.

Diagnose: Find the first failing component and its newest .logs file. Separate source checkout, image build/push, role and application-update errors.

Correct: Repair the dependency identified by that log. Use the private connectivity or build-pool entries above when appropriate. Do not assume every component failure is a registry-permission problem.

Verify: Retry the failed workflow and inspect the actual image, intended revision and startup logs, not only the child command's exit status.

docs.title: Deploy succeeds but the UI or administrative panel does not start
docs.text:
Symptom: Child commands succeed, but the latest revision is unhealthy. Logs name OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_ID, OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_SECRET, OAUTH_AZURE_AD_TENANT_ID or missing panel OAuth settings.

Diagnose: Inspect the intended revision and image. A previous healthy placeholder can still serve HTTP 200 while the new revision fails.

Correct: Configure delegated authentication. Store the credential in Key Vault and publish its reference, not its value, under label agent-lz. Reload configuration through the supported lifecycle workflow.

Verify: Check revision health, the Entra login redirect, real user login, OBO and rejection of unauthenticated panel data requests. Do not disable the panel or authentication to turn a missing-authentication error into a pass.

docs.title: Search shared private links are not ready
docs.text:
Symptom: Private native azureBlob source configuration reports pending approval, denied Search reads or a readiness timeout.

Diagnose: Inspect the exact reported Search service, link name, target and group. Runner private access and successful ARM provisioning do not prove Search-managed outbound access. Each required source link must report both Approved and Succeeded.

Correct:

  • Pending: Have an authorized administrator investigate and approve only the exact target request using Microsoft's procedure. Configuration does not approve requests automatically.
  • ARM 401/403: Review the runner's Microsoft.Search/searchServices/sharedPrivateLinkResources/read permission. Target approval does not replace it.
  • Approved but provisioning: Allow propagation and inspect the failed link's state. Readiness polling has a 600-second budget, 10-second intervals and requests bounded by 30 seconds and the remaining budget.
  • Missing long-name manifest: Re-provision the updated template through an authorized deployment to publish SEARCH_SHARED_PRIVATE_LINKS under agent-lz. Do not invent a hashed name or edit metadata to approve another request.

Verify: Rerun post-provision from a connected host, then verify source processing and authorized retrieval. The gate runs before dependent Search mutation and source creation. Do not approve unrelated requests, enumerate target connections as a workaround, enable public access or bypass the gate. See Private native Blob ingestion.

docs.title: Ingestion selection does not match the source configuration
docs.text:
Symptom: A fresh environment has no ingestion Container App, a source combination fails validation, or attachment behavior differs from expectations.

Diagnose: Fresh bundled deployments default DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP=false, independently of orchestrator hosting. Native source ingestion covers supported Foundry IQ sources, not all ingestion application features or conversation uploads. Existing environments and custom definitions retain their component intent.

Correct: Check the resolved component selection, retrieval backend, source kind and index bindings using Ingestion. To retain or restore the application, select it explicitly and run the full workflow, not only azd deploy. An externally populated index must be named explicitly where required.

Older UI compatibility

The upload gate was introduced with platform v4.3.0 / UI v3.3.0. On platform v4.2.3 / UI v3.2.2, retain DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP=true until the coordinated upgrade is complete. Clearing ingestion endpoints or editing the attachment widget is not a supported opt-out. Never switch to anonymous authentication to hide uploads.

Verify: Confirm the effective agent-lz key and intended UI revision. With supported opt-out, attachment controls must be hidden and direct/stale uploads rejected, while text chat, authentication, retrieval and document authorization still work. A missing key retains legacy behavior; explicit false activates the gate. Do not delete existing apps, documents or indexes as incidental cleanup.

docs.title: Shared-source permission options are rejected or unexpected
docs.text:
Symptom: Source configuration rejects FOUNDRY_IQ_INGESTION_PERMISSION_OPTIONS, or a source has unexpected permission metadata.

Diagnose: Omitted or actual-null values retain ["rbacScope"]; explicit [] means something different. For active native Blob ingestion, an empty list deliberately selects shared access only for recognized non-ADLS azureBlob configuration. Unsupported or ambiguous active sources fail closed. In non-native ai_search or foundry_iq/searchIndex modes, accepted [] is unused metadata, not shared-source activation.

Correct: Supply valid JSON for the intended source policy. For protected Blob ingestion, restore ["rbacScope"]. Nonempty non-ADLS Blob lists support only rbacScope and sensitivityLabels. Review the full input contract for source/pattern constraints and the historical managed alias.

Verify: Rerun source configuration, inspect permission metadata and test document allow/deny behavior. Do not use [] to bypass private-link, RBAC or authentication failures.

docs.title: Firewall DNS proxy is enabled but clients still resolve incorrectly
docs.text:
Symptom: Private names resolve incorrectly after enabling the DNS proxy.

Diagnose: ENABLE_FIREWALL_DNS_PROXY defaults to false; its opt-in applies only with firewall deployment and isolation enabled. It does not change VNet/VPN client DNS settings or build-feed egress.

Correct: Inspect the affected client's DNS server, zone links and forwarding path. Make client DNS changes deliberately and separately from proxy enablement. See Firewall DNS proxy.

Verify: Resolve the required names and test private TLS from the actual client. Do not enable public access as a workaround.

docs.title: Hosted configuration TLS handshake stalls
docs.text:
Symptom: Hosted bootstrap stalls while loading App Configuration or Key Vault references.

Diagnose: Distinguish name resolution, routing, TLS and HTTP authorization errors at both endpoints. Confirm the actual runtime identity. MTU is not an established cause of every timeout.

Correct: Only for the confirmed transport compatibility case, use the endpoint-scoped TLS profile. It was introduced in platform v4.2.3 with orchestrator v5.2.1. Supply the actual KEY_VAULT_URI, deliberately select APP_CONFIG_TLS_COMPATIBILITY=true and deploy the corrected agent version. To restore SDK defaults, use false and redeploy. Never disable certificate verification, downgrade TLS globally or broaden roles to conceal a transport failure.

If bootstrap resolves a UI-only secret, inspect the actual label selectors: in the SDK, None selects all labels, while "\0" selects only unlabelled settings. Use the corrected selector, not weaker vault permissions or deleted labels.

Verify: The new version completes configuration using valid TLS and the intended identity. Test real application behavior separately.

docs.title: Search preflight region and quota
docs.text:
Symptom: Preflight checks AZURE_LOCATION despite AZURE_SEARCH_LOCATION, or counts only one service when two will be created.

Diagnose: Earlier hooks had region/count defects corrected in v4.2.3. An empty AZURE_SEARCH_LOCATION falls back to AZURE_LOCATION. Both workload and newly created Agent Service Search must be accounted for.

Correct: Check the effective region and selected resources using Search region and quota. Verify local hooks and repository-owned infrastructure match the intended coordinated source. Request quota or deliberately select a supported region; do not set PREFLIGHT_SKIP or AGENTLZ_REGIONAL_PREFLIGHT_SKIP.

Verify: Preflight checks the effective region and full creation count, then provisioning succeeds. Preflight does not reserve capacity.

docs.title: Quota check rejects an unchanged existing deployment
docs.text:
Symptom: Re-provision reports insufficient remaining model quota for the same account, deployment and configured capacity.

Diagnose: The v4.2.2 preflight compared full requested capacity with unused regional quota, without crediting an existing matching deployment. This could block the second provision of a hosted deployment.

Correct: Verify environment, account region, deployment, model/version and SKU. Use the coordinated correction introduced in v4.2.3 (PR #773). It credits only verified successful matching capacity and aggregates quota pools. Fresh allocations and changed/unverified targets still need capacity.

Verify: Both preflight gates evaluate the intended incremental request. Do not delete the existing deployment, reduce capacity just to pass or disable the gate. Model availability checks still apply.

docs.title: Foundry rejects evaluation API-key creation
docs.text:
Symptom: Failed to list key. disableLocalAuth is set to be true.

Diagnose: The account requires Entra ID. Legacy v4.2.2 post-provision still attempted evaluation-key injection; its final success message did not prove the secret existed.

Correct: Keep local authentication disabled and use Entra ID for evaluation. The correction introduced in v4.2.3 (PR #773) skips inapplicable key injection and surfaces unexpected key/Key Vault errors.

Verify: Post-provision reports the expected Entra-only path and evaluation works with the intended identity. Do not enable keys to hide the error.

docs.title: Administrative panel cannot resolve its Cosmos database
docs.text:
Symptom: DEPLOY_ADMINISTRATIVE_PANEL is true but DATABASE_ACCOUNT_NAME is not set.

Diagnose: Legacy v4.2.2 panel role setup expected process inputs even when DATABASE_ACCOUNT_NAME and DATABASE_NAME were published in App Configuration.

Correct: Confirm the two settings under agent-lz for the selected environment. Use the coordinated correction introduced in v4.2.3 (PR #773), which reads published settings when process inputs are absent.

Verify: Panel configuration resolves the actual account/database and preserves container-scoped grants. Do not guess a database name or broaden permissions to the whole account.

docs.title: Missing endpoint output
docs.text:
Symptom:

Missing <KEY>. Run provisioning and load the selected azd environment outputs before this stage.

Diagnose: The selected environment lacks a required output such as APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT, AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT or AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_ENDPOINT.

Correct: Confirm the environment first. If it is already provisioned and you moved machines, use azd env refresh. If provision is incomplete, follow Deploy infrastructure only. Do not invent endpoint values to satisfy a guard.

Verify: The environment's outputs refer to its actual provisioned resources, then retry the failed stage.

docs.title: Private post-provision prerequisites failed
docs.text:
Symptom:

Private post-provision prerequisites failed. Connect through VPN/VNet and rerun postProvision; configuration has not started.

Diagnose: Provisioning completed, but the runner cannot reach private App Configuration, so configuration has not started.

Correct: Connect through an approved jumpbox, VPN or peered VNet. Follow Complete a deferred post-provision.

Verify: The configuration hook actually completes from the connected host. Do not infer success from resource provisioning alone.

docs.title: Post-provision was deferred
docs.text:
Symptom:

Post-provision configuration explicitly deferred; application setup is incomplete.

Diagnose: An explicit deferral can exit successfully without configuring the application. In isolated mode, RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX=false (also 0, no, skip) or a truthy AZURE_SKIP_NETWORK_ISOLATION_WARNING without a truthy RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX selects deferral.

Correct: Complete the deferred step from a connected host. A truthy RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX requests connectivity checking; it does not provide connectivity.

Verify: Post-provision logs show completed configuration rather than another deferral before resuming application deployment.

docs.title: NETWORK_ISOLATION is not a boolean
docs.text:
Symptom: A hook rejects the isolation value.

Diagnose: The selected environment contains a value other than literal true or false.

Correct: Restore the value required by the intended network design, for example azd env set NETWORK_ISOLATION true for an isolated environment. Do not flip it to false merely to pass connectivity checks.

Verify: The effective value matches the intended topology and validation passes before any provisioning changes.

docs.title: Provisioning fails in Azure
docs.text:
Symptom: A resource deployment fails after preflight.

Diagnose: Open Resource group > Deployments in the Azure portal and inspect the first failed operation, including its policy, quota, region or resource-name error.

Correct: Resolve that specific cause. Region/name changes can replace stateful resources, so review their impact before retrying the foundation workflow. Never delete an existing resource just because its name is occupied.

Verify: The failed deployment and post-provision configuration both complete. Incremental ARM success is not application acceptance.

docs.title: The orchestrator returns HTTP 422
docs.text:
Symptom: The agent rejects a request with validation details.

Diagnose: The stateless Responses 2.0.0 adapter rejects non-null previous_response_id, empty asks and message arrays not ending with a user message. Top-level conversation is ignored by this adapter, not itself the reason for a rejection. The UI's /invocations?api-version=v1 uses another request shape.

Correct: Use the returned validation detail and the correct calling contract. For stateless Responses, remove state selectors and supply complete, ordered context.

Verify: A valid request succeeds through the intended endpoint. Do not interchange endpoint request bodies.

docs.title: Hosted chat works but history is unavailable
docs.text:
Symptom: A greeting works, but history is unavailable or panel history returns 503.

Diagnose: Hosted runtime is stateless. Without separately activated continuity, context is limited to the active UI session. Application Cosmos DB in hosted-panel stores owner/index and feedback metadata, not transcripts. Agent Service backing resources alone do not enable UI history.

Correct: Review continuity activation, panel gates, owner binding and agent-scoped permissions in Hosted agents. Apply deliberate configuration changes through the full workflow. Do not register the Container App/Dapr history layer for hosted chat or grant broad conversation access to the hosted container.

Verify: Test intended persistence across sessions, same-owner access and cross-user denial. A greeting or a page reload is not sufficient evidence.

docs.title: The application starts but does not answer
docs.text:
Symptom: The application loads but an authenticated task fails.

Diagnose:

  1. Confirm the intended image and revision or routed hosted version using health checks.
  2. Read startup and request logs using correlated diagnostics.
  3. Inspect the effective configuration using the actual component selectors.
  4. Follow the first failing model, retrieval, tool or identity dependency.

Correct: Repair the identified dependency, then use the appropriate runtime-setting lifecycle or redeployment. Do not assume a restart can apply infrastructure or process-only settings.

Verify: Repeat the same authenticated task and test document authorization when retrieval is involved. Keep credentials and content out of diagnostics.

docs.title: Access denied between services
docs.text:
Symptom: A dependency returns HTTP 401/403 or names a denied action.

Diagnose: Identify the caller's actual principal, target, denied action and scope. A project identity, deployment principal and hosted runtime identity are not interchangeable. Also distinguish a service call from delegated-user authorization.

Correct: Compare the deployed grants with capability profiles and the hosted runtime access model. Allow new assignments to propagate before requesting additional access. Use hosted recovery where required; do not assign blanket roles manually.

For application-component configuration failures, the catalog's implicit base profile is a useful checklist:

Role Intended resource scope Purpose App Configuration Data Reader Selected App Configuration store Read runtime settings AcrPull Selected container registry Pull images Key Vault Secrets User Selected Key Vault Resolve secret references

Additional grants depend on declared profiles, selected resources and topology. Hosted bootstrap, continuity and panel permissions are reconciled separately; this table is not a script for assigning identical grants to every principal.

Verify: The same intended identity can perform the required operation while unauthorized users/documents remain denied.

docs.title: Check application health
docs.text:
For Container Apps, list the latest and latest-ready revisions:

az containerapp list -g "<resource-group>" --query "[].{name:name,state:properties.runningStatus,latest:properties.latestRevisionName,ready:properties.latestReadyRevisionName}" -o table
az containerapp revision list -g "<resource-group>" -n "<container-app-name>" --query "[].{name:name,active:properties.active,health:properties.healthState,image:properties.template.containers[].image}" -o json

Compare the intended image/revision with the ready revision and traffic routing. An older placeholder can return HTTP 200 while the intended application fails. Inspect system and startup logs for that exact revision.

For a Foundry hosted orchestrator, inspect its routed version, immutable image and Foundry runtime logs separately. Container Apps commands cover the UI, optional ingestion and Container App orchestration, not hosted agent compute.

docs.title: Stream logs from a container app
docs.text:
Select the failing revision explicitly:

az containerapp logs show -g "<resource-group>" -n "<container-app-name>" --revision "<revision-name>" --follow

If the revision has multiple replicas or containers, select the relevant ones using the command's --replica and --container options. Avoid treating output from another healthy revision as evidence about the failed image.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Use Application Insights > Transaction search to correlate a request with its dependencies and traces. Use Log Analytics for container output and platform events. Confirm diagnostic settings and the selected workspace if expected logs are absent.

Recent Container Apps errors:

ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Log_s has_any ("ERROR", "Exception", "Traceback")
| project TimeGenerated, ContainerAppName_s, Log_s
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Revision, scaling and startup events:

ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| project TimeGenerated, ContainerAppName_s, Reason_s, Log_s
| order by TimeGenerated desc

These queries depend on the configured Container Apps log destination and schema; they do not query Foundry hosted runtime logs. No matching rows does not establish application health.

UI records containing exception_type and failure_site intentionally omit dependency error payloads. Correlate the static operation, code location and request reference with dependency telemetry. Do not enable raw token, cookie, claim, signed-URL or document logging to fill that gap. A failed optional panel index write needs repair even when the chat continues; it is not proof the index was persisted.

Telemetry content capture is a separate, default-off privacy choice, not a prerequisite for successful chat or safe diagnosis.
