docs.title: Cost guide
docs.text:
Estimate the deployment you intend to run, not an all-services-enabled template. Begin with the resource inventory and scenario estimates, then build a regional estimate in the Azure Pricing Calculator. Use the sizing guide to identify the capacity assumptions you need to test.

Estimate dates and pricing evidence

The earlier version of this guide contained East US USD estimates dated November 5, 2025, linked to this saved calculator example. That example is not a current default deployment or a quote. The separate resource inventory identifies its own pricing date and assumptions. This guide's October 18, 2026 editorial review did not reprice Azure services. Recalculate for your region, agreement, currency and selected resources before approving spend.

docs.title: Build an estimate in five steps
docs.text:
1. Select the implementation and topology. Record whether you are estimating a foundation alone or the application too. For Agent Landing Zone, use its manifest.json, deployment definition and resolved configuration, not the standalone foundation's example defaults.
  2. Count the actual resources. Include separate Agent Service backing resources where created. Account for existing resources without counting their full shared cost twice.
  3. Separate allocation from usage. Estimate always-running capacity, variable consumption and one-time migration or indexing work separately.
  4. Price the region and tier. Use current calculator rates and your organization's applicable pricing. Record a date and shareable estimate.
  5. Validate after deployment. Compare the estimate with Cost Management, usage and performance. Revisit it after traffic, model, data or topology changes.

docs.title: What to include
docs.text:
The categories below are a costing checklist, not a statement that every resource is deployed by default. Check the selected template and effective parameters.

Category Include when selected or required Main cost drivers Models and Foundry Account/project, selected model deployments and agent/tool services Input/output tokens, model and deployment type, provisioned capacity, separately metered tools Search and ingestion Workload Search, Agent Service Search where created, native ingestion or the optional ingestion application Service count, SKU, replicas/partitions, semantic or agentic retrieval, indexing/enrichment and embedding usage Application hosting Selected Container Apps, Foundry hosted-agent compute, build services and Container Registry Active compute, minimum replicas, allocated workload-profile nodes, registry tier/storage and build-agent pool allocation Data Workload and Agent Service Storage/Cosmos DB as applicable Account count, throughput mode, requests, stored data, redundancy, backup and restore Configuration and secrets App Configuration and Key Vault Tier, requests and secret/key operations Observability Log Analytics, Application Insights and configured tests Ingested data, retention, queries and test execution; avoid double-counting workspace-based ingestion Private networking Private endpoints/DNS, firewall, NAT, peering, Bastion and connected-runner VMs where deployed Allocated hours, processed data, endpoint count, DNS queries, VM disks and data transfer Ingress and optional tools Application Gateway/WAF, API Management, Speech, Grounding with Bing or other selected services Tier and capacity, allocated hours, requests, tokens and data transfer

docs.title: Avoid common counting mistakes
docs.text:
• Agent backing resources are separate. Standard Agent Service setup can create its own Search, Storage and Cosmos DB resources in addition to workload resources. Count what is actually created or reused.
  • Application Cosmos DB depends on topology. Omitting the application's database does not imply that Agent Service has no backing database.
  • Ingestion is a separate choice. Omitting the optional ingestion app does not remove Search, source-processing, embedding or indexing charges.
  • Private networking is not a fixed package. Endpoint count and services depend on isolation, selected resources and existing platform integration. Count firewall, Bastion, NAT, VMs and disks only where present.
  • Optional does not mean free. Add API Management, public ingress and tools only when selected, with their own pricing assumptions.

docs.title: Record your sizing assumptions
docs.text:
Use measured or explicitly estimated inputs rather than a single unexplained monthly total:

Input What to record User and agent traffic Active users, turns per day, concurrency, peak rate and retries/tool calls per task Model usage Input/output tokens per task, context size, model choice and embedding volume Retrieval and ingestion Document count/size, update frequency, query volume and index growth Compute Hosting mode, instance size, minimum/maximum capacity and expected active hours Data protection Retention, backups, replication and recovery requirements Network and monitoring Outbound/cross-region data, private endpoint count, log volume and retention

Search's allocated capacity is only part of its cost: inspect separately billed features and usage. For Cosmos DB, distinguish provisioned or autoscale capacity from serverless request consumption. A stopped VM can still incur disk and network charges.

docs.title: Optimize without changing the security contract
docs.text:
Start with idle or oversized capacity, unnecessary duplicate resources and excessive telemetry. Validate each proposed saving against service limits and workload acceptance tests.

  • Schedule supported development VMs, while preserving the connected-runner access needed for private deployments.
  • Tune Container Apps minimum replicas and workload-profile allocation using measured startup and latency requirements. Consumption hosting is a design choice, not a drop-in instruction to replace the deployed application.
  • Choose Search capacity and replica counts according to index size, throughput and availability requirements, not price alone.
  • Evaluate commitments only after measuring sustained utilization.
  • Set intentional log retention and avoid unnecessary content capture without losing operational or compliance evidence.
  • Reuse shared networking only when ownership, routing and access requirements are satisfied. Do not disable firewall, authentication or private access to meet an arbitrary savings percentage.

Removing a component is not routine cost cleanup. Back up data, review dependencies and explicitly authorize retirement. For Agent Landing Zone, follow the full-stack lifecycle guidance rather than deleting individual resources behind the deployment's state.

docs.title: Monitor actual spend
docs.text:
Use Azure Cost Management to group spend by resource and environment, set budgets/alerts and investigate unexpected usage. Budgets are notifications, not an automatic cap on spending. Review both platform-shared and workload-specific charges with their owners.

Useful pricing references:

  • Azure Pricing Calculator
  • Azure OpenAI pricing
  • Azure AI Search pricing
  • Container Apps pricing
  • Azure Monitor pricing

docs.title: Design Checklist
docs.text: Use this checklist when designing an AI workload landing zone, before approving a deployment, and when reviewing a significant change. For each applicable row, record your decision, owner and verification evidence. These are design recommendations, not a list of features automatically enabled by a template. Check the selected implementation and deployment parameters before assuming a control is present.

docs.title: Compute and cost
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References C-R1 Where will models, agents and application components run? Choose compute for each component's scaling, network and operational needs. Standardize where useful, but do not assume model hosting and application hosting have identical requirements. Compute decision guide CO-R1 What is the workload's monthly cost and usage model? Estimate the selected resources, model tokens, indexing and observability before deployment. Include optional services and separate shared-platform costs. Cost guide, Foundry cost planning CO-R2 Is model traffic predictable enough for provisioned throughput? Compare measured utilization and commitment costs with pay-as-you-go. If using spillover, explicitly design gateway routing and test quota exhaustion. Provisioned capacity is not automatically cheaper. Provisioned throughput, Multi-backend gateway CO-R3 Which model deployment type meets residency, latency and cost requirements? Compare regional, data-zone and global options for the chosen model. Verify processing-location requirements before choosing a lower advertised token price. Deployment types CO-R4 Which nonproduction resources can stop outside working hours? Schedule shutdown only for supported resources that can tolerate downtime. Check disks, networking and other charges that continue while compute is stopped. VM auto-shutdown

docs.title: Data
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References D-R1 Where are agent state, uploaded files and application data stored? Identify the selected Agent Service setup and its backing resources. Record retention, access, backup and deletion requirements separately for each data store. Standard agent setup D-R2 Which resources may be shared across projects? Review supported resource-sharing constraints and choose explicit isolation boundaries. Separate application storage from Agent Service backing storage where required. Capability hosts and backing resources D-R3 Does the workload need data from Microsoft Fabric? Evaluate the Fabric data agent's supported access model, permissions and regional availability before selecting it as an agent tool. Fabric data agent tool

docs.title: Governance
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References G-R1 Which policies apply to the deployed services? Assign relevant built-in or custom policies at the appropriate scope. Review audit results and exemptions before enforcing deny effects. AI services policies, Search policies G-R2 Which regulatory and organizational obligations apply? Map risks and applicable controls to evidence. A policy initiative or checklist does not establish compliance by itself. NIST AI RMF, Regulatory compliance initiatives G-R3 How will responsible AI risks be evaluated? Define evaluation datasets, human review, acceptance thresholds and escalation for the actual agent tasks. Do not assume a machine-learning dashboard supports every generative AI workflow. Generative AI evaluation G-R4 What content safety controls are needed? Select supported filters and Content Safety APIs for the model and modalities in use. Test prompts, outputs and failure handling. Content filtering does not replace authorization. Content Safety overview G-R5 Which models may teams deploy? Review the applicable model-deployment policies. Start in audit mode, assess impact, then enforce approved restrictions and remediate existing noncompliant deployments separately. Model deployment policies

docs.title: Identity and access
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References I-R1 How do services authenticate to one another? Prefer managed identity where supported, with narrowly scoped roles for each runtime principal. Keep deployment, project and runtime identities distinct. Managed identities I-R2 How is privileged human access controlled? Require MFA and use just-in-time privileged access where available. Use a private administrative path when resources are isolated. MFA, Privileged Identity Management I-R3 Can clients use Microsoft Entra ID rather than static keys? Use identity-based authentication where supported. Where a key is necessary, store it securely, limit distribution and define rotation and recovery. AI services authentication I-R4 Which sign-in conditions should be enforced? Evaluate risk, device and location policies for human access. Test workload identities separately; interactive Conditional Access is not a replacement for service authorization. Conditional Access I-R5 What can each user and service read or modify? Grant minimal control-plane and data-plane permissions at the smallest supported scope. Verify document allow/deny behavior, not just successful authentication. Foundry RBAC I-R6 Can local key authentication be disabled? Confirm every dependent client supports Entra ID, then disable local authentication where supported. Plan a tested migration rather than breaking existing clients. Azure OpenAI managed identity authentication

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References M-R1 What signals establish workload health? Define service-level objectives for availability, latency, task outcomes and data freshness. Monitor models, resources and data against those objectives. AI workload management M-R2 Which failures require an alert? Enable applicable baseline alerts and route them to an owner. Tune thresholds and test delivery rather than enabling alerts without a response plan. Azure Monitor Baseline Alerts M-R3 Can one failed request be traced across dependencies? Correlate application, model and retrieval calls. Protect prompts, documents and user data; content capture must be a deliberate privacy decision. Foundry tracing M-R4 Which resource logs must be retained? Configure supported diagnostic categories and retention for key services. Confirm that logs reach the intended destination and restrict access to them. Diagnostic settings M-R5 How will quality changes be detected? Re-evaluate representative tasks after model, prompt, tool and data changes. Investigate regressions before deciding whether to change data, prompts or models. Evaluation metrics M-R6 Can private connectivity failures be diagnosed? Test DNS, routes, TLS and service authorization separately from the affected network. Use network diagnostics supported by the resource. Network Watcher

docs.title: Reliability and resource organization
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References R-R1 What are the recovery time and recovery point objectives? Plan backup, restore and regional recovery for each stateful dependency. Test recovery and application routing. A second region alone does not guarantee continuity. Azure OpenAI continuity, Storage disaster recovery, Cosmos DB backup RO-R1 Are the required services and models available in the selected regions? Check current service, model, deployment-type and feature availability. Do not rely on a fixed region list copied into a design document. Products by region, Model availability RO-R2 Is there enough quota for every resource to be created? Count all selected service instances, including separate Agent Service backing resources. Validate regional model capacity and request increases before deployment. Azure limits and quotas RO-R3 How will growth affect subscription and regional limits? Record capacity headroom, ownership and the process for requesting quota. A passing preflight is not a guarantee of service capacity at deployment time. Quota overview RO-R4 What are the account, project and billing boundaries? Align Foundry accounts and projects with access, network and operational boundaries. Verify supported isolation instead of assuming a project is a complete security boundary. Foundry architecture

docs.title: Security
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References S-R1 Which deployed AI risks can be monitored? Evaluate Defender for Cloud's supported AI posture and threat-protection features, coverage, prerequisites and cost for this workload. AI security posture S-R2 Which service security controls are required? Map applicable Azure security baselines and Well-Architected guidance to the services actually deployed. Security baselines, Service guides S-R3 How is sensitive data discovered and protected? Assess data classification, oversharing and insider-risk requirements. Evaluate Purview coverage and licensing without assuming it enforces retrieval permissions. Purview Insider Risk Management S-R4 Which AI-specific attack paths need testing? Threat-model tools, model calls, retrieved content and data access. Use established AI risk frameworks to define tests and mitigations. MITRE ATLAS, OWASP generative AI risks S-R5 How will prompt injection be handled? Evaluate Prompt Shields for supported inputs and test failures. Keep tool permissions and document authorization enforced independently of model output. Prompt Shields

docs.title: Networking
docs.text: ID Design consideration Recommended decision or check References N-R1 Does public ingress need DDoS protection? Assess coverage for the actual public IP resources. Reuse platform protection where appropriate; VNet DDoS protection does not cover every PaaS endpoint. DDoS Protection overview N-R2 How will operators reach private resources? Use an approved VPN, connected runner or jumpbox. Reuse central Bastion and administrative access when available rather than adding unnecessary public VM access. Azure Bastion N-R3 Which services require private endpoints? Design private ingress and service-managed outbound links separately. Verify DNS and disable public access only after the intended path works. Foundry account/project networking is not interchangeable with hub-based managed networking. Foundry private networking N-R4 Where should NSGs enforce traffic policy? Apply supported NSG rules to subnets or network interfaces, not to a VNet itself. Preserve service-specific subnet and platform connectivity requirements. Network security groups N-R5 Is a regional or global web application firewall needed? Select Application Gateway or Front Door according to ingress requirements. Verify routing, authentication and backend access as well as WAF rules. Azure WAF N-R6 Does the workload need an AI gateway? Evaluate API Management for routing, token controls and authentication. Confirm tier support and configure policies explicitly. Avoid logging raw prompts or responses by default. AI gateway capabilities N-R7 Which outbound traffic must traverse a firewall? Reuse a platform firewall where appropriate. Verify routes, supported service paths and required destinations before enforcing egress restrictions. Azure Firewall N-R8 How will private service names resolve from every client network? Plan zone links, conditional forwarding and connected-network resolution. Private DNS provides name resolution, not traffic routing or authorization. Private endpoint DNS integration N-R9 What outbound destinations are allowed? Restrict egress to verified service and build dependencies where supported. Review exceptions and test recovery without opening unrestricted internet access as a troubleshooting shortcut. AI services data-loss prevention

docs.title: How do Azure Landing Zones and AI Landing Zones relate?
docs.text:
Azure Landing Zones distinguish between a platform landing zone, which provides shared services and governance, and workload landing zones, which contain the resources for individual workloads.

An AI Landing Zone is a workload landing zone designed for AI services and applications. It can integrate with an existing platform landing zone or provide a standalone foundation when shared platform services are not available.

docs.title: Should I integrate with a platform landing zone or deploy standalone?
docs.text:
Use platform integration when your organization already provides shared connectivity, DNS, firewall and administrative access. This keeps those services centrally managed while AI-specific resources remain in the workload landing zone.

A standalone deployment is useful when no shared platform exists or the workload needs a separately managed foundation. Its team must then operate the required networking and governance services. Standalone does not, by itself, guarantee network isolation or remove the need for security controls.

See the Azure Landing Zones guidance and design checklist before choosing a deployment model.

docs.title: Building Accelerators on the AI Landing Zone (Submodule Pattern)
docs.text:
This page explains how an accelerator repository can reuse the AI Landing Zone Bicep implementation without copying or forking it.

This is an implementation pattern for other accelerators, not an Agent Landing Zone deployment procedure. Agent Landing Zone owns its infra/ source and no longer uses this submodule pattern. To deploy, use Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack. Version numbers below illustrate pin mechanics, not a current-release recommendation.

The pattern is simple: the accelerator owns the application code and its scenario-specific parameter file, while the shared AI Landing Zone Bicep code is brought in as a git submodule under infra/.

In one sentence

Use infra/ as a submodule that points to Azure/bicep-ptn-aiml-landing-zone, then run a preprovision script before azd provision so the submodule is initialized, pinned to the expected tag, and overlaid with the accelerator's own main.parameters.json.

Implementation references:

  • Azure/live-voice-practice
  • Agent template contract — the distinct repository-owned-source model

docs.title: When to use this pattern
docs.text:
Use this approach when you are building a new accelerator that should deploy on top of the AI Landing Zone but should not maintain its own copy of the Bicep modules.

It gives you:

  • Reuse: common infrastructure stays in the AI Landing Zone repository.
  • Scenario defaults: the accelerator can provide its own main.parameters.json.
  • Version control: the accelerator pins the AI Landing Zone to a tested tag, such as v2.0.2.
  • azd init support: the setup works even when an accelerator is downloaded as a ZIP by azd init -t.
  • Custom checks: add accelerator-specific validation before AI Landing Zone checks.

docs.title: The pattern in one picture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Accelerator["Accelerator repository"]
        APP["Application code"]
        AZD["azure.yaml"]
        GM[".gitmodules"]
        PP["scripts/preProvision.sh<br/>scripts/preProvision.ps1"]
        PARAMS["main.parameters.json"]
        MANIFEST["manifest.json<br/>(optional)"]
    end
    subgraph Infra["infra/ submodule"]
        LZ["Azure/bicep-ptn-aiml-landing-zone<br/>(checked out locally)"]
        BICEP["infra/main.bicep<br/>(azd entry point)"]
        LZPARAMS["main.parameters.json<br/>(overwritten before provision)"]
        CHECKS["scripts/Invoke-PreflightChecks.ps1"]
    end
    GM -- "declares URL + tag" --> LZ
    AZD -- "infra.path + module" --> BICEP
    PARAMS --> PP
    MANIFEST --> PP
    PP -- "copies overlay" --> LZPARAMS
    PP -- "runs" --> CHECKS

At provision time, azd uses infra/main.bicep from the submodule, but it does not use the default parameters from the submodule. The accelerator's root-level main.parameters.json is copied into infra/main.parameters.json first.

That copy is intentional. It lets each accelerator keep its scenario defaults close to the application code while still reusing the shared Bicep implementation.

docs.title: Required files
docs.text:
The pattern is made of five small pieces.

1. .gitmodules

Declares the AI Landing Zone repository as a submodule and records the version the accelerator expects.

[submodule "infra"]
    path = infra
    url = https://github.com/Azure/bicep-ptn-aiml-landing-zone.git
    branch = v2.0.2
    ignore = dirty

Important details:

  • path = infra must match infra.path in azure.yaml.
  • branch = v2.0.2 is used as the version pin. In practice this value should be a tag.
  • ignore = dirty avoids noisy git status output because the preprovision script overwrites files inside infra/.

Note

Git submodules are normally pinned by a gitlink commit. The accelerator scripts also read the branch value from .gitmodules and force-checkout that ref inside infra/. This makes .gitmodules the easy-to-read source of truth for the AI Landing Zone version.

2. azure.yaml

Tells azd that the Bicep entry point lives in infra/ and registers the hook that prepares that folder.

name: my-accelerator
metadata:
  template: my-accelerator
infra:
  provider: bicep
  path: infra
  module: main
hooks:
  preprovision:
    posix:
      shell: sh
      run: scripts/preProvision.sh
      interactive: true
    windows:
      shell: pwsh
      run: scripts/preProvision.ps1
      interactive: true

The important line is infra.path: infra. It must point to the submodule folder.

3. scripts/preProvision.sh and scripts/preProvision.ps1

These scripts are the glue. They run before azd evaluates Bicep parameters.

They should:

  1. Initialize the infra/ submodule.
  2. Fall back to a direct clone when azd init -t downloaded the accelerator as a ZIP.
  3. Checkout the AI Landing Zone tag declared in .gitmodules.
  4. Copy the root main.parameters.json into infra/main.parameters.json.
  5. Copy manifest.json into infra/manifest.json when the accelerator has one.
  6. Run any accelerator-specific checks.
  7. Delegate to infra/scripts/Invoke-PreflightChecks.ps1.

For a new accelerator, download the starter scripts instead of copying code from this page.

Linux/macOS hook preProvision.sh Shell starter for azd environments that execute the POSIX hook. Windows/PowerShell hook preProvision.ps1 PowerShell starter with the same submodule, parameter copy, and preflight flow.

They cover the generic flow: prepare infra/, copy accelerator parameters and run foundation preflight. See Azure/live-voice-practice for nested boolean rewriting. Do not copy current Agent platform hooks as submodule starters: their repository-owned-source contract is different.

4. main.parameters.json

This file lives in the accelerator repository root. During preprovision, it replaces the submodule's infra/main.parameters.json.

Use it to set the accelerator defaults:

{
  "$schema": "https://schema.management.azure.com/schemas/2019-04-01/deploymentParameters.json#",
  "contentVersion": "1.0.0.0",
  "parameters": {
    "environmentName": { "value": "${AZURE_ENV_NAME}" },
    "location": { "value": "${AZURE_LOCATION}" },
    "principalId": { "value": "${AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID}" },
    "appConfigLabel": { "value": "my-accelerator" },
    "networkIsolation": { "value": "${NETWORK_ISOLATION=false}" },
    "deployContainerApps": { "value": "true" },
    "deploySearchService": { "value": "true" }
  }
}

This is not a JSON merge

The script copies the file with overwrite semantics. Your root main.parameters.json must be complete for the AI Landing Zone tag you pinned. When you upgrade the tag, compare your file with the new infra/main.parameters.json.

5. manifest.json (optional)

Use this only when you want to record release metadata, such as the accelerator tag and the AI Landing Zone tag it was tested with.

{
  "tag": "v0.1.0",
  "repo": "https://github.com/myorg/my-accelerator.git",
  "ailz_tag": "v2.0.2",
  "components": []
}

docs.title: What happens during azd provision
docs.text:
The preprovision hook prepares infra/ before azd compiles and deploys Bicep.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer or CI
    participant AZD as azd
    participant Hook as preprovision hook
    participant Git as git
    participant FS as files
    participant Azure as Azure
    Dev->>AZD: azd provision
    AZD->>Hook: run preprovision
    Hook->>Git: initialize infra submodule
    alt normal git clone
        Git-->>FS: infra/ is populated
    else azd init ZIP download
        Hook->>Git: clone AI Landing Zone into infra/
    end
    Hook->>Git: ensure infra/ is on the tag from .gitmodules
    Hook->>FS: copy main.parameters.json into infra/
    Hook->>FS: copy manifest.json into infra/ if present
    Hook->>FS: run preflight checks
    Hook-->>AZD: infra/ is ready
    AZD->>Azure: deploy infra/main.bicep

Two implementation details are worth understanding:

ZIP fallback: azd init -t <repo> can download a ZIP instead of doing a full git clone. ZIP files do not preserve submodule metadata, so infra/ may be empty. The script detects this and clones the AI Landing Zone directly using the URL and tag from .gitmodules.

Version re-pin: this runs after both paths. In a normal git clone, the submodule may already be on the expected version, so this step is usually just a confirmation. In the ZIP fallback path, it is required because the script cloned infra/ directly. In both cases, the readable tag in .gitmodules is treated as the version the accelerator expects.

Nested boolean compatibility note

This is about the values an accelerator passes into the AI Landing Zone Bicep module. If the accelerator parameterizes a boolean field that lives inside an AI Landing Zone object parameter, configure that conversion in the accelerator's preProvision hook with nestedBooleanRewrites. The hook runs after main.parameters.json is copied into infra/ and before preflight checks, so the deployment receives a real JSON boolean instead of the string produced by environment-variable substitution.

For example, this accelerator parameterizes the nested enabled field:

{
  "publicIngress": {
    "value": {
      "enabled": "${PUBLIC_INGRESS_ENABLED=false}",
      "frontendHostName": "${PUBLIC_INGRESS_FRONTEND_HOSTNAME=}"
    }
  }
}

In that case, configure the starter preProvision template to normalize only publicIngress.value.enabled.

PowerShell starter:

$nestedBooleanRewrites = @(
    @{
        Parameter = 'publicIngress'
        PropertyPath = @('enabled')
        EnvironmentVariable = 'PUBLIC_INGRESS_ENABLED'
        Default = $false
    }
)

Shell starter:

NESTED_BOOLEAN_REWRITES='[
  {
    "parameter": "publicIngress",
    "propertyPath": ["enabled"],
    "environmentVariable": "PUBLIC_INGRESS_ENABLED",
    "default": false
  }
]'

Leave the configuration empty when the accelerator does not parameterize this kind of nested boolean field.

docs.title: Step-by-step setup
docs.text:
Follow these steps when creating a new accelerator.

1. Add the submodule

git submodule add -b v2.0.2 https://github.com/Azure/bicep-ptn-aiml-landing-zone.git infra

Then edit .gitmodules and add ignore = dirty:

[submodule "infra"]
    path = infra
    url = https://github.com/Azure/bicep-ptn-aiml-landing-zone.git
    branch = v2.0.2
    ignore = dirty

2. Add azure.yaml

Create an azure.yaml with:

  • infra.provider: bicep
  • infra.path: infra
  • infra.module: main
  • hooks.preprovision pointing to both scripts/preProvision.sh and scripts/preProvision.ps1

Use the example in Required files as the starting point.

3. Copy the preprovision scripts

Create both scripts from the starter templates in Required files:

  • scripts/preProvision.sh
  • scripts/preProvision.ps1

Keep the generic submodule, overlay, and AI Landing Zone preflight behavior. Add accelerator-specific checks only where the templates say to add them.

4. Create the root main.parameters.json

Start from the infra/main.parameters.json file from the AI Landing Zone tag you pinned. Copy it to the accelerator repository root and then change only the values needed by your scenario.

Typical changes include:

  • enabling or disabling services;
  • setting appConfigLabel;
  • setting model, search, networking, or container defaults;
  • adding accelerator-specific parameters.

5. Add manifest.json only if useful

If your accelerator needs release traceability, add manifest.json. If not, skip it.

6. Ignore local azd state

Add .azure/ to .gitignore.

.azure

7. Validate the integration

Use the accelerator's reviewed source, complete parameter overlay and a nonproduction environment. Exercise its lifecycle with its own supported runbook; there is no additional generic deployment recipe here.

During provisioning, the script should print messages similar to:

Initializing infrastructure submodule...
Pinning infra submodule to 'v2.0.2'...
Applying project main.parameters.json to infra...
Running landing-zone preflight checks...

docs.title: Upgrade and local workflow
docs.text:
To upgrade the AI Landing Zone version:

  1. Change branch = v2.0.2 in .gitmodules to the new tag.
  2. Checkout the same tag inside infra/.
  3. Reconcile your root main.parameters.json with the new tag's default file.
  4. Update manifest.json if you use it.
  5. Test with azd provision in a non-production environment.

Example:

cd infra
git fetch --tags
git checkout v2.1.0
cd ..
git add infra .gitmodules main.parameters.json manifest.json
git commit -m "Bump AI Landing Zone to v2.1.0"

For local development:

  • Clone with git clone --recurse-submodules <repo-url>.
  • If infra/ is empty, run git submodule update --init --recursive.
  • To see the current AI Landing Zone version, run git -C infra describe --tags.
  • Do not edit infra/main.parameters.json directly. Edit the root main.parameters.json; the hook will copy it into infra/.

docs.title: Code agent checklist
docs.text:
Use this checklist when automating the pattern in a new accelerator.

Required changes:

  1. Add the infra submodule pointing to https://github.com/Azure/bicep-ptn-aiml-landing-zone.git.
  2. Ensure .gitmodules has path = infra, branch = <tag>, and preferably ignore = dirty.
  3. Ensure azure.yaml has infra.path: infra, infra.module: main, and a preprovision hook for POSIX and Windows.
  4. Copy scripts/preProvision.sh and scripts/preProvision.ps1 from a reference accelerator.
  5. Keep the generic script behavior: initialize submodule, handle ZIP fallback, checkout the pinned tag, copy parameters, copy manifest if present, and run AI Landing Zone preflight checks.
  6. Create a complete root main.parameters.json for the pinned AI Landing Zone tag.
  7. Add manifest.json only if the accelerator needs release metadata.
  8. Add .azure/ to .gitignore.

Validation checks:

test -f infra/main.bicep
grep -q 'bicep-ptn-aiml-landing-zone' .gitmodules
grep -q 'path: infra' azure.yaml
grep -q 'preprovision:' azure.yaml
jq . main.parameters.json > /dev/null

Invariants to preserve:

  • azure.yaml and .gitmodules must both point to infra.
  • The .gitmodules branch value should be a released AI Landing Zone tag.
  • The root main.parameters.json must match the schema expected by the pinned AI Landing Zone tag.
  • Accelerator-specific checks should run before the AI Landing Zone preflight checks.
  • Preserve preflight validation and fail on findings; offline checks do not establish Azure deployment readiness.

docs.text:
Use this optional runbook to automate the AI Landing Zone Bicep foundation with Azure DevOps. It explains the upstream CI/CD assets, service connections and protected Environment checks. For the Agent Landing Zone application and strict DEV → TEST → PROD promotion, use the application CI/CD runbook.

For an interactive Agent Landing Zone deployment, use Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack.

The pipeline assets live in the landing zone repository under pipelines/azuredevops/. This page is the source of truth for setup and usage; the YAML files in that folder are the assets it references.

Foundation, not the full application

These assets belong to Azure/bicep-ptn-aiml-landing-zone and run from that repository's root. They provision the foundation, not the Agent Landing Zone runtime. For application deployment from your platform repository, use the application Azure DevOps runbook. Copying these YAML files into the platform repository without adapting paths and lifecycle steps is not a full-stack pipeline.

docs.title: What the pipelines do
docs.text:
There are two pipelines that work together.

CI pipeline (ci-pipeline.yml) validates the Bicep templates. It runs on pull requests and on pushes to main, filtered to the paths that affect the deployment (*.bicep, *.json, modules/, constants/, and pipelines/azuredevops/). It has a single Validate stage that:

  • installs the Bicep CLI,
  • compiles the template with az bicep build,
  • lints the template with az bicep lint,
  • publishes the repository as a pipeline artifact named bicep-templates.

No Azure sign-in or provisioning happens in CI. It checks template build/lint, not Azure readiness, security or application acceptance, and publishes an artifact for traceability.

CD pipeline (cd-pipeline.yml) deploys the landing zone. It does not trigger automatically (trigger: none and pr: none); you run it on demand and choose which environments to deploy to. Its Build stage downloads and republishes the CI artifact for traceability, but each deployment job uses checkout: self and runs from that source checkout. The existing pipeline does not guarantee deployment of the downloaded artifact. Compare the CI revision with the CD checkout before deployment; use an explicitly artifact-based workflow when that guarantee is required.

flowchart LR
  PR[PR or push to main] --> CI[CI pipeline\nbuild + lint]
  CI --> ART[(bicep-templates\nartifact)]
  ART --> CD[CD pipeline\ntraceability download]
  SRC[CD source checkout] --> Dev
  CD --> Dev[DEV]
  Dev --> Test[TEST]
  Test --> Prod[PROD]

docs.title: Deployment stages and gating
docs.text:
When you queue the CD pipeline, you pick the environments to deploy with three boolean parameters: Deploy to DEV, Deploy to TEST, and Deploy to PROD. All default to off, so a run deploys only what you opt into.

Stage dependencies order Dev after the artifact download, Test after Dev and Prod after Test. However, the existing not(failed()) condition allows skipped earlier environments: this is not strict promotion. Each selected environment deploys with the reusable deploy-bicep.yml template, which runs azd provision against that environment.

flowchart LR
  Build[Download CI artifact] --> Dev[DEV\nno approval]
  Dev --> Test[TEST\napproval gate]
  Test --> Prod[PROD\napproval gate]

Approvals are not defined in YAML. They live on the Azure DevOps Environment resource, so you control them from the portal without editing the pipeline. The recommended setup is no approval on dev and a required approval on test and prod. When an approval is configured, the pipeline pauses before that stage until an approver allows it to continue.

docs.title: Reusable templates
docs.text:
The pipelines are built from small templates under pipelines/azuredevops/templates/:

  • validate-bicep.yml compiles and lints the template and publishes the artifact. Used by CI.
  • deploy-bicep.yml installs azd and the Bicep CLI, resolves the deploying principal, sets the azd environment, and runs azd provision with an optional retry loop. Used by each CD stage.
  • preview-bicep.yml runs azd provision --preview (a what-if) against a target environment. It is provided but not called by the existing CD stages. Adding a preview requires explicitly wiring the template and its inputs.
  • variables.yml holds the shared values you fill in for your environment.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before the first run, set up the following in Azure DevOps.

1. Service connections. Create one Azure Resource Manager service connection per environment you plan to use (Dev, Test, Prod). Each service principal needs Contributor and User Access Administrator on the target subscription, because the landing zone creates resources and assigns roles. You will reference these connection names in variables.yml.

In Project settings > Service connections > New service connection, select Azure Resource Manager, then workload identity federation with an app registration or an existing user-assigned managed identity, as permitted by your organization. Set the intended tenant and subscription and use distinct names such as azure-ailz-dev, azure-ailz-test and azure-ailz-prod. Do not grant access to all pipelines: authorize only the deployment pipeline. Follow Microsoft's federated service connection setup for the available identity creation options.

An administrator assigns deployment permissions to the service principal object ID, not the application/client ID. A client ID identifies the application; an object ID identifies its principal in the target tenant. The deployment template tries to resolve this with az ad sp show; if directory lookup is restricted, provide the administrator-verified object ID as AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID and AZURE_PRINCIPAL_TYPE=ServicePrincipal. Do not add directory permissions or subscription Owner merely to bypass a lookup failure.

Verify assignments on the target subscription in Access control (IAM). Contributor creates resources; User Access Administrator permits role assignments. A hub in another scope needs separately approved network permissions there. These infrastructure roles do not prove access to application data planes. The deploy task signs in through its service connection and sets azd config set auth.useAzCliAuth true so azd uses that Azure CLI session; do not add interactive az login to an unattended job.

2. Environments. Create Azure DevOps Environments named dev, test, and prod. Add an approval check on test and prod so deployments to those environments pause for a human. Leave dev without an approval for fast iteration.

In each environment, open Approvals and checks > Approvals, select the approvers, and disallow self-approval where required by policy. Restrict who can administer these checks. The YAML environment: name must match the protected resource exactly. A stage dependency orders execution; it does not create an approval.

3. Variable group. Create a variable group named ailz-secrets and add a secret variable secretOrRandomPassword. This value is used as the jumpbox VM admin password in Zero Trust deployments. Link the group to the CD pipeline.

Create it under Pipelines > Library > Variable groups, mark the password as secret, and grant the CD pipeline access under Pipeline permissions. Never place the password in YAML, a repository, a published artifact or a command that echoes it. Treat local azd environment state and deployment logs as sensitive.

4. Fill in variables.yml. Edit pipelines/azuredevops/templates/variables.yml and set the values for your environment:

Variable What to set azureServiceConnectionDev Name of the Dev ARM service connection azureServiceConnectionTest Name of the Test ARM service connection azureServiceConnectionProd Name of the Prod ARM service connection location Azure region for the deployment, for example eastus2 environmentName Base azd environment name, default ailz-bicep deploymentMode zeroTrust for network isolation, or basic for public networking agentPool Hosted image name such as ubuntu-latest; see the self-hosted change below deployRetryCount Extra azd provision attempts on transient Azure failures, default 0 templateFile Bicep entry point, default main.bicep

The deploymentMode value maps directly to network isolation. zeroTrust sets NETWORK_ISOLATION true (VNet, private endpoints, Bastion), and basic sets it to false for public networking. This is the same toggle described in How to Deploy.

deploymentMode in this variables file means network isolation (basic or zeroTrust), not the Bicep topology parameter deploymentMode (standalone or ailz-integrated). Configure hub integration separately using the hub-and-spoke runbook.

For a self-hosted pool, replace each applicable pool: { vmImage: $(agentPool) } with pool: { name: '<connected-agent-pool>' }; changing the variable alone is not sufficient. Preinstall the documented tools and provide routes, private DNS and required outbound access. A Microsoft-hosted agent has no automatic access to private endpoints. An ACR Tasks pool builds images; it is not an Azure Pipelines runner and does not supply connectivity to pipeline jobs.

Note

The pipelines deploy with the Azure Developer CLI (azd provision), which handles resource group creation, parameter filtering, and principal ID resolution. You do not need to pre-create the resource group.

docs.title: How to wire it up in Azure DevOps
docs.text:
1. Create the CI pipeline. In your Azure DevOps project, go to Pipelines, New pipeline, point it at this repository, and select pipelines/azuredevops/ci-pipeline.yml. Name it exactly AI Landing Zone - CI. The CD pipeline references the CI pipeline by that name to pull its artifact, so the name must match.

2. Create the CD pipeline. Create a second pipeline from pipelines/azuredevops/cd-pipeline.yml. Link the ailz-secrets variable group to it (Edit, Variables, Variable groups).

3. Run a deployment. Run the CD pipeline manually. Turn on Deploy to DEV to start, and add Deploy to TEST or Deploy to PROD when you are ready to promote. The run downloads the CI-validated artifact, then deploys to each selected environment in order, pausing at any environment that has an approval gate.

Before the first CD run, authorize its CI pipeline resource, service connections, agent pool and variable group when Azure DevOps reports Permission needed. Confirm the selected CI run succeeded and record both the CI and CD source revisions. Successful setup means CI publishes bicep-templates, CD resolves its identity, and each selected Environment records a successful deployment. Then verify the actual resources. For an Agent Landing Zone environment, use the acceptance checks in Deploy infrastructure only.

Tip

For strict promotion, Test must require dependencies.Dev.result to equal Succeeded, and Prod must likewise require a successful Test. The default condition uses not(failed()), which lets you deploy directly to Test or Prod without deploying Dev first. See the complete strict promotion example.

docs.title: Relationship to the pre-flight checks
docs.text:
Every deployment runs the repository pre-flight script, scripts/Invoke-PreflightChecks.ps1, through the azd preprovision hook before the template deployment. The hook is not a guarantee that azd has not initialized a resource group. The pipelines do not call the script directly. They run azd provision, and azd runs the hook.

The script is read-only and never changes Azure state. It catches the common topology mistakes that otherwise surface as deep, late ARM errors, such as conflicting Private DNS settings, mutually exclusive hub-integration parameters, invalid IP allow-list shapes, subnet prefixes that overflow or overlap, subnets too small for the services that use them, and bring-your-own resources that were promised but do not exist. It also checks regional readiness, including provider registration, jumpbox VM SKU availability, and AI model quota.

If a check fails, the pipeline reports the failure before submitting the template deployment (azd may already have initialized its resource group). You can narrow or skip checks with the script switches and environment variables documented in the script header, for example LZ_PREFLIGHT_REGIONAL_SKIP or PREFLIGHT_SKIP. These are diagnostic controls, not fixes for quota, permission, region or network failures. Resolve the cause rather than treating a skipped check as deployment readiness.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The CD pipeline cannot find the CI artifact. Confirm the CI pipeline is named exactly AI Landing Zone - CI and that it has run successfully at least once, so the bicep-templates artifact exists.

Deployment fails with a missing password error. Confirm the ailz-secrets variable group is linked to the CD pipeline and contains a secret variable named secretOrRandomPassword.

Deployment fails resolving the deployment principal. Set the AZURE_PRINCIPAL_ID pipeline variable to the Entra object ID of the deploying identity. The deploy template tries to resolve it automatically from the service connection, but you can set it explicitly if resolution fails.

Role assignment errors during provisioning. Confirm the service principal behind the environment's service connection has both Contributor and User Access Administrator on the target subscription.

docs.title: Deployed Resources & Cost Estimates
docs.text:
This page answers the two questions operators always ask before approving an AI Landing Zone deployment:

  1. What does this template actually deploy? — every resource, broken down by always-on baseline, default-on (toggleable), BYO-capable, and opt-in add-on.
  2. What will it cost? — an order-of-magnitude monthly estimate for three common scenarios, with the variable (token / call / data) drivers called out separately.

Foundation scope

This inventory describes the independent Bicep foundation, not the Agent application footprint. Agent Landing Zone composes its own services, topology and component selection. Foundry backing resources are separate from application stores, and conditional creation/reuse applies across all resource families. Check the selected source's current parameters, deployment preview and Agent choices. Cost scenarios below are dated example configurations, not current defaults or full Agent deployment quotes.

Cost figures are estimates, not a quote

All numbers here are USD/month, East US 2 PAYG retail pricing, as of 2026-05-29, with empty data and a quiet workload (~1 user). Your bill will vary with region, currency, EA/MCA discounts, reserved capacity, autoscale behavior, data volumes, model token consumption, AI Search index size, and Application Gateway capacity units. Always validate with the Azure Pricing Calculator before committing.

docs.title: The "Standard Agent Setup" gotcha — read this first
docs.text:
By default the landing zone deploys AI Foundry with the Standard Agent Setup (deployAiFoundry=true + deployAfProject=true + deployAAfAgentSvc=true). The Agent Service requires its own data plane, so when this combination is on the template provisions a second, dedicated set of supporting resources just for Foundry:

Resource family Default count when Agent Service is enabled Why Azure AI Search 2 — one for Foundry agents, one for the workload Agent Service stores agent state, thread embeddings, and tool indices in its own Search service so workload index churn never affects agents Storage account 2 — one for Foundry artifacts, one for workload blobs Agent files, run outputs, and Foundry connections live in the Foundry-owned account Cosmos DB account 2 — one for Foundry agent threads/state, one for workload documents Foundry-owned account holds thread/run/message documents Key Vault 1 workload vault, plus an optional VM vault deployVmKeyVault=false by default; a VM vault requires explicit selection and applicable resource conditions

How to opt out of the duplicate Foundry data plane

  • Bring your own — set aiSearchResourceId, aiFoundryStorageAccountResourceId, and aiFoundryCosmosDBAccountResourceId to existing resource IDs of a dedicated Foundry-only trio that belongs exclusively to this Foundry instance. Don't share the Agent Service data plane with the workload or with other Foundry instances — only use BYO to reattach a trio already provisioned out-of-band for this same Foundry.
  • Disable the Agent Service — set deployAAfAgentSvc=false (and optionally deployAfProject=false). The Foundry account stays, but the second Search / Storage / Cosmos are not created. Use this when you only need model deployments and don't use Foundry agents.
  • Foundry AI Search defaults to 1 partition × 1 replica (lowered from 3 replicas in v2.0.5; see CHANGELOG) — scale it back up to 3 replicas in-place if you need Azure AI Search's read/write SLA.

docs.title: Estimated monthly cost — by scenario
docs.text:
The three scenarios correspond to the most common shapes operators ask about. Each shows:

  • Fixed monthly cost — what you pay even with zero traffic and empty data (the resource exists and is billed by allocation).
  • Variable driver — what makes the line grow over the fixed floor.

Quick mental model

Most of the fixed cost comes from a small number of allocation-based resources: the two AI Search services, Application Gateway (if any), Azure Firewall (if any), Bastion, ACR Premium, App Configuration, and any pinned D4 workload-profile node. Everything else is essentially zero at idle but scales fast with use.

docs.title: Methodology and caveats
docs.text:
• Pricing snapshot: Azure retail PAYG, East US 2, 2026-05-29.
  • Currency: USD; convert at your contract rate.
  • Discounts not applied: EA, MCA, CSP, reservations, savings plans, Azure Hybrid Benefit, dev/test rates — all of these can materially lower the floor.
  • Empty-data assumption: Storage, Log Analytics, and Cosmos data charges are shown as ~$0 fixed because the resource itself is free at zero bytes; they grow linearly with data.
  • Quiet workload assumption: variable token / call / processing line items are listed without a number because they depend entirely on your traffic — model the load you actually expect in the Pricing Calculator.
  • Foundry Cosmos floor reflects the minimum autoscale band (400 RU/s) commonly used by the AVM Foundry module; the exact number depends on the Foundry CapabilityHost configuration.
  • Container Apps: the D4 workload-profile baseline assumes 1 node remains active because the default orchestrator app pins min_replicas=1 on profile_name: "main". With Consumption-only deployments the baseline drops to $0.
  • Region matters: AI Search, Azure Firewall, and Application Gateway can vary by ±20 % across regions.
  • Page is a snapshot, not a contract: when in doubt, the Azure Pricing Calculator is the source of truth.

docs.title: Hub-and-spoke network reference
docs.text:
A private spoke can reuse an existing hub's controlled egress, operator access, DNS and monitoring rather than recreate them. This page defines the ownership and inputs for that design. It does not deploy a hub or provide a separate landing-zone deployment recipe.

Apply these choices in Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack. For a network without shared hub dependencies, use the standalone reference.

docs.title: Agree ownership and permissions
docs.text:
Owner Contract before deployment Workload team Dedicated spoke scope, nonoverlapping addresses, workload resources, private endpoints and identities Hub/network team Hub VNet, firewall policy, forward/return routes, both peering directions, Bastion/VPN and shared route tables DNS team Zone inventory, zone groups/records, links or resolver forwarding, cross-scope permissions and conflict prevention Monitoring team Shared workspace/component access, retention and any central Azure Monitor Private Link Scope (AMPLS)

Contributor and role-assignment authority on the workload do not automatically authorize hub operations. Peering needs permissions at both VNet scopes, including remote peer/action. Shared-zone operations need zone join access; link creation needs zone/link write and VNet join permissions. Authorize monitoring access separately. Cross-subscription resources require appropriate provider registration and scoped access.

The deployment host needs private DNS resolution and network/data-plane access. An ACR Tasks pool is not a connected deployment host. Bastion is interactive VM access, not a VPN for a workstation.

Test fixtures are not shared-platform deployments

Upstream tests/hub/ and tests/scripts/ simulate a hub. Do not deploy them into an operational connectivity subscription or copy their empty route, disabled Search, skipped bootstrap or skipped preflight settings.

docs.title: Address and subnet contract
docs.text:
Review the complete address plan against hub, spokes, VPN/on-premises and future networks. A VNet prefix alone does not update its default subnets. Store the approved native parameters in the selected source's root parameter file.

For an existing VNet, preserve externally owned subnets, NSGs and delegations. With USE_EXISTING_VNET=true, the template does not create forward peering; the network team owns both directions. Do not update isolated existing subnets with DEPLOY_NSGS=false: retain managed NSGs or set DEPLOY_SUBNETS=false and have the network owner prepare the complete configuration.

docs.title: Hub integration inputs
docs.text:
DEPLOYMENT_MODE=ailz-integrated records intent. The explicit inputs below select resources and behavior; the preset alone does not enable isolation or wire a hub.

Environment input Intended value or role NETWORK_ISOLATION true DEPLOY_AZURE_FIREWALL false when using hub egress DEPLOY_BASTION, DEPLOY_NAT_GATEWAY false when not deploying local counterparts DEPLOY_JUMPBOX Explicit choice; true creates a workload jumpbox EXISTING_BASTION_RESOURCE_ID Exact approved hub Bastion ID HUB_INTEGRATION_HUB_VNET_RESOURCE_ID Exact hub VNet ID HUB_INTEGRATION_CREATE_HUB_PEERING true creates spoke→hub for a new isolated VNet; false leaves it externally managed HUB_INTEGRATION_EGRESS_NEXT_HOP_IP Hub firewall/NVA private IP for the workload default route HUB_INTEGRATION_EXISTING_ROUTE_TABLE_RESOURCE_ID Alternative approved route table; mutually exclusive with next-hop IP EXISTING_LOG_ANALYTICS_WORKSPACE_RESOURCE_ID Approved shared workspace, if reused EXISTING_APPLICATION_INSIGHTS_RESOURCE_ID Optional reused component; also supply its protected EXISTING_APPLICATION_INSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING

With a next-hop IP, the template creates a spoke route table with 0.0.0.0/0 to the hub appliance. A supplied route table is reused, not rewritten. Neither input being set does not enforce hub egress. Confirm region, association permissions and routes before choosing a shared table.

Allow required spoke source CIDRs and destinations before bootstrap, image pulls and data-plane configuration. Review the foundation egress reference and the Agent platform's build-egress requirements. Check return paths, DNS transport, NSGs and forwarded traffic rather than opening unrestricted Internet access. Peering is not transitive.

Reusing a central workspace does not automatically create local AMPLS. Local private monitoring has its own conditions; the central monitoring owner must provide private ingestion/query connectivity when needed. Confirm a reused Application Insights component belongs to the selected workspace. Do not enable mixed workspaces just to suppress validation.

docs.title: Private DNS ownership
docs.text:
Choose one ownership model:

Model Responsibility Locally managed Template creates applicable zones and links Per-zone BYO Exact existing zone IDs suppress local creation and automatic VNet links; owners supply links/resolution Azure Policy-managed POLICY_MANAGED_PRIVATE_DNS=true suppresses template DNS zones/zone groups; clear BYO overrides and agree the Policy-owned records/groups/links

Peering does not propagate DNS zone links. Every client VNet needs a direct link or explicit DNS resolver/forwarding path to a linked network. With custom DNS, a zone link alone does not reconfigure clients. Avoid duplicate authoritative zones that hide records.

Use actual approved zone IDs, not guessed names or synthesized cross-scope IDs. The following suffixes complete EXISTING_PRIVATE_DNS_ZONE_<SUFFIX>_RESOURCE_ID for Azure public cloud:

Suffix Zone COGSVCS privatelink.cognitiveservices.azure.com OPENAI privatelink.openai.azure.com AISERVICES privatelink.services.ai.azure.com SEARCH privatelink.search.windows.net COSMOS privatelink.documents.azure.com BLOB privatelink.blob.core.windows.net KEYVAULT privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net APPCONFIG privatelink.azconfig.io CONTAINERAPPS privatelink.<region>.azurecontainerapps.io — must match the deployment region ACR privatelink.azurecr.io AZUREMONITOR privatelink.monitor.azure.com OMSOPSINSIGHTS privatelink.oms.opinsights.azure.com ODSOPSINSIGHTS privatelink.ods.opinsights.azure.com AZUREAUTOMATION privatelink.agentsvc.azure.automation.net APPINSIGHTS privatelink.applicationinsights.io

Monitoring overrides apply only when the corresponding local private-monitoring resources are created; they do not configure a central AMPLS. Provide only applicable zones. See the full parameter reference. Use unique link names where multiple spokes share zones; DNS_ZONE_LINK_SUFFIX only affects links the template itself creates.

docs.title: Peering and bootstrap ordering
docs.text:
A fresh spoke can require the network operator during the first provision. As soon as the VNet exists, complete the authorized reverse peering and DNS links so bootstrap and private configuration can resolve and reach dependencies. Waiting for those stages to finish first can cause a recoverable failure.

The template creates spoke→hub only, for a new isolated VNet when enabled. The hub owner creates the matching hub→spoke peering with forwarded traffic and VNet access. If peering is externally managed or the VNet is BYO, the network owner creates both. Record exact spoke-specific names for retirement.

Gateway transit is a separate design choice. To consume the hub's gateway, the hub side allows gateway transit and the spoke uses remote gateways (HUB_INTEGRATION_PEERING_USE_REMOTE_GATEWAYS=true for template-managed peering). Do not set the spoke's ALLOW_GATEWAY_TRANSIT to consume a hub gateway; that is the opposite direction.

docs.title: Verify the network contract
docs.text:
Use exact selected names and IDs:

az network vnet peering list -g <hub-resource-group> --vnet-name <hub-vnet> \
  --subscription <hub-subscription-id> -o table
az network vnet peering list -g <spoke-resource-group> --vnet-name <spoke-vnet> \
  --subscription <spoke-subscription-id> -o table
az network private-dns link vnet list -g <dns-resource-group> \
  --zone-name <private-zone-name> --subscription <dns-subscription-id> -o table

Expect both peerings Connected with the approved forwarded-traffic/gateway settings, and required DNS links Completed. Inspect effective routes on a running workload/jumpbox NIC and route-table associations on managed subnets:

az network nic show-effective-route-table --ids <running-jumpbox-nic-id> -o table
az network vnet subnet list -g <spoke-resource-group> --vnet-name <spoke-vnet> \
  --query "[].{name:name,prefix:addressPrefix,routeTable:routeTable.id}" -o table

Expect the intended hub VirtualAppliance default route or approved shared route policy. Confirm the actual deployment host's private DNS/TCP/TLS path with the standalone connectivity checks. Check service authorization and a new test trace in the intended workspace. Connected alone proves none of those data-plane results.

For interactive access, use the hub's Bastion or approved VPN, not a local Bastion that this design disabled. Native RDP requires supported client/SKU and tunneling. An authorized portal password reset is safer than placing credentials in shell history or adding a public VM IP.

docs.title: Recovery and spoke retirement
docs.text:
Symptom Inspect before retry Peering not connected Both IDs, overlap, remote-scope permissions and reverse peering Public/NXDOMAIN answers inside the network Zone IDs, groups/records, links for the actual client VNet and resolver forwarding Bootstrap, pull or package timeout Effective UDR/NSG, reverse peering and firewall denies for the actual source subnet/destination Missing central telemetry Workspace/component permissions and association, AMPLS, DNS and ingestion/query paths Quota, Policy or expired token Failed deployment operations and the specific approved capacity, policy or authentication repair

Retry with the same approved revision, parameters and environment after repair; do not disable Search, open endpoints or skip checks for a green result. Use foundation reconfiguration.

For safe removal, obtain workload/data-retention approval and inventory dependencies first. Retire only recorded reverse peering and DNS links dedicated to this spoke with their owners. Preserve shared zones, hub VNet, Bastion, firewall, route tables, workspace and Application Insights. Confirm other spokes remain healthy.

docs.title: Bicep documentation
docs.text: This page is no longer part of the Bicep documentation flow. Continue with How to Deploy.

docs.title: Bicep foundation overview
docs.text: The AI Landing Zone Bicep implementation provides an Azure foundation for AI workloads. Its source is maintained in Azure/bicep-ptn-aiml-landing-zone. Agent Landing Zone incorporates foundation source under its own infra/ tree and adds application composition, service configuration and deployment hooks.

docs.title: Deployment modes
docs.text:
The network design is distinct from the Agent application's orchestrator topology. deploymentMode records intent; explicit flags and resource IDs determine the actual resources, routing and reuse.

Foundation shape Intent Reference Self-contained standalone; public service endpoints or an explicitly isolated local network Standalone network Existing hub integration ailz-integrated; explicit private networking, hub routing, peering, DNS and shared-service inputs Hub-and-spoke network

The hub test fixture is not a third production topology. Neither preset automatically supplies an operational hub, DNS resolver or connected deployment host.

docs.title: What gets deployed
docs.text:
Enabled parameters select Foundry/model services, workload data services, container runtimes, configuration/secrets, observability, network resources and optional add-ons. Service-specific conditions and existing-resource inputs determine which are created, reused or omitted.

The independent foundation's default Container App is a hello-world placeholder. It is not the Agent application. Foundry Agent Service backing resources are also distinct from workload data stores. Review the resource inventory and cost scenarios for foundation scope and the parameter reference for supported inputs. Do not infer the Agent application footprint from the upstream defaults.

docs.title: Access and validation
docs.text:
Managed identities and scoped role assignments provide service-to-service access; Permissions describes the foundation's default assignments. Effective application grants depend on the selected definition, capabilities and topology.

The preprovision hook checks inputs, BYO resource references, network constraints and regional readiness. A passing check is not proof of regional capacity, private DNS resolution, data-plane authorization or application readiness. Resolve findings instead of skipping the checks.

docs.title: Use the canonical runbooks
docs.text:
• Deploy infrastructure only — choose independent Bicep foundation or Agent foundation.
  • Deploy the full stack — deploy the Agent foundation and selected application.

For implementation details, see Bicep deployment considerations, parameterization and Application Gateway ingress.

docs.title: Parameterization
docs.text:
This reference describes the independent Bicep foundation. Its root main.parameters.json supplies native parameter values and ${VARIABLE_NAME} substitutions. Use azd env set only for substitutions actually present in the selected source file; native arrays and objects need reviewed file changes.

Agent Landing Zone composes its own root parameter file and regenerates infra/main.parameters.json. Its definition and topology can override foundation choices. See Agent configuration rather than assuming every foundation deploy toggle is an Agent environment variable. Execute changes through the infrastructure or full-stack runbook.

# Example: set a parameter via azd
azd env set NETWORK_ISOLATION true

Tip

Parameters set via azd env set are stored locally in the azd environment and override the defaults in main.parameters.json at provisioning time. This only works for parameters whose default value uses the ${...} syntax.

docs.title: Solution Storage controls
docs.text:
Available in v2.7.0 - live Azure validation not verified

These inputs are available in Bicep implementation v2.7.0 for Azure/bicep-ptn-aiml-landing-zone#160. Use a compatible implementation revision. Release availability and successful CI are not evidence of a successful live Azure deployment; scanner and client behavior still require environment-specific validation.

These three inputs apply only to the solution Storage account controlled by deployStorageAccount, not auxiliary AI Foundry Storage, VM storage, or other services. The Storage AVM dependency remains br/public:avm/res/storage/storage-account:0.26.2.

Parameter Bicep type Default Description storageAccountNetworkAclsBypass String-literal union 'AzureServices' Value passed to the solution account's networkAcls.bypass. Only the exact strings listed below are accepted. storageAccountResourceAccessRules Array of sealed objects with required resourceId: string and tenantId: string fields [] Complete desired list of resource-instance network rules passed to networkAcls.resourceAccessRules. Additional object properties are not accepted. storageAccountAllowSharedKeyAccess bool true Value passed to allowSharedKeyAccess. Disabling Shared Key authorization is an explicit, compatibility-sensitive opt-in.

The bypass union accepts exactly these eight values, with the spelling, comma-space separators, and ordering shown:

  • 'None'
  • 'AzureServices'
  • 'Logging'
  • 'Metrics'
  • 'AzureServices, Logging'
  • 'AzureServices, Metrics'
  • 'AzureServices, Logging, Metrics'
  • 'Logging, Metrics'

Do not combine None with another value or use a differently ordered or unspaced string.

docs.title: Native parameter values and defaults
docs.text:
These inputs use native JSON values in main.parameters.json: a string, an array of objects, and a boolean. They do not introduce environment-variable substitutions, environment-variable names, or JSON-string aliases. In particular, do not quote booleans or serialize the rules array into a string.

Top-level null selects defaults

Bicep 0.42.1 treats an explicit top-level null for these defaulted parameters as omission/default selection: AzureServices, [], and true, respectively. This is compiler behavior, not a new runtime fallback or a change to product defaults. For the stricter profile, explicitly set bypass to None and Shared Key access to false, not null; use [] when no resource-instance exceptions are desired.

This top-level behavior does not permit malformed nested rule fields. Each rule still requires non-empty string resourceId and tenantId fields; missing fields, nested null, wrong types, empty strings, and extra properties are invalid. Wrong bypass enum values and other wrong parameter types remain invalid.

Omitting all three inputs from a compatible parameter file uses the defaults. The equivalent explicit defaults are shown below as a fragment of the file's parameters object, not as a complete deployment parameter file:

{
  "storageAccountNetworkAclsBypass": {
    "value": "AzureServices"
  },
  "storageAccountResourceAccessRules": {
    "value": []
  },
  "storageAccountAllowSharedKeyAccess": {
    "value": true
  }
}

Keep customizations in your reviewed, version-controlled parameter-file overlay. With the accelerator submodule pattern, the overlay replaces the parameter file; it is not a JSON merge and must remain complete for the pinned ALZ revision. Do not patch generated infrastructure or change the pinned AVM to apply these settings. See the deployment and migration guidance.

docs.title: Network rules are desired state, not discovered exceptions
docs.text:
storageAccountResourceAccessRules declares the entire desired rules list. A redeployment removes resource-instance rules not included in it, including undesired or manually added exceptions. An empty array, including the omitted-input default, does not preserve rules that exist on the live account. There is no live-state merge or automatic discovery of Defender scanner exceptions.

Each entry must use the exact, approved, existing Azure resource's full ARM resource ID and its tenant ID. Do not use wildcards, tenant/subscription/resource-group-wide scopes, or a synthesized scanner ID. Resource instances must belong to the same Microsoft Entra tenant as the Storage account, although their subscriptions can differ. A sealed object validates the input shape, not the resource's existence, supported type, tenant eligibility, or permissions; those remain Azure-side checks. A resource-instance network rule provides network eligibility, not data permissions. The resource's managed identity still needs the appropriate data-plane authorization, managed separately.

These inputs do not change the existing networkIsolation, public network access (PNA), allowedIpRanges, defaultAction, or private-endpoint behavior. Bypass None alone does not make an account private. Conversely, PNA Disabled does not make trusted-service or resource-instance exceptions irrelevant: previously configured exceptions can remain effective. Review them explicitly using the Storage firewall limitations and network access rules.

An approved existing Defender scanner can be included explicitly in the rules list when needed. These inputs do not enable a Defender plan or create a scanner, its managed identity, or role assignments. Defender's own configuration is a separate prerequisite; see resources deployed by malware scanning.

docs.title: Shared Key compatibility boundary
docs.text:
Before opting into storageAccountAllowSharedKeyAccess=false, inventory and migrate all account-key clients, key-based connection strings, service SAS and account SAS consumers, and Azure Files clients and tools. Validate each required protocol and workflow before rollout. Microsoft Entra authorization and Blob user delegation SAS are distinct from key-signed service/account SAS; disabling Shared Key does not disable the former, but they still require suitable network access and data permissions. See prevent Shared Key authorization.

This is a data-plane authorization control, not a promise of a key-free management-plane deployment. AVM 0.26.2 retains secure outputs that use listKeys; setting this input to false does not remove those outputs or their management-plane requirements.

docs.title: Deploy toggles
docs.text:
Each toggle controls whether a specific service is provisioned. Set to true to deploy or false to skip.

Parameter Default Description deployAiFoundry true AI Foundry account and project deployAiFoundrySubnet true Dedicated subnet for AI Foundry agents deployAppConfig true Azure App Configuration store deployAppInsights true Application Insights instance deployCosmosDb true Azure Cosmos DB account and database deployContainerApps true Container Apps (based on containerAppsList) deployContainerRegistry true Azure Container Registry deployContainerEnv true Container Apps Environment deployNsgs true Network Security Groups deployMcp true MCP (Model Context Protocol) server deployGroundingWithBing false Bing Grounding service deployKeyVault true Azure Key Vault deployVmKeyVault — Separate Key Vault for VM secrets (DEPLOY_VM_KEY_VAULT) deployLogAnalytics true Log Analytics workspace deploySearchService true Azure AI Search service deployStorageAccount true Azure Storage account deployJumpbox null (inherits from preset) Jumpbox VM deployBastion null (inherits from preset) Azure Bastion host deployNatGateway null (inherits from preset) NAT Gateway for outbound traffic deploySoftware true Pre-install development tools on the Jumpbox VM

Jumpbox, Bastion, and NAT Gateway

These components are controlled independently with deployJumpbox, deployBastion, and deployNatGateway, so each topology can choose only the pieces it needs.

docs.title: Resource naming
docs.text:
By default, generated resource names follow the Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) pattern type-workload-environment-region-instance, for example kv-a1b2c3-dev-eus2-001. You do not have to set anything: every CAF token has a safe default, so a plain azd provision produces valid, readable names.

Parameter Env variable Default Description resourceNamingMode RESOURCE_NAMING_MODE caf Naming strategy: caf (default) or legacy (older resourceToken-based names). cafWorkloadName CAF_WORKLOAD_NAME short deterministic hash Workload token. When empty, derived from subscription, environment, and location. Override with a meaningful name such as contosoai. cafEnvironmentName CAF_ENVIRONMENT_NAME azd environment name Environment token, for example dev or prod. cafRegionName CAF_REGION_NAME mapped from AZURE_LOCATION Region token. eastus2 becomes eus2. cafInstance CAF_INSTANCE 001 Instance token. Increment only for a second parallel copy of the same workload in the same environment and region.

Names are length-bounded automatically so they stay within Azure limits (storage 24, Key Vault 24, Container Apps environment 32, and so on). Because the tokens are deterministic, redeploying the same environment produces the same names, so naming stays idempotent.

Override a single token

azd env set CAF_WORKLOAD_NAME contosoai

Upgrading an existing deployment

CAF is now the default. To keep the older resourceToken-based names and avoid renaming existing resources, pin the legacy mode before provisioning: 

azd env set RESOURCE_NAMING_MODE legacy

docs.text:

docs.title: Existing resource IDs (BYO)
docs.text:
All of the parameters below are optional. Leave them empty to let the template create the resource; set any of them to a resource ID to reuse an existing resource instead. Cross-resource-group and cross-subscription IDs are supported throughout.

Use these for hub-and-spoke and workload landing zone designs where a platform team owns shared services. Resource reuse needs explicit scoped permissions and connectivity; a resource ID alone does not supply them.

docs.title: Workload data services
docs.text: Parameter Env variable Description aiSearchResourceId — (native string) Reattach a dedicated Foundry backing Search service; this is not the workload Search reuse input. aiFoundryStorageAccountResourceId — (native string) Reuse dedicated Foundry backing Storage. aiFoundryCosmosDBAccountResourceId — (native string) Reuse dedicated Foundry backing Cosmos DB. keyVaultResourceId — (native string; add to reviewed root file if needed) Existing workload Key Vault ID. Review its deployment and access conditions.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Parameter Env variable Description existingLogAnalyticsWorkspaceResourceId EXISTING_LOG_ANALYTICS_WORKSPACE_RESOURCE_ID Reuse a central Log Analytics workspace. All diagnostic settings, AMPLS linkage, and the App Configuration entries point at this workspace. existingApplicationInsightsResourceId EXISTING_APPLICATION_INSIGHTS_RESOURCE_ID Reuse an existing Application Insights component. Pair with existingApplicationInsightsConnectionString so downstream consumers (Container Apps Environment, App Configuration) receive a working connection string without needing access to the AppInsights resource. existingApplicationInsightsConnectionString EXISTING_APPLICATION_INSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING Connection string for the reused AppInsights component (az monitor app-insights component show -g <rg> -a <name> --query connectionString -o tsv).
