docs.text: Parameter Env variable Description existingVnetResourceId EXISTING_VNET_RESOURCE_ID Existing VNet to deploy the workload subnets into. Used together with useExistingVNet=true. hubIntegrationHubVnetResourceId HUB_INTEGRATION_HUB_VNET_RESOURCE_ID Resource ID of the hub VNet to peer with. When set and hubIntegrationCreateHubPeering=true, the deployment creates the spoke→hub peering automatically (the reverse hub→spoke direction is the operator's responsibility — see tests/scripts/Add-HubSpokePeering.ps1). hubIntegrationExistingRouteTableResourceId HUB_INTEGRATION_EXISTING_ROUTE_TABLE_RESOURCE_ID Existing Route Table to attach to the spoke workload subnets. When set, the deployment skips local RT creation and assumes the RT is already configured with the correct default route.

docs.title: Hub jumpbox / Bastion / NAT
docs.text:
An existing ID influences the matching nullable deploy* default; an explicit deploy flag wins. Review the effective flags together rather than assuming the ID alone suppresses every local resource.

Parameter Env variable Description existingBastionResourceId EXISTING_BASTION_RESOURCE_ID Hub-managed Bastion host that has line-of-sight to the spoke jumpbox via peering. existingNatGatewayResourceId EXISTING_NAT_GATEWAY_RESOURCE_ID Hub-managed NAT Gateway to associate with the spoke subnets for outbound egress. existingJumpboxResourceId EXISTING_JUMPBOX_RESOURCE_ID Reference to a hub-managed jumpbox VM. Informational — surfaced to runbooks and post-provision scripts.

docs.title: Private DNS zones
docs.text:
Each applicable zone can be brought from a central platform subscription. An existing zone ID suppresses its local creation and automatic spoke link. Every client VNet needs a zone link or explicit DNS forwarding path to a linked network; peering alone does not propagate DNS zone links. With policyManagedPrivateDns=true, use the Policy-owned DNS model instead of BYO overrides and agree who creates zone groups, records and links.

docs.title: Hub integration
docs.text:
For deploymentMode=ailz-integrated or hybrid hub-and-spoke designs. See the hub-and-spoke reference for ownership, DNS and peering.

Parameter Default Description hubIntegrationCreateHubPeering true When true and hubIntegrationHubVnetResourceId is set, the deployment creates the spoke→hub peering inline. Set to false to defer peering creation to the platform team. hubIntegrationEgressNextHopIp null Private IP of the hub Azure Firewall / NVA. When set, the spoke UDR for 0.0.0.0/0 points here. Effective only when deployAzureFirewall=false and networkIsolation=true. hubIntegrationPeeringAllowGatewayTransit false allowGatewayTransit flag on the spoke→hub peering. Set to true only when the spoke owns a VPN / ExpressRoute gateway. hubIntegrationPeeringUseRemoteGateways false useRemoteGateways flag on the spoke→hub peering. Set to true to route on-premises traffic through a hub-owned gateway.

The BYO IDs that drive this section (hubIntegrationHubVnetResourceId, hubIntegrationExistingRouteTableResourceId) are listed in the Networking BYO table above.

docs.text: Parameter Default Env variable Description useExistingVNet false USE_EXISTING_VNET Use an existing VNet instead of creating a new one. docs.text:

docs.title: Public Ingress with Application Gateway
docs.text:
Network-isolated deployments keep Container Apps private by default. The Container Apps environment is internal-only and is normally reached from inside the virtual network, for example from the jumpbox.

Use Public Ingress when one Container App needs a controlled public entry point. The Bicep template provisions Azure Application Gateway WAF v2 in front of the private Container Apps environment, without making the environment itself public.

This is a configuration reference, not another landing-zone deployment procedure. Apply its reviewed parameter changes through Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack.

Cost and teardown

Application Gateway WAF v2 and Standard Public IP incur hourly charges while deployed. Turning publicIngress.enabled back to false does not delete resources that were already created by an incremental ARM deployment. Use azd down for full teardown, or manually delete the gateway, Public IP, WAF policy, NSG, and gateway identity.

docs.title: What gets created
docs.text:
When publicIngress.enabled=true, and the deployment also has networkIsolation=true, deployContainerEnv=true, deployContainerApps=true, and at least one app in containerAppsList, the template creates:

Resource Purpose Application Gateway WAF v2 Public HTTPS entry point for one Container App backend. Standard Public IP Public address for the gateway. WAF policy Managed WAF rules, using Prevention mode by default. User-assigned identity Lets Application Gateway read the TLS certificate from Key Vault. NSG for AppGatewaySubnet Keeps the gateway closed until source CIDRs are configured. Diagnostic settings Sends gateway logs and metrics to Log Analytics.

The backend defaults to the first app in containerAppsList. Use publicIngress.backendAppIndex to point to a different app.

docs.title: Operating states
docs.text:
Public Ingress is intentionally a two-step workflow.

State Configuration Behavior Skeleton mode enabled=true, but frontendHostName or sslCertSecretId is empty The gateway resources exist, but Internet traffic is not opened through the NSG. Live mode enabled=true, frontendHostName and sslCertSecretId are set, and allowed source CIDRs are provided HTTPS on 443 is enabled, HTTP redirects to HTTPS, and only configured CIDRs can reach the gateway.

This keeps the post-provision configuration in source control instead of relying on portal edits that can be overwritten later.

docs.title: Gateway skeleton configuration
docs.text:
In main.parameters.json, enable Public Ingress:

"publicIngress": {
  "value": {
    "enabled": true
  }
}

Apply this through the canonical provisioning step, then capture PUBLIC_INGRESS_PUBLIC_IP from its outputs or the resource-group deployment outputs in the Azure portal.

docs.title: Hostname and certificate ownership
docs.text:
Choose the public hostname, for example:

app.contoso.com

From the jumpbox, use the ACME client installed by the bootstrap script:

C:\tools\win-acme\wacs.exe

Use a DNS-01 flow with your DNS provider, then import the certificate into the landing-zone Key Vault. The jumpbox managed identity has the Key Vault certificate permissions needed for this workflow.

After import, copy the versionless Key Vault secret URI for the certificate:

https://<key-vault-name>.vault.azure.net/secrets/<certificate-name>

Use the versionless URI, not a URI that includes a certificate version.

docs.title: Public DNS
docs.text:
In your public DNS provider, create or update an A record:

Record Value app.contoso.com PUBLIC_INGRESS_PUBLIC_IP

Wait for DNS propagation before validating the endpoint.

docs.title: Live configuration
docs.text:
Update main.parameters.json with the hostname, certificate secret URI, and source CIDRs that are allowed to reach the gateway:

"publicIngress": {
  "value": {
    "enabled": true,
    "frontendHostName": "app.contoso.com",
    "sslCertSecretId": "https://<key-vault-name>.vault.azure.net/secrets/<certificate-name>",
    "allowedSourceAddressPrefixes": ["203.0.113.0/24"]
  }
}

Apply the reviewed change through the canonical provisioning step again. The template configures the HTTPS listener, attaches the Key Vault certificate, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, and opens the NSG only for the configured source CIDRs.

docs.title: Validation expectations
docs.text:
From an allowed source:

curl -v https://app.contoso.com/
curl -v http://app.contoso.com/

Expected behavior:

Test Expected result https://app.contoso.com/ Returns the Container App response. http://app.contoso.com/ Redirects to HTTPS. Source outside allowedSourceAddressPrefixes Cannot reach the gateway on 443.

docs.text:

  enabled: bool
  backendAppIndex: int?
  frontendHostName: string?
  sslCertSecretId: string?
  allowedSourceAddressPrefixes: string[]?
  wafMode: ('Prevention' | 'Detection')?
  wafCustomRules: object[]?

  sslPolicy: object?
}

Required for live mode. sslCertSecretId Empty Versionless Key Vault secret URI for the TLS certificate. Required for live mode. allowedSourceAddressPrefixes [] CIDRs allowed to reach HTTPS on 443. Empty keeps the gateway closed. wafMode Prevention WAF mode. wafCustomRules [] Optional custom WAF rules. capacity { minCapacity: 0, maxCapacity: 2 } Application Gateway autoscale capacity. sslPolicy {} Optional Application Gateway SSL policy block.

docs.text: For full teardown use safe environment removal. If the rest of the landing zone must remain, obtain approval to retire only the gateway resources and dependencies: Application Gateway, Public IP, WAF policy, NSG and gateway identity. Confirm none are shared before deletion.

docs.title: Regional Considerations
docs.text: Choosing the right Azure region for an AI Landing Zone deployment is more than provider/location support. Some resources can be listed as supported in a region but still fail at provision time because of transient regional capacity that is not exposed by any reliable pre-create quota API.

docs.title: Why provider/location support is not enough
docs.text: Azure Resource Manager only tells you whether a resource type is registered and available in a region. It does not tell you whether that region has free capacity right now for your subscription tier and SKU. The control plane only attempts allocation when the deployment actually runs, and capacity-related failures surface as errors such as InsufficientResourcesAvailable or ServiceUnavailable minutes into a provision that otherwise looked healthy.

docs.title: Resources with known transient capacity caveats
docs.text:
The following resource types are part of the AI Landing Zone and have been observed to fail at provision time even when the region lists them as supported. Treat these as regions to validate, not regions to trust blindly:

  • Azure AI Search — may return InsufficientResourcesAvailable for the chosen SKU/region combination. There is no pre-create quota API to consult.
  • Azure Cosmos DB — may return high-demand ServiceUnavailable errors during account creation in popular regions.
  • Azure Container Apps Environment — managed environment creation can fail in regions under heavy demand, especially for workload profile environments.

This is not an exhaustive list; AI Foundry and AI Services model deployments are governed instead by regional model quota, which can be checked ahead of time and should be validated separately for each model SKU you plan to deploy.

docs.title: Recommended practice
docs.text:
• Pick a primary region and an alternate region up front. If the primary fails on capacity, you want to fail over quickly rather than redesign.
  • Validate model quota first. Use az cognitiveservices usage list --location <region> for the model SKUs you need. This is the one signal you can trust before provisioning. As of landing zone v2.0.3 the azd preprovision hook does this automatically for every format=OpenAI entry in modelDeploymentList and fails fast (MODEL_QUOTA_INSUFFICIENT) if (limit − currentValue) < sku.capacity for any of them.
  • Separate a fresh capacity test from an existing deployment. If a fresh deployment fails on InsufficientResourcesAvailable or ServiceUnavailable, review failed operations and approved regional alternatives. A different region needs a new environment and dedicated scope; do not move existing data-bearing resources or silently change their locations.
  • Preserve partial deployments until recovery is decided. Inventory created resources and data, then retry the same approved inputs or obtain approval for safe removal. A capacity failure is not permission to delete or purge a resource group.

What the preflight now covers (v2.0.3+)

Starting with v2.0.3 (issue #72), scripts/Invoke-PreflightChecks.ps1 extends its read-only validation with a regional readiness pass that runs from the azd preprovision hook. It checks: subscription drift vs. the azd env, provider/location support per resource type (AI Search, Cosmos DB, Container Apps, AI Foundry/Cognitive Services, Key Vault, Storage, App Configuration, Log Analytics, Application Insights), jumpbox VM SKU availability in the region, and AI model quota. Each check is gated on the corresponding deploy* feature flag.

Warning

Even with v2.0.3+, the preflight surfaces transient regional capacity caveats for AI Search, Cosmos DB, and Container Apps Environment as WARN (non-blocking) findings only, because Azure does not expose that signal before allocation. A passing preflight does not guarantee a successful provision in a capacity-constrained region — the WARN just makes it obvious what to retry in your alternate region if provisioning later fails.

Offline validation cannot establish live regional readiness. Resolve findings in the approved environment; do not skip preflight to recover a provisioning failure.

docs.title: Standalone network reference
docs.text:
A standalone foundation manages its own workload network rather than relying on a shared hub. With isolation enabled it can include local private DNS, private endpoints, firewall, Bastion and a jumpbox. For shared network services, use the hub-and-spoke design.

Execute Deploy infrastructure only for either the independent Bicep foundation or the Agent foundation. Execute Deploy the full stack when the Agent application is required. This page is the network reference for those procedures, not a third deployment path.

docs.title: Ownership and scope
docs.text:
The workload team owns resources, backups and cost in its dedicated group. The network/security owners approve addresses, egress and public exceptions. Confirm regional capacity, resource-provider registration and scoped deployment permissions before provisioning.

The upstream Bicep foundation creates a hello-world Container App, not the Agent application. Agent Landing Zone instead uses its repository-owned infra/ and additional hooks. Do not deploy both sources into one environment. The inventory and cost estimates describe the independent foundation; selected Agent application resources can differ.

docs.title: Address planning
docs.text:
Reserve a VNet range that does not overlap other VNets, VPN/on-premises ranges or future hub connections. The upstream default VNet is 192.168.0.0/21. Changing only that prefix does not change the individual subnet prefixes.

The following is a complete illustrative allocation, not a universally safe range. Replace it as a unit if it conflicts with your approved design.

Native parameter Example allocation vnetAddressPrefixes ["10.200.0.0/21"] agentSubnetPrefix 10.200.0.0/24 acaEnvironmentSubnetPrefix 10.200.4.0/23 peSubnetPrefix 10.200.2.0/26 azureBastionSubnetPrefix 10.200.2.64/26 azureFirewallSubnetPrefix 10.200.2.128/26 gatewaySubnetPrefix 10.200.2.192/26 azureAppGatewaySubnetPrefix 10.200.3.0/27 jumpboxSubnetPrefix 10.200.3.64/27 devopsBuildAgentsSubnetPrefix 10.200.3.96/27

These native values belong in the selected source's reviewed root main.parameters.json; there is no VNET_ADDRESS_PREFIXES mapping. Keep the complete file with the deployment inputs and carry it to a connected host. Environment refresh does not restore file customizations.

Every subnet must fit without overlap. Keep AzureBastionSubnet and AzureFirewallSubnet at least /26. Reserve private-endpoint capacity and growth. The workload-profile Container Apps environment example uses the recommended /23; current preflight enforces /27 minimum and warns below the recommendation. That minimum is not a future-scale guarantee.

docs.title: Private network choices
docs.text:
Input Private standalone intent DEPLOYMENT_MODE standalone; records intent, not a replacement for explicit flags NETWORK_ISOLATION true DEPLOY_AZURE_FIREWALL true for local inspected egress DEPLOY_JUMPBOX, DEPLOY_BASTION, DEPLOY_NAT_GATEWAY Independently selected; the canonical runbook shows the self-contained choice BASTION_SKU_NAME, BASTION_ENABLE_TUNNELING Standard/Premium with tunneling for native RDP DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL Upstream defaults off; the Agent platform selects it for private remote builds

The NAT gateway supports its configured subnet; it is not a firewall or a substitute for reviewing effective routes. Inspect the local firewall route and required destinations in the upstream egress reference. Agent platform build egress also includes its own dependency-specific inputs. An ACR Tasks pool does not make the deployment host VNet-connected.

With empty native allowedIpRanges, private service endpoints are the intended path. A nonempty approved list can enable IP-restricted public access. Storage trusted-service/resource-instance exceptions and Shared Key access remain independent controls; see Storage controls. Optional Application Gateway ingress is a separate, explicitly reviewed public entry point.

docs.title: Existing VNet and DNS ownership
docs.text:
With USE_EXISTING_VNET=true, decide who manages each subnet, NSG, route table and delegation. Do not update existing subnets under isolation with DEPLOY_NSGS=false; retain managed NSGs or use DEPLOY_SUBNETS=false and have the network owner prepare the complete subnet configuration.

Choose local DNS, per-zone BYO IDs or Azure Policy-managed DNS deliberately. Shared zones require links or forwarding for every actual client VNet; peering alone does not propagate zone links. Avoid duplicate authoritative zones. See private DNS parameters and Policy ownership.

The BYO-VNet reserved AzureBastionSubnet is excluded from generic NSG attachment when Bastion is disabled; enabled Bastion uses its dedicated compliant NSG. Do not rename subnets, renumber prefixes or reapply an older workaround automatically on existing deployments. Plan such migrations explicitly.

docs.title: Provisioning boundary
docs.text:
Return to preview and provision after the network inputs are approved. Preflight validates parameters and regional readiness, not successful bootstrap or data-plane access. Inspect the VM Custom Script Extension result if software bootstrap is selected; it is not evidence that all Agent prerequisites are installed.

For a new build subnet created in a BYO VNet, the ACR Tasks pool depends on the conditional subnet deployment. With DEPLOY_SUBNETS=false, subnet readiness is the external network owner's responsibility. A first-attempt cold-start check must start with that subnet absent, record successful operations and the pool's final state, and distinguish retries from the first attempt. Source availability and offline CI do not prove this live result.

docs.title: Verify private connectivity
docs.text:
Inspect the actual endpoint names and approvals in the selected resource group:

az containerapp list -g <resource-group> \
  --query "[].{name:name,fqdn:properties.configuration.ingress.fqdn}" -o table
az network private-endpoint list -g <resource-group> \
  --query "[].{name:name,state:provisioningState,connections:privateLinkServiceConnections[].privateLinkServiceConnectionState.status}" -o json

From the actual connected Windows host, repeat these checks for the app, Search, Storage, App Configuration and registry hostnames:

Resolve-DnsName -Name <service-hostname> -Type A
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName <service-hostname> -Port 443

Expect private answers matching the intended endpoint NICs and successful TCP connections. Test HTTPS with normal certificate validation and the intended authorized identity. A 401/403 can show an endpoint responds, but is not a successful data-access authorization test. Confirm telemetry reaches the intended workspace.

For the independent foundation's placeholder app, an HTTPS 200 from inside the network is a runtime/network smoke test only. Agent acceptance also requires sign-in, agent/tool execution and positive/negative document-access tests. An unconnected workstation must not serve a private app or read private data; public DNS outside the VNet alone does not establish exposure.

Use the portal's Bastion connection or approved VPN for interactive access. Native Bastion RDP requires a supported Windows client, Standard/Premium SKU and tunneling. Use the provisioned VM credential or an authorized portal reset (default username testvmuser); never put passwords in command history or add a public VM IP as a shortcut.

docs.title: Recovery and retirement
docs.text:
Inspect failed deployment operations, system logs and firewall denies. Correct the specific quota, Policy, DNS, route, egress or role failure; preserve the same approved inputs on retry. Do not disable isolation, purge a partially deployed group or move existing resources to another region as generic recovery.

Use foundation reconfiguration and safe removal. If this environment later adopted a hub, preserve shared services and retire only its own attachments with their owners.

docs.title: AI Landing Zone — Portal Deployment Guide
Overview
docs.text:
The Portal-based AI Landing Zone deploys a secure, enterprise-ready AI/ML infrastructure on Azure through a guided wizard experience in the Azure Portal. It uses ARM linked templates backed by Azure Verified Modules (AVM) and deploys resources including Azure AI Foundry, networking, security, monitoring, and application services.

Deploy to Azure:

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• An Azure subscription with Contributor role (or Owner if enabling Microsoft Defender)
  • A resource group in a supported region
  • If using Platform Landing Zone mode: existing Private DNS Zones for the services being deployed
  • Sufficient quota for the selected VM sizes and AI model deployments

docs.text: The deployment wizard consists of 7 tabs, described in detail below.

docs.title: 1. Full Standalone (Greenfield)
docs.text:
Settings: All defaults, Platform LZ = No

Deploys the complete reference architecture with: - Full networking stack (VNet, Firewall, Bastion, NAT Gateway, NSGs) - All AI services (Foundry, Search, Cosmos DB, Storage, Key Vault) - Application platform (Container Apps, ACR, App Config, APIM, App Gateway) - DevOps infrastructure (Build VM, Jump VM) - Full monitoring (Log Analytics, App Insights, Private Link Scope) - All Private DNS Zones and Private Endpoints

Best for: New projects, PoCs, isolated environments, teams without existing platform infrastructure.

docs.title: 2. Platform Landing Zone Integration (Brownfield)
docs.text:
Settings: Platform LZ = Yes, select existing DNS zones

Best for: Enterprise environments with existing hub-spoke networking, central DNS management, and shared security appliances.

docs.text:
Settings: Disable Firewall, APIM, App Gateway, Build VM, Jump VM, Cosmos DB, Bing Grounding

Best for: Development/test environments, quick experimentation, cost-conscious deployments.

Settings: Deploy VNet = No → select existing VNet → map subnets

docs.text:
The deployment automatically completes these post-provisioning steps:

  1. AI Foundry Connections — Search, Storage, and App Insights are wired to the Foundry hub

  3. RBAC Role Assignments — Managed identity granted access to AI services, Cosmos DB, Storage, Key Vault

  6. Private Endpoint DNS — All PaaS services accessible via private DNS names within the VNet

docs.title: Terraform foundation reference
docs.text:
Strategy under review

The Terraform deployment strategy is currently under review.

The Terraform AI Landing Zone module provides infrastructure building blocks and examples. Use its source and input reference for Terraform-managed foundations.

For the Agent Landing Zone application, follow Deploy infrastructure only or Deploy the full stack. Those runbooks describe the Bicep/azd workflow, including application configuration, identity and image preparation. A Terraform apply is not an application deployment.

docs.title: Choose an example
docs.text:
The implementation lives in its own repository, not in a terraform directory of the documentation or Agent Landing Zone repository.

Example Purpose Standalone Foundation without an existing platform landing zone. Default Demonstrates platform integration with an example hub. It creates demonstration hub resources too. Standalone with an existing VNet Starting point for a standalone foundation using an existing virtual network. Default with an existing VNet Starting point for platform integration using an existing virtual network.

Examples require a security and cost review

The examples are test configurations, not production-ready security policies. For example, the standalone example includes test-runner public Key Vault access, some disabled diagnostic settings and purge-on-destroy settings. Review the actual source before applying it. Adapt networking, data protection and monitoring to your requirements rather than copying those settings into production.

docs.title: Prepare the deployment
docs.text:
You need:

  • Terraform matching the selected example's required_version constraint.
  • Azure CLI, an Azure subscription and quota for the services and models you select.
  • Resource creation permissions at the intended deployment scope. If the configuration creates role assignments, the deployment identity also needs the appropriate role-assignment permissions. Contributor alone cannot create role assignments.
  • A runner that can reach the required private data-plane endpoints.
  • An approved state-storage and recovery plan before creating resources.

For interactive use, authenticate and confirm the subscription:

az login
az account set --subscription "<subscription-id>"
az account show --query "{subscription:id, tenant:tenantId}" --output table
$env:ARM_SUBSCRIPTION_ID = "<subscription-id>"

For automation, prefer your runner's supported managed identity or federated identity configuration. Follow the AzureRM provider authentication guidance for the selected method. Do not put client secrets in .tf files, shell history or persistent user environment variables.

Clone the implementation and open the example you reviewed:

git clone https://github.com/Azure/terraform-azurerm-avm-ptn-aiml-landing-zone.git
Set-Location terraform-azurerm-avm-ptn-aiml-landing-zone
Set-Location examples\standalone
terraform version

Inspect main.tf, variables.tf and the example README. Confirm the region, names, models, network access, backing services and all enabled add-ons. Some example settings are literal values in main.tf; setting an unrelated variable will not override them. Use the selected module's input definitions when creating your own root configuration.

docs.title: Protect Terraform state
docs.text:
State and saved plans can contain secrets and sensitive resource details. Do not commit them or share unredacted terraform show output. Keep state encrypted, access-controlled, backed up and separate for each environment.

For team use, configure an approved Azure Storage backend before the first terraform init, using identity-based authentication and state locking. Grant only the required backend data access. If resources already exist, plan state migration explicitly; do not initialize a new empty backend and apply against the same resources.

docs.title: Validate, plan and apply
docs.text:
Run these commands from the selected example or your reviewed root module:

terraform init
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=deployment.tfplan
terraform show deployment.tfplan

Review additions, updates and deletions, including provider registration, role assignments, public access and recurring charges. Commit the reviewed dependency lock file according to your repository policy. Do not use terraform init -upgrade as a generic repair for authentication or network failures.

Apply only the approved plan:

terraform apply deployment.tfplan

Applying a saved plan does not ask for another approval. Protect it and use your normal approval process before this command. If configuration or the environment has changed since planning, create and review a new plan.

docs.title: Verify the foundation
docs.text:
1. Confirm Terraform reports a successful apply.

  2. Inspect resources in the actual resource group named in your configuration or plan, not a fixed example name:

    az resource list --resource-group "<resource-group>" --output table

  3. Verify private DNS, network access and identities from the intended runner and application network. Resource existence does not prove data-plane access.

  4. Check the intended Foundry project and model deployments, diagnostic settings and data-protection controls.
  5. Record the source revision, lock file, reviewed plan and verification results without exposing sensitive values.

docs.title: Diagnose common failures
docs.text: Symptom Diagnosis and corrective action Verify Authentication fails or the subscription is missing Identify whether Terraform uses Azure CLI, managed identity or federation. Confirm the tenant/subscription for that method; an interactive az login does not repair an unrelated CI identity. Re-run terraform plan with the intended identity. AuthorizationFailed while assigning a role Check the denied action and exact scope. Ask an authorized administrator for the minimum required permission, not blanket Owner access. Retry the plan/apply after propagation and inspect the intended assignment. Resource provider is not registered Inspect the provider named in the error. Have an authorized identity register only the required provider and wait for Registered. Query az provider show --namespace "<namespace>" --query registrationState. Quota or model availability blocks creation Compare the selected region, model and SKU with current availability and subscription quota. Request capacity or deliberately revise the design. Review a new plan before applying a region or model change. Key Vault or another private endpoint returns a connection error Check runner DNS, routes, TLS and data-plane permissions separately. Move to an approved connected runner; do not enable public access just to pass the deployment. Test the endpoint from the actual runner and retry the failed operation. A resource with the ID ... already exists Determine who owns the resource and which state manages it. Use a reviewed import or a deliberately different resource identity where appropriate. Do not delete it blindly. Review the resulting plan for unintended replacement or deletion. Module/provider download fails Check the reported registry URL, proxy and egress rules. Preserve the state and lock file while investigating. Re-run terraform init without a speculative provider upgrade.

docs.title: Changes and retirement
docs.text:
Treat configuration changes as reviewed plans. Changing a region or a resource name may replace resources and lose data; it is not an in-place migration procedure.

Before retiring a foundation, confirm ownership, backups, retention obligations and dependent applications. Inspect the example's purge settings and keep the state backend available for recovery.

terraform plan -destroy -out=retirement.tfplan
terraform show retirement.tfplan

Only after the deletion plan is explicitly approved:

terraform apply retirement.tfplan

Do not run deletion to repair a failed apply, and do not remove shared resources or the state backend as incidental cleanup. Follow the module repository's README for implementation-specific requirements.
